articles.title: Mexico’s most powerful cartels adapt as arrests and leadership battles reshape their ranks
articles.description: Mexico’s most powerful cartels adapt as arrests and leadership battles reshape their ranks AP News Capture of drug lord on FBI's most wanted list leads to more violence, arrests in Mexico CBS News Alleged drug lord 'El Chapo Isidro' will be tried in Mexico despite US extradition request Reuters Violence in Mexican state raises travel concerns near Arizona border AZ Family After a kingpin’s arrest, Sinaloa’s drug war
articles.content: MEXICO CITY (AP) — The arrest of another Mexican drug lord over the weekend added to a string of actions against cartels as Mexico intensifies its crackdown on organized crime under mounting pressure from U.S. President Donald Trump and with U.S. intelligence support. The capture of Fausto Isidro Meza Flores, known as “El Chapo Isidro,” was hailed by both governments as a security win that may shift the balance of power within the Sinaloa Cartel. Yet violence persists among rival criminal groups across Mexico, where two powerful organizations — the Sinaloa Cartel and the Jalisco New Generation Cartel — continue to dominate the criminal landscape. Both groups have been designated foreign terrorist organizations by the U.S., but experts say they still retain strong power in Mexico and abroad. Here’s a look at the balance of power between the two groups and how it has shifted under President Claudia Sheinbaum. In late July 2024, two months before Sheinbaum took office, one of the Sinaloa Cartel’s founders, Ismael “El Mayo” Zambada, was arrested in the U.S. following a Hollywood-esque airplane kidnapping orchestrated by “Los Chapitos,” the sons of his former partner, Joaquín “El Chapo” Guzmán. Shortly afterward, the Sinaloa Cartel plunged into a long-term internal war that continues to ravage the northern state of Sinaloa. A year and a half later, the Mexican army killed Nemesio Oseguera Cervantes, “El Mencho,” leader of the Jalisco New Generation Cartel, or CJNG, one of Mexico’s most powerful criminal groups. His death set off a violent response across 20 Mexican states that left more than 70 people dead, but it lasted only a few days. The U.S. celebrated both operations. Zambada is serving a life sentence there, and two of his sons are cooperating with U.S. authorities. Mexico accused Washington of interference in the Zambada case although U.S. officials denied it. With those kingpins out of the picture, both groups began restructuring. Zambada’s arrest caused a split in the Sinaloa Cartel — a confederation of criminal groups — and sparked a bloody battle between two factions, “Los Mayos” and “Los Chapitos”. The fighting sent violence soaring across the state and put Sheinbaum under intense pressure. The government reinforced its military presence several times. About 23% of its troops are now deployed in the state, and security forces have arrested hundreds of people from both factions. But the violence continued as the criminal groups offset the arrests by recruiting increasingly younger people, said Miguel Calderón of the State Public Security Council, a Sinaloa citizens’ group. Pressure from Washington increased after it accused ruling party officials in Sinaloa of ties to drug trafficking and called for their arrests. Sheinbaum refused. Meza Flores, who was arrested over the weekend, played a significant role in this landscape. This undated image released by the U.S. Department of State shows Fausto Isidro Meza-Flores. (U.S. Department of State via AP) This undated image released by the U.S. Department of State shows Fausto Isidro Meza-Flores. (U.S. Department of State via AP) He led his own criminal group heavily involved in drug trafficking that kept a tight grip on northern Sinaloa but also had a presence in southern Mexico. His group first allied with “Los Chapitos” and later with Zambada’s followers, according to authorities. Meza Flores was known for his ability to corrupt local authorities, meaning his arrest could provide clues about politicians’ links to the cartel, said Sinaloa journalist Ismael Bojórquez. Meanwhile, the United States is offering rewards of up to $10 million each for two top Sinaloa Cartel figures, Iván Archivaldo and Jesús Alfredo Guzmán Salazar. These “Chapitos” are described as members of a new generation of drug traffickers experimenting to produce the world’s most potent fentanyl. CJNG, which has a pyramidal command structure, underwent a leadership transition without the internal fighting seen in Sinaloa, allowing the group to benefit from its enemy’s weakness and continue its business despite pressure from authorities, security analyst David Saucedo said. For a time, there were fears that two potential successors would clash. But two months after killing Oseguera Cervantes, Mexico arrested one of them, Audias Flores Silva, leaving the cartel boss’ Mexican-American stepson, Juan Carlos González Valencia, as leader. The U.S. is offering a reward of $25 million for González Valencia. Mexico continued arresting regional leaders, including members of a cell responsible for extensive violence in Michoacán, which Saucedo said indirectly strengthened González Valencia. Among the figures now most wanted by both countries are Julio Alberto Castillo Rodríguez, “El Mencho’s” son-in-law; Hugo Gonzalo Mendoza Gaytán, who was linked to a ranch that exposed the cartel’s horrors; and Ricardo Ruiz Velasco, considered a member of CJNG’s special forces and responsible for propaganda. Soldiers drive past a burned out cargo truck on a highway between Guamuchil and Guasave in Sinaloa state, Mexico, Saturday, Nov. 21, 2026, following overnight violence after Mexican authorities captured cartel boss Fausto Isidro Meza Flores, better known as ‘El Chapo Isidro’, in Guasave. (AP Photo/Martin Urista) Photo taken with a smartphone. Soldiers drive past a burned out cargo truck on a highway between Guamuchil and Guasave in Sinaloa state, Mexico, Saturday, Nov. 21, 2026, following overnight violence after Mexican authorities captured cartel boss Fausto Isidro Meza Flores, better known as ‘El Chapo Isidro’, in Guasave. (AP Photo/Martin Urista) Photo taken with a smartphone. Sheinbaum’s strategy marked a shift from the “hugs, not bullets” approach of her political mentor and predecessor, Andrés Manuel López Obrador, which entailed avoiding direct confrontations with cartels. But Vanda Felbab-Brown, a researcher at the Brookings Institution, said it is still too early to know whether the strategy will succeed. The approach has helped Mexico defuse Trump’s threats of military intervention, while allowing Washington to claim successes and receive nearly 100 criminals for prosecution. But violence has not been brought under control, Felbab-Brown added. Homicides have declined, but disappearances and extortion have not. Authorities also have failed to regain territory seized by the cartels, break their grip on businesses or politicians, or cut off the northward flow of drugs. Still, she welcomed U.S. efforts, in cooperation with Mexico, to begin targeting the middle operational ranks of criminal groups, particularly along the border. Meza Flores’ capture fits that approach, she said. “That’s a far more effective and far more comprehensive strategy than just going after the capos,” she said.

articles.title: Uncle Kracker’s homecoming leads metro area’s holiday music weekend
articles.content: He may live in Nashville now — where country star Morgan Wallen coach-pitches for his youngest son’s baseball team — but home is where Uncle Kracker’s heart is, at least on Thanksgiving weekend. The singer, songwriter and former member of Kid Rock’s Twisted Brown Truck Band (real name Matt Shafer) began the tradition of playing on Thanksgiving night in 2002. He’s since moved it to the holiday weekend and is nothing but happy that he’s still doing it after all these years. “Y’know, what means the most to me is the fact people still keep showing up,” says Kracker, 52, who released the first of his six solo recordings in 2000. He’s had Top 10 hits such as “Follow Me,” “Smile” and a rendition of Dobie Gray’s “Drift Away” and dueted with Kenny Chesney on the country chart-topper “When the Sun Goes Down.” “I’m just baffled that after all these years, we’re still doing it. It means a lot to me that people can still come together and want to hear the songs.” Kracker plans to give them more of those, sooner rather than later. Acknowledging that “I don’t have a big enough body of work here,” he’s been writing in earnest this year and hopes to have a new single out in the spring, with an album to follow. “Nowadays, you can’t just slap an album out there, ’cause it falls on deaf ears,” he explains. “You just start peeling (songs) out one at a time, do the social media gauntlet and all that. I’m still learning about that mess.” He did, however, collaborate on “Broken Hearted People,” a song on Kid Rock’s new album “Halfway 2 Jesus.” “One day, I was out at (Rock’s) house. He had that one started, so we sat down and finished it,” says Kracker, who co-wrote Rock hits such as “Bawitdaba,” “Cowboy,” “Only God Knows Why” and “All Summer Long.” “The process of songwriting is what I love the most,” he adds, “the recording of songs and getting it to where you thought it was supposed to be. When you can nail that, you’re really happy.” Uncle Kracker performs Friday, Nov. 27, at District 142, 142 Maple St., Wyandotte. Doors at 6 p.m. district142live.com. articles.title: Judge declines to issue a long-term ban on taxpayer-funded, pro-Trump ads critics called propaganda
articles.description: Judge declines to issue a long-term ban on taxpayer-funded, pro-Trump ads critics called propaganda AP News Judge sides against Democrats on taxpayer-funded pro-Trump ads The Hill Democrats Lose Bid to Block Taxpayer-Funded Pro-Trump Ads Newsweek Judge declines to issue long-term ban on taxpayer-funded pro-Trump ads CBS News Federal judge makes major ruling on future of $20 million taxpayer funded Trump ads The Indep
articles.content: NEW YORK (AP) — A federal judge on Wednesday sided against Democrats on the federal government’s taxpayer-funded ads that promoted partisan messages and President Donald Trump ahead of the midterm elections, declining to extend a temporary ban. The Democratic National Committee had argued the TV spots were illegal government-sponsored propaganda intended to promote the president’s campaign message just weeks before November’s midterm elections. The ruling by U.S. District Judge Loren AliKhan comes after another judge in a similar case in New York also declined a long-term ban on the ads. AliKhan noted that a previous temporary restraining order against the ads had been issued when the election was less than a week away. “But the November 2026 midterm elections have come and gone,” she wrote, adding that the DNC was now claiming the party could be harmed by the ads in December congressional runoff elections or even because the 2028 presidential cycle has already begun. AliKhan took issue with the DNC’s argument that the “permanent” nature of campaigns justified an injunction against the ads. “Such an argument, taken to its logical conclusion, would allow the DNC to seek preliminary relief in perpetuity because it could always point to the occurrence of some election somewhere in the country,” she wrote. Democrats sued the Trump administration in October after it began airing ads that were paid for at least in part by a $20 million Department of Homeland Security contract. In court papers, the DNC challenged at least 11 government-created ads that either aired on TV or appeared on Trump administration social media feeds. Some of the ads glorified the president with highlight reels of scenic speeches, promoted his tax cuts and emphasized support for law enforcement. One of them repurposed a clip that had been used by Trump’s 2024 presidential campaign, showing him walking down a hallway as his voice can be heard warning of a “final battle” against “globalists” and “warmongers.” A spokesperson for the DNC, Angelo Fernández Hernández, said in a statement that the organization was “disappointed” by the judge’s decision, adding that the DNC “will fight on to put an end to the Trump administration’s attempts to undermine our democracy.” The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment. AliKhan in the earlier temporary restraining order blocked the Trump administration from developing, airing or distributing some of the challenged ads through Nov. 25. In the separate case in New York, the judge blocked a broader collection of the advertisements and required the government to pull three of them from official government websites and social media sites. While she declined to extend her ban against the ads, AliKhan said the DNC was likely to succeed on its claim that the use of public money for the ads violated the law. The White House has defended the ads as public service announcements akin to what past administrations have made to promote various policies. But the recent ads differ from many past public service announcements because they don’t try to help the public benefit from specific government programs, the plaintiffs have argued. Ahead of the ruling, the Justice Department argued in court papers that there was no threat of harm because the government had already ceased using public funds to air the ads and the midterm elections had passed.

articles.title: Trump says he will meet El-Sayed to discuss ‘TrumpCare’
articles.content: WASHINGTON (VINnews) – President Donald Trump said Tuesday he plans to meet with Michigan Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed to discuss a proposal for universal health care that the progressive Democrat has branded “TrumpCare,” suggesting the two could find common ground despite their political differences. In an interview with the New York Post in the Oval Office, Trump praised El-Sayed’s idea of naming a government-funded health care plan after him, calling the branding “very smart” and describing the senator-elect as a “smart guy.” “I know I’ll be meeting with him,” Trump told the Post, without specifying a date. “Maybe there’s some place in the middle that we could go.” El-Sayed, who campaigned on Medicare for All, proposed a gold-colored insurance card bearing Trump’s name, offering to put the president’s branding on a plan guaranteeing health coverage for every American. Trump also expressed optimism about working with Democrats after they take control of Congress in January, saying the two sides could accomplish “great things together,” although he threatened to veto legislation before negotiations begin. El-Sayed has welcomed the prospect of a meeting, saying he is willing to put Trump’s name on the proposal if it helps secure universal coverage. The proposal faces significant Republican opposition because of its potential cost to the federal government. A single-payer system would shift much of the nation’s health care spending to the government, while potentially reducing patients’ out-of-pocket expenses. The exchange marks a notable change in tone between Trump and El-Sayed, who traded sharp personal attacks during the campaign. Trump previously called El-Sayed a “jihadist lunatic,” while El-Sayed accused Trump of running a hateful campaign. The meeting would come as Democrats prepare to control both chambers of Congress, creating an opportunity for negotiations on health care and other major policy issues.

articles.title: Championship days: Romeo eyeing first state title since 2015, while Almont looking to be crowned for first time
articles.content: It’s safe to say that there is that there is some great football being played along the Van Dyke and M-53 corridors these days. Both Romeo and nearby Almont – which are separated by 8.8 miles with Romeo in northern Macomb County and Almont just over the border in southeastern Lapeer County – have both put together remarkable seasons on the gird-iron over the past three-plus months and both will be playing for state championships this weekend at Ford Field in Detroit. Not bad for neighboring, one high school towns. Unbeaten Romeo (13-0) will play at 7 p.m. Saturday against longtime state powerhouse Novi Detroit Catholic Central, which has earned 11 MHSAA state titles dating back to 1979. Romeo has one state title (2015) in its first state title game appearance. Meanwhile, Division 6 Almont is 0-2 all-time in state finals appearances, previously losing in the title game in both 2019 and 2023. The Raiders are also a perfect 13-0 on the campaign and hope to run the tables by claiming the school’s first state title in the sport. Almont faces top-ranked and defending state champion Jackson Lumen Christi, which knocked the Raiders out of the postseason in the state semifinals round last November. NO. 2 NOVI DETROIT CATHOLIC CENTRAL (12-1) VS. NO. 6 ROMEO (13-0), 7 P.M. SATURDAY: Both of these schools hail from two of the top conferences in the state and both have more than earned the right to play for a state title. Romeo is 13-0 for the first time in school history and are one win away from a perfect 14-0 campaign. That will have to come against once-beaten Detroit Catholic Central, one of the premier Class A/Division 1 programs in the state since the MHSAA first began hosting a state tournament back in 1975. “I think the effort that these kids have put in over the last couple of years is a big reason why we’re still in this (tournament,” said veteran Romeo coach Curt Rienas, whose team toppled top-ranked Detroit Cass Tech 30-29 on Nov. 21 in a state semifinals thriller – a game that literally wasn’t decided until the waning moments. “They have won games in a variety of ways. These kids do not give up.” Romeo, the Macomb Area Conference Red Division, had outscored the opposition 526-201 this season, which is around 40.5 points a game offensively and 15.5 points allowed defensively. The Bulldogs – who toppled Detroit Cass Tech 41-27 back in the 2015 Division 1 state finals clash – have defeated nine schools that reached the state tournament, including the four opponents during the postseason run. “I think our schedule is really tough. Not only do we play in the MAC Red, which I agree is one of the best leagues, but we always seem to play a bunch of (Oakland Activities Association) schools each year in the tournament. We are very battle-tested. It seems every time we make a run, we have to beat a team or two from the OAA,” noted Rienas. “It’s never easy.” Romeo is 4-0 against OAA schools (all from the Red or White divisions). The Bulldogs won the MAC Red Division title at 5-0, while the team is also 3-0 against schools from the MAC White Division and 1-0 against schools from the Detroit Public School League. Seniors Troy Smith (RB/DB/WR), Tyler DeCardenas (QB), Landen Fetty (RB/LB), Parker Cohoon (RB/DB), Tayshawn Proctor (DL/FB), Brayden Watson (DE/TE) and Ethan Green (DL) along with juniors Shane Plutschuck (DE) and Antonio LaLama (LB) are amongst several Bulldogs who have began to earn plenty of postseason honors and there are more major contributors on the roster. Detroit Catholic Central, the defending Division 1 state champions, was on every media outlet’s No. 1 spot in the Super 25 lists that came out back in the summer. The uber-talented Shamrocks, led by fourth-year head coach Justin Cessante, has talent galore all over the map and even some Blue Chip-type athletes on the roster. Catholic Central, the Catholic High School League Central Division co-champions at 5-1, only lost one game and that was a Week 9 defeat by Division 2 No.1-ranked Birmingham Brother Rice (31-25) in overtime – a game where the Shamrocks were missing some key players due to injury. But Catholic Central is also 9-0 against postseason teams form Michigan and Ohio, while the Shamrocks are also is 3-0 against schools from the OAA Red Division. DCC has defeated several other quality teams along the way and defeated No. 3-ranked and previously unbeaten East Kentwood in the state semifinals (31-17) last weekend. Mr. Football candidate Gideon Gash (WR/DB) is a threat on both sides of the ball to make things happen for the Shamrocks. Seniors Ryan Jaafar (RB/SS), Duke Banta (QB) and Eric Anderson (OL/DL) are amongst the leaders for Catholic Central, which has roster chalk full of future NCAA Division I and Division II athletes. Without the revolving door of injuries, might have been 13-0 entering this game, as the Shamrocks were always on everyone’s shortlist of title contenders. “Catholic Central – they’re always really good,” said Rienas. “That’s not a secret. We will get to work and get ready for them.” For Watson, who caught a late-game touchdown against Detroit Cass Tech in the state semifinals, the Bulldogs won’t back down from anyone. “We’ve worked so hard to get there and we will give everything we have,” said Watson. “The seniors on this team – we’ve been playing together for a long time, ever since middle school,” continued Watson. “This is what we dreamed about and now we’ll have our chance. Ever since the day after we lost to (Rochester) Adams last year in the regional (finals), we got to work for this season.” NO. 2 ALMONT (13-0) VS. NO. 1 JACKSON LUMEN CHRISTI (11-2), 4 P.M. FRIDAY: Almont tasted defeat only one time last season. That came in the Division 6 state semifinals – an extremely-heartbreaking loss to say the least. The Raiders misfired on a fourth quarter extra point and had a couple of costly penalties down the stretch. Then-unbeaten Almont ended up losing 25-19 to eventual state champion Jackson Lumen Christi – a program that has won an incredible 15 state titles in its history – in a game that lasted three overtime periods before the Titans escaped with the six-point win. Do you think that hasn’t weighted on the minds of each player and coach for the last year? “We’re kind of glad it’s going to be Jackson Lumen Christi,” said Almont coach James Leusby. “The boys really wanted another shot at them. To be the best, you have to beat the best and Lumen Christi is the defending state champs. We’ll get ready for them. “To be honest. These two teams are not the same as last year even though the game with them was only a year ago,” added Leusby. “Both teams graduated some key guys and have new guys playing this season. And that’s okay. We have worked really hard to get this far and now we have our shot.” Almont, which captured its fourth straight Blue Water Area Conference championship this season, has pounded teams in the postseason. Only two schools have even scored over 20 points on the Raiders. Almont has outscored the opposition 455-190 this season, averaging 35.0 points a game on the offensive end while conceding 14.6 points an outing defensively. Several times this season the Raiders pulled their starters during the second half as part of blowouts. Almont’s closest game was against Division 4 schools Macomb Lutheran North (28-27) during BWAC play and Marysville (14-13) in a non-league contest. Seniors Blake Lane (QB/DB), Brody Corneau (RB/DB) and Ayden Battani (LB/RB) and junior Colten Karbel (RB/LB) are amongst several players that have already earned All-BWAC and All-Region honors. Jackson Lumen Christi left the Interstate 8 Athletic Conference four years ago and now competes in the CHSL-AA Division, where the Titans were 4-1 this season and finished second to Division 4 state finalist Dearborn Divine Child. Lumen Christi, under the direction of one of the winningest high school coaches in state history in Herb Brogan (443-98 over 47 seasons). The Titans own a 489-262 scoring edge during a ever-tough schedule. Lumen Christi had averaged 37.6 points an outing while yielding 20.2 points a game on the defensive end. Seniors Wes Learned (WR/DB), Jake Contat (FB/LB), Benny Gatson (QB) and Owen Powers (DL/OL), junior Brennan Brogan (LB/OL) and sophomore Ayden Gatewood (RB) are some of the many standouts for Lumen Christi. “They are so well-coached. They have one of the best coaches in the state,” said Leusby of Brogan. “That team is always very good and I think we are 0-3 against them all-time. We know what is at stake. The (returning p[layers) were heartbroken last season and now we’ll get another shot at it. “We’re 0-2 in state finals games,” continued Leusby. “We’re hoping the third time will be the charm.”

articles.title: Michigan AG’s office reissues holiday consumer safety warnings, joins another federal lawsuit
articles.description: The Michigan Attorney General is warning residents to be on the lookout for scams this holiday season.
articles.content: The Michigan Attorney General's Office is launching a campaign aimed at helping people avoid scams over the holiday season.( Michigan Attorney General on Instagram)The Michigan attorney general is warning residents to be on the lookout for scams this holiday season.A new “scampaign” from the AG's office will focus on reminding Michiganders of different shady practices to watch out for.Attorney General Dana Nessel said that could include spoofed websites that can steal information, or real stores possibly charging some people more based on shopping habits — and she said it's especially important to be careful in Michigan, because the state lacks some important protections for consumers that other states have implemented.“Sometimes it’s these total criminal actors, other times it’ll be more legitimate retailers but they’re finding new and different ways to take advantage of consumers. And there are laws that Michigan does not have that many other states do to better protect consumers,” Nessel said.Some tips involve paying with a credit card so victims can dispute fraudulent charges, and taking time to ensure sellers are legitimate. Resources are available at the department’s website.Nessel said people should still report suspicious activity to get justice and stop others from falling victim, though she mentioned Michigan’s laws not requiring disclosure of data as an example where Michigan fell behind.Some of Nessel’s hopes for the Attorney General’s Office will have to wait until next year, when Attorney General-elect Eli Savit takes office, along with a new governor and Legislature. The next class of lawmakers could decide to crack down on so-called “surveillance pricing,” and data breaches, and give her office more resources.A bright spot for consumer protection, Nessel said, was a court decision earlier this year. The ruling against insulin manufacturer Eli Lilly gives her office more power to investigate alleged wrongdoing like price gouging.“Instead of saying to a consumer, ‘I’m sorry but you are complaining about a product that is regulated by some other agency so there’s nothing we can do about it,’ we’re able to get started and launch those investigations to know that we will one day be able to bring a case,” Nessel said.Despite her leaving office at the end of this year, Nessel said new lawsuits are already being put together.Outside of consumer protection, she joined Michigan in another multi-state lawsuit against the Trump administration this week.The coalition is suing to block a federal rule that would take away family housing assistance from households where at least one resident doesn’t qualify. The rule, from the Department of Housing and Urban Development, would target families where a member may be in the country without permission from immigration authorities.It would affect Section 214 of the Housing and Community Development Act of 1980. Its rules generally try to limit HUD resources to serving citizens and eligible residents.“This proposed rule would bring HUD's Section 214 implementing regulations into greater alignment with the wording and purpose of Section 214,” the agency wrote in explaining the new decision.Nessel accused the Trump administration of trying to overturn long-standing federal policy and keep funding from Michigan residents.“People want to have their top law enforcement official, their top consumer protector and their top protector of civil liberties for their state fighting back against a very criminal and chaotic and corrupt administration,” Nessel said.The Michigan Attorney General’s Office has signed onto several lawsuits, often related to federal funding, since Trump began his second term. The office said it’s protected or recouped more than $3.5 billion for Michigan.Federal agencies have often said the disputed actions to cut funding are to better protect tax dollars and cut wasteful government spending.

articles.title: Almost 2,000 migrants arrive on Spain’s Canary Islands in a single day, breaking a record
articles.description: Almost 2,000 migrants arrive on Spain’s Canary Islands in a single day, breaking a record AP News Migrant arrivals in Spain's Canary Islands break single-day record Reuters Spain: Canary Islands witness 1-day migration record DW.com Record 2,100 migrants land on Canaries in single day The Times Record number of migrants land on Canaries tourist island The Telegraph
articles.content: BARCELONA, Spain (AP) — Spanish authorities said nearly 2,000 migrants arrived on Spain’s Canary Islands on Tuesday, a record high for migrants reaching the archipelago on a single day. The islands located off the coast of West Africa saw a surge in arrivals just before Spain holds a national election later this week, when migration will be a major concern for many voters. Spain’s maritime rescue service said that 1,990 people arrived on 15 different boats as search and rescue vessels accompanied one dinghy after another to the small island of El Hierro. “Sadly, this is a historic day,” the Canary Islands’ regional leader Fernando Clavijo said in an interview with Spanish radio Cadena Ser. There were around 100 minors among Tuesday’s arrivals, including a 4-day-old baby who had been born during the journey, Clavijo said. In this photo provided by Black Forest Collective/Humanitarian Pilots Initiative, migrants crowd a wooden boat as they sail on the Mediterranean sea, Spain, Monday, Nov. 23, 2026. (Sarah Ziegler/Black Forest Collective/Humanitarian Pilots Initiative, via AP) In this photo provided by Black Forest Collective/Humanitarian Pilots Initiative, migrants crowd a wooden boat as they sail on the Mediterranean sea, Spain, Monday, Nov. 23, 2026. (Sarah Ziegler/Black Forest Collective/Humanitarian Pilots Initiative, via AP) The Canary Islands, a tourist hotspot for many Europeans drawn to year-round mild weather, have for years been a key entry point for migrants desperate to reach Europe. The route is also extremely dangerous with thousands dying in the attempted crossing. Although the islands lie about 65 miles (105 kilometers) from the nearest African coast, many migrants take longer routes to evade security forces. The journeys can last days or weeks, with many boats missing their target and drifting into the open Atlantic. Over 26,000 people have reached the Canary Islands this year, with half that total coming in November. The previous single-day record was hit just two weeks before, when 1,400 people arrived at Gran Canaria on Nov. 7. In June, Pope Leo XIV warned people smugglers that they will face God’s wrath for exploiting the desperation of migrants when the pontiff visited the islands. Departures from West Africa are seasonal, and November often sees spikes in numbers as many leave before the ocean becomes rough during winter. The seas have been calm recently, which has contributed to the high number of departures. Most of the boats that arrived on Tuesday were from Senegal and Gambia, Clavijo said. Despite the European Union’s efforts in West Africa to reduce the number of migrants, many believe that leaving is their only option to find work and build a better life. “The sailing conditions were favorable and there was a full moon, so these people looking for a better future ended up on our shores,” Clavijo said. Clavijo said that El Hierro, the westernmost member of the archipelago, with a population of 12,000, could not handle such a large influx of people, many of whom arrived exhausted and in poor condition. He said that overall he was satisfied with the transfer of adult migrants to mainland Spain, but added that he asked for help from other regions to take in unaccompanied minors who need to be taken care of by authorities. Migrants disembark at the port of La Restinga on the Canary Island of El Hierro, Spain, Tuesday, Nov. 24, 2026. (AP Photo) Migrants disembark at the port of La Restinga on the Canary Island of El Hierro, Spain, Tuesday, Nov. 24, 2026. (AP Photo) Spain’s conservative Popular Party is aiming to unseat the ruling Socialist-led central government in Sunday’s elections. To do so, it would likely have to form a government with the far-right Vox party, which is campaigning heavily on expelling migrants and social policies that favor Spaniards over foreigners who have recently arrived. Without mentioning Vox, Clavijo, who belongs to the regional Canary Coalition party, denounced any attempts to demonize the migrants, calling it “a xenophobic discourse of bad people.” The Canary Island leader also slammed the recent deal by Austria, Denmark, Germany, Greece and the Netherlands to send migrants to Rwanda, calling it “ridiculous.” “Europe is on the wrong path,” Clavijo said. Migrants crowd a wooden boat as they arrive at the port of La Restinga on the Canary Island of El Hierro, Spain, Tuesday, Nov. 24, 2026. (AP Photo) Migrants crowd a wooden boat as they arrive at the port of La Restinga on the Canary Island of El Hierro, Spain, Tuesday, Nov. 24, 2026. (AP Photo) ___ Associated Press writer Monika Pronczuk in Dakar, Senegal, contributed to this report. Follow AP’s coverage of migration issues at https://apnews.com/hub/migration

DTE Energy places 350 lineworkers on call ahead of windy Thanksgiving Day weather
articles.content: With strong winds and heavy rain weather in the forecast for Thanksgiving Day, DTE Energy plans to have dozens of lineworkers on call and ready to respond if the power is knocked anywhere in Southeast Michigan. Utility officials say they have a plan ready to be implemented if the lights go out in Macomb, Oakland, and Wayne counties and elsewhere on Thursday, Nov. 25. “We know our customers are counting on reliable power as they gather with family and friends this Thanksgiving,” said Brian Calka, senior vice president, DTE Energy. “That’s why we’re preparing now, with 350 lineworkers on call and ready to respond if the weather turns tomorrow. I’m especially grateful for our team members stepping up this Thanksgiving, just as they do throughout the year to serve our customers and communities.” According to the National Weather Service, scattered showers are expect to begin late Thursday morning, with periods of heavy rain possible between 4 p.m. and midnight. The forecast calls for around 1 inch of rain and wind gusts of 36 mph. The breezy conditions may also impact America’s Thanksgiving Parade in downtown Detroit, but as of Wednesday morning, no cancellations of floats scheduled to be part of the procession were announced. Five giant balloons are scheduled to appear along Woodward Avenue. On Wednesday, New York City Mayor Zohran Mamda announced Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade will be postponed until Saturday, Nov. 28, because of weather conditions in the New York City area and on the East Coast. DTE says its has been closely monitoring the forecast and preparing crews and resources ahead of the holiday. The company will continue monitoring conditions and is prepared to adjust staffing and resources if the forecast changes. articles.title: Mamdani Wins Against Landlords in Rent Freeze Lawsuit
articles.content: Judge upholds rent freeze on roughly 1m rent-stabilized apartments in victory for Democratic socialist mayor A New York City judge has upheld a rent freeze on the roughly 1m rent-stabilized apartments in New York City, delivering a big victory for the city’s Democratic socialist mayor, Zohran Mamdani. In an order published Wednesday, Manhattan supreme court judge Brendan Lantry dismissed a lawsuit brought by a group of landlords seeking to block the policy, which freezes rents on one- and two-year leases for rent-stabilized units beginning on or after 1 October. A spokesperson for Mamdani also did not immediately respond to the Guardian. But, in a statement to the New York Times, Mamdani described the decision as “a victory for tenants, for affordability and for the principle that working New Yorkers deserve a city they can afford to live in”. “Because housing is not a luxury,” Mamdani said. “It is a basic necessity.” The lawsuit was filed after the city’s rent guidelines board approved the measure in June. The landlords argued that the order was a result of a “sham process” and claimed that the board “ignored evidence of soaring landlord costs and manipulated the data to understate the impact of these costs”. In the judge’s order on Wednesday, he wrote that “the court’s review is not whether the Board’s determination was wise or if it may cause negative collateral consequences to the overall real estate market” but rather that it is to review whether the order “has a rational basis, that is, that it is not unreasonable, arbitrary, or capricious”. The judge concluded that the petitioners had “failed to establish” that the passing of the order “was unreasonable, arbitrary, or capricious” and thus, the court found that freeze “has a rational basis and must therefore be upheld as valid”. The ruling marks a win for Mamdani, who campaigned on the pledge “freeze the rent” for rent-stabilized tenants. Much of his campaign focused on making New York City more affordable, as many residents face rising costs for housing, food and more. But the rent freeze for rent-stabilized units, and its approval by the board, drew criticism from landlords and from some in the real estate industry, who argued that freezing those rents, while insurance, taxes, maintenance and other operating costs rise, will place additional financial strain on building owners. In the ruling on Wednesday, the judge criticized the mayor’s campaign pledge to “freeze the rent” calling it “reckless and irresponsible” as he noted that mayors have “no authority to unilaterally raise, ‘freeze’ or otherwise adjust the rent of stabilized units in this City”. That authority rests with the board. But, ultimately, the judge wrote that the group of landlords had “failed to establish” that the passing of the order by the rent guidelines board in June was “unreasonable, arbitrary or capricious” and found that the freeze “has a rational basis and must therefore be upheld as valid”. It is not clear whether the landlords will appeal. One of the lawyers representing the plaintiffs, Randy Mastro, a former first deputy mayor under Eric Adams, said in a statement to the Guardian that he was “disappointed by the court’s ruling” and said that “we are continuing to review the ruling and considering next steps”.

articles.title: New York court upholds Mayor Mamdani's rent freeze
articles.content: NEW YORK: A New York court has upheld Mayor Zohran Mamdani’s rent freeze for nearly one million rent-stabilised apartments, dismissing a lawsuit by landlords who argued that the decision was politically influenced and ignored rising property operating costs. Manhattan Supreme Court Justice Brendan Lantry ruled on Wednesday that the city’s Rent Guidelines Board had acted within its legal authority when it approved zero-per cent rent increases for one- and two-year lease renewals. The decision allows the freeze, which took effect on October 1, to remain in place until September 30, 2027. The ruling represents a major victory for Mamdani, who made freezing rents a central promise of his mayoral election campaign. It also protects more than two million New Yorkers living in rent-stabilised homes from increases during the period covered by the decision. The landlords who brought the lawsuit accused the nine-member Rent Guidelines Board of reaching a predetermined decision to fulfil Mamdani’s campaign pledge. They argued the board had failed to properly account for rising expenses, including insurance, utilities, maintenance and property taxes. The landlords also questioned the board’s independence, pointing to Mamdani’s appointments of members who supported his housing affordability agenda. However, Justice Lantry found that the board had considered the economic evidence and statutory requirements before reaching its decision. He ruled that the landlords had failed to establish the freeze was unreasonable, arbitrary or unlawful. The judge acknowledged the decision could have negative consequences for New York’s residential property industry but said the court could not substitute its judgment for that of the board. He also criticised Mamdani’s campaign pledge, describing an election promise guaranteeing a rent freeze as “reckless and irresponsible”. The judge stressed that the mayor ‘did not have the authority to unilaterally freeze or adjust rents’ in the city’s rent-stabilised apartments. That responsibility rested exclusively with the Rent Guidelines Board. The board approved the freeze in June in a 7-1 vote, marking the first time it had set zero-per cent increases for both one- and two-year lease renewals. Landlords challenged the decision shortly afterwards, arguing the board underestimated operating costs and overstated rental income. The dispute reflects a wider conflict over housing affordability in New York, where millions of residents face high rents, and landlords contend with rising building maintenance and operating expenses. Tenant organisations welcomed the ruling, arguing that the freeze would provide relief to households struggling with the cost of living. READ ALSO: New York Mayor Mamdani Opposes Event Featuring RSS Chief Mohan Bhagwat Landlord representatives, however, warned that the decision could put additional pressure on small property owners, whose operating expenses continue to rise even as regulated rents remain unchanged. The decision leaves Mamdani’s signature housing policy intact while reinforcing an important distinction: the mayor can appoint members to the Rent Guidelines Board and advocate a policy, but the board itself retains the legal authority to determine rent adjustments. The landlords filed suit in July, arguing that the Rent Guidelines Board had bowed to Mamdani’s election promise, manipulated financial data and ignored rising costs, including insurance, maintenance and property taxes. They can now appeal Justice Lantry’s ruling to a higher court, seeking to overturn the freeze. Unless an appeal succeeds, the zero-increase order will remain in force for eligible lease renewals through September 2027. articles.title: ‘Free of everything evil’: Kilmar Abrego Garcia speaks out from Spain, after fleeing US
articles.description: WASHINGTON — Kilmar Abrego Garcia, the wrongly deported immigrant who fought the Trump administration’s efforts to re-deport him to one of several African nations, said Wednesday that he felt joyful to choose to voluntarily depart from the United States to Spain. “I feel happy,” Abrego Garcia said in Spanish, shortly after arriving in Madrid. “I […]
articles.content: Kilmar Abrego Garcia speaks to people who held a prayer vigil and rally on his behalf outside the Immigration and Customs Enforcement building in Baltimore, Maryland, on Aug. 25, 2025. Lydia Walther Rodriguez with CASA interprets for him. (Photo by William J. Ford/Maryland Matters)WASHINGTON — Kilmar Abrego Garcia, the wrongly deported immigrant who fought the Trump administration’s efforts to re-deport him to one of several African nations, said Wednesday that he felt joyful to choose to voluntarily depart from the United States to Spain. “I feel happy,” Abrego Garcia said in Spanish, shortly after arriving in Madrid. “I feel free, free of everything evil that has followed me up until this point.” The federal government agreed to allow Abrego Garcia, a longtime Maryland resident, to voluntarily leave the U.S. for Spain late Tuesday, apparently concluding a 20-month legal saga that cast a national spotlight on the president’s aggressive deportation campaign after Abrego Garcia was erroneously deported to a brutal Salvadoran prison. He appeared during a Wednesday virtual press conference with the immigration advocacy group that has spearheaded his case, We Are CASA. “The government did not decide where my story continues,” Abrego Garcia said. “My family and I decided.” One of his attorneys, Simon Sandoval-Moshenberg, said Abrego Garcia’s time in Spain would be temporary and that he plans to wait for a new administration to take office before making an effort to return to the U.S. His wife and their three children remain in Maryland. He is in Spain on a tourist visa, which lasts for about 90 days, Sandoval-Moshenberg said. He declined to give details about where Abrego Garcia would go next after his tourist visa expires. Sandoval-Moshenberg said because Abrego Garcia is married to a U.S. citizen, there is a legal avenue they could pursue, but in order for Abrego Garcia to be allowed back into the country, he’ll need a certain waiver from the State Department. A U.S. citizen married to a noncitizen can petition for a visa for their spouse, which could eventually lead to a green card, or lawful permanent residence. “It is going to be up to the next administration to reunite this family as quickly as possible and to bring Mr. Abrego Garcia back to Maryland, but this does not require an act of extraordinary executive grace,” Sandoval-Moshenberg said. “There is an existing immigration pathway.” ‘Any country that is willing to accept him’ The federal judge overseeing his case, Paula Xinis, on Wednesday unsealed a court order from Oct. 6, where Abrego Garcia’s attorneys and Department of Justice lawyers agreed to let Abrego Garcia self-deport from the U.S. “to any country that is willing to accept him,” with a date set for Nov. 24. In self-deportation, the government makes life so difficult for people without legal status that they choose to leave. The Trump administration has pressured immigrants to self-deport by offering monetary incentives or threatening to levy hefty fines or detention against those who don’t leave on their own. Because U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement kept Abrego Garcia’s passport after he was released from immigrant detention, he could not leave the country without permission from the federal government. As part of a condition of his release from detention, he was also placed on electronic monitoring. In the October order, Xinis ordered federal immigration agents to remove Abrego Garcia’s ankle monitor before he was set to board his flight to Madrid, and remove any prohibitions that blocked him from leaving the U.S., such as a no-fly list. On Wednesday, in a separate order, Xinis, dissolved all injunctions that barred the Trump administration from removing him to a third country, finding the case moot after Abrego Garcia left the U.S. on Tuesday. In a late Tuesday statement, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said the Trump administration was “delighted to announce that Kilmar Abrego Garcia has self-deported from the United States to Spain.” Maryland Democratic Sen. Chris Van Hollen, who traveled to El Salvador to visit Abrego Garcia and advocate for his return to the U.S., said during Wednesday’s press conference that the Trump administration’s efforts to remove him to several African countries was “a vendetta against Kilmar Abrego Garcia because he stood up for his constitutional rights.” “This is a case where the court system did ultimately work, despite the efforts of the Trump administration to trample over our Constitution, and so this is a good moment,” he said. Van Hollen added that he met with Spain’s ambassador to the U.S., Ángeles Moreno Bau, and informed her of “all the wrongs that have been committed by the Trump administration, the U.S. government, against Kilmar Abrego Garcia.” Speaking tour next In the meantime, Abrego Garcia plans to go on a speaking tour in Spain and elsewhere to tell his story of being mistakenly deported in March 2025 to a brutal prison in El Salvador, despite having legal protections that prevented him from being removed to his home country. He is also expected to relate the legal battles the Trump administration waged against him and the efforts to remove him to several African nations. While he was at the mega-prison in El Salvador, he said in court filings he experienced physical and psychological torture. Federal and appeals courts, including the Supreme Court, found he was illegally removed, and the lower courts ordered the Trump administration to return him. When Abrego Garcia was brought back to the U.S., it was because the Department of Justice charged him with an indictment that stemmed from a traffic stop in Tennessee. A federal judge in Nashville threw out the case, finding that the Department of Justice was being vindictive against Abrego Garcia. The Department of Justice offered Abrego Garcia a deal that if he pleaded guilty to the Tennessee charges of two counts of human smuggling, he would be allowed to be removed to Costa Rica, but he pleaded not guilty. For more than a year, he agreed to be removed to Costa Rica, but the Trump administration has tried to remove him to the African nations instead. Xinis found the Trump administration had not made a good faith effort to remove Abrego Garcia to Costa Rica, which agreed to accept him and give him refugee status. The Trump administration tried to send him to Eswatini, Liberia, Ghana, and Uganda. Abrego Garcia said his decision to leave the U.S. means that “this time I’m leaving with my freedom, not like before when they took me out inhumanely.” Xinis, who oversaw his wrongful deportation case, was also presiding over his second case, where he challenged his immigration detention, known as a habeas corpus claim. She ordered that U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement release Abrego Garcia from detention because the agency was not making an effort to remove him, making his detention unlawful.

articles.title: Federal court blocks second Trump order on birthright citizenship
articles.description: WASHINGTON — A federal judge in the District of Columbia Wednesday issued a classwide injunction to prevent the Trump administration from implementing its second attempt at redefining the constitutional right to birthright citizenship. The order from Judge Christopher Reid Cooper will remain in effect while litigation continues. A classwide injunction blocks action affecting a defined group […]
articles.content: Demonstrators from the immigration advocacy organization CASA chant "Up up with liberation, down down with deportation" outside of the U.S. Supreme Court on Thursday, May 15, 2025, as justices heard oral arguments on the Trump administration's legal challenge to birthright citizenship. (Photo by Ashley Murray/States Newsroom)WASHINGTON — A federal judge in the District of Columbia Wednesday issued a classwide injunction to prevent the Trump administration from implementing its second attempt at redefining the constitutional right to birthright citizenship. The order from Judge Christopher Reid Cooper will remain in effect while litigation continues. A classwide injunction blocks action affecting a defined group of individuals, as opposed to a nationwide injunction. In a memorandum opinion, Cooper noted the Supreme Court earlier this year denied President Donald Trump’s executive order that would deny citizenship to babies born from immigrants either in the country unlawfully or on a temporary basis, in the case Barbara v. Trump. “Yet Barbara’s ink had scarcely dried when the President issued a second executive order—Executive Order 14418, at issue here—directing federal agencies to withhold recognition of citizenship from additional categories of U.S.-born children with noncitizen parents,” he wrote. “As the Supreme Court has made clear, however, the President cannot carve out new exceptions to birthright citizenship for children born within the United States and subject to its laws.” The American Civil Liberties Union, which led the first challenge against the Trump administration’s birthright citizenship order and is leading the second, welcomed the ruling. “Enough is enough,” Cody Wofsy, deputy director of the ACLU’s Immigrants’ Rights Project, said in a statement. “The Supreme Court has twice rejected efforts to gut birthright citizenship, in 1898 and again earlier this year. Third time is not the charm, and the President needs to accept that birthright citizenship is the law of the land.” The Department of Justice did not respond to States Newsroom’s request for comment. Earlier this month, Cooper seemed skeptical of the legality of the Trump administration’s second attempt to redefine the constitutional right to birthright citizenship. The president’s recent executive orders would deny citizenship to babies born in the United States to parents deemed part of a designated terrorist organization and to parents who purposefully came to the United States to gain citizenship in what critics call “birth tourism.” The executive order also aimed to deny citizenship to children born to foreign diplomatic staff and children born in U.S. territories where Congress has not passed a law granting citizenship. There is already a small carve out for birthright citizenship, extended to children born to foreign diplomats.

articles.title: Temporary Protected Status to expire for Lebanese immigrants in the US
articles.description: WASHINGTON — Humanitarian protections for thousands of Lebanese immigrants living in the United States are set to expire by Nov. 27, and the Department of Homeland Security has not indicated if their Temporary Protected Status will be renewed. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin in May renewed TPS for an estimated 11,000 nationals from Lebanon for […]
articles.content: Markwayne Mullin, at the time a Republican senator from Oklahoma, speaks to reporters at the U.S. Capitol on March 3, 2026. Mullin is now the secretary of the Department of Homeland Security. (Photo by Ashley Murray/States Newsroom)WASHINGTON — Humanitarian protections for thousands of Lebanese immigrants living in the United States are set to expire by Nov. 27, and the Department of Homeland Security has not indicated if their Temporary Protected Status will be renewed. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin in May renewed TPS for an estimated 11,000 nationals from Lebanon for six months, citing instability in the region due to the U.S.-Israel-backed war in Iran, which is still active. Nationals who hail from a country deemed too dangerous for return, due to war, violence or other extreme instability, are granted anywhere from six-month to 18-month cycles of protections to remain and work in the U.S. A DHS spokesperson did not answer State Newsroom’s questions about the renewal status for Lebanese immigrants with TPS. “An announcement on Lebanon’s TPS will be made at the appropriate time,” a DHS spokesperson said in a statement. “Until such an announcement is made, Lebanese individuals present in the U.S. under TPS retain protection.” DHS has made the same announcement for nationals with TPS from El Salvador, Sudan and Ukraine. TPS for people from all those countries expired this year, but DHS for now will allow those immigrants to also keep their work authorization and deportation protections. Overall, the Trump administration has aimed to wind down the program created by Congress in the 1990s. At the start of the second Trump administration, 17 countries were designated under TPS, but now only Lebanon has the status, until Nov. 27. The moves have resulted in more than 1 million immigrants having their TPS stripped, and opening them to the president’s mass deportation agenda. The remaining TPS holders whose protections expired but who maintain deportation protections include roughly 200,000 Salvadorans, 100,000 Ukrainians and 2,000 Sudanese. Congressional Democrats have tried to pass legislation to extend TPS broadly, and for certain nationals such as Haitians and Afghans, but have been unable to with Republicans controlling both chambers. In January, Democrats will hold the majority in the House and Senate, and members of both chambers have expressed immigration reform as a top priority. However, passage of any legal protections for immigrants will likely face a veto from President Donald Trump, and need a two-thirds majority to override. The president has expressed interest in making a deal with Democrats regarding legal status for some immigrants in certain industries such as hospitality and agriculture. But his new White House Chief of Staff Stephen Miller has often taken a hard-line approach to any forms of immigration, including legal immigrant workers.

articles.title: Veterans’ abortion restrictions likely to stay in place for months as lawsuit timeline stretches
articles.description: Despite a lawsuit and opposition from newly empowered congressional Democrats, the U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs’ tight abortion restrictions are likely to remain in place for at least six months, if not longer. The VA policy, in effect for nearly a year, has drawn significant criticism from some veterans and other groups. But the timeline […]
articles.content: The U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs medical campus in Rapid City, South Dakota. A lawsuit challenging the VA’s decision in 2025 to end nearly all abortion care and abortion counseling is ongoing, but will likely extend late into next year before any action from the appeals court. (Photo by Seth Tupper/South Dakota Searchlight)Despite a lawsuit and opposition from newly empowered congressional Democrats, the U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs’ tight abortion restrictions are likely to remain in place for at least six months, if not longer. The VA policy, in effect for nearly a year, has drawn significant criticism from some veterans and other groups. But the timeline may be extended on the legal challenge, and there’s seemingly little that a new congressional majority can do to change the policy without passing legislation, which would take some time. Under the military’s medical benefits package, since the 1990s, abortion care was provided if the pregnancy was a result of rape or incest, or if necessary to save the pregnant patient’s life. Beginning in 2022, the VA provided abortions for health-preserving reasons as well, and implemented a policy allowing members to be reimbursed for having to travel for care if they were stationed in a state with a ban. But at the end of 2025, the VA announced it would not provide any abortion care for veterans even in cases of rape and incest, would not allow any abortion counseling, and would rescind the reimbursement policy. The VA responded to thousands of public comments about the proposed rule, saying it would make no changes as a result of the feedback. It was finalized on Dec. 31, 2025. One of Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth’s first directives when he took office in January 2025 was about rescinding the 2022 policy, and the formal rule adoption process began in August that year. Trump administration officially ends veteran abortion access The legal arguments surrounding the case rely on a specific section of law written in the 1990s that the VA says excluded infertility services, abortion and pregnancy care from veteran medical benefits. But those opposing the rule say even that section, which they disagree should be applied as narrowly as the administration is using it, does not exclude abortion counseling. The department said ectopic pregnancy terminations and miscarriages are not considered abortions and can be treated. The policy led to a lawsuit filed in May by Minority Veterans of America, an organization with more than 3,600 members in 49 states and the District of Columbia. The organization argues that the VA made the change without a reasonable explanation, violating administrative law, and says its members have already been harmed by not being able to discuss options with care providers. The lawsuit is ongoing, but it may be at least six more months before oral arguments are heard in the case, making any department-level changes unlikely anytime soon. U.S. Department of Justice attorneys representing the VA asked the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Federal Circuit for an extension until Feb. 8 to file a response, which was originally due on Dec. 9. The court hasn’t yet approved that request, but if it does, it will extend the overall timeline of the case by several months. Sides weigh in In the complaint, Minority Veterans of America argued that veterans of reproductive age have high rates of chronic medical and mental health conditions that can increase risks associated with pregnancy, including post-traumatic stress disorder, hypertension and kidney disease. Those conditions can heighten the risk of hemorrhage and placental issues. According to a friend of the court brief submitted by 212 congressional Democrats, the VA told their staff in February 2025 that records showed about 462,000 women veterans of reproductive age were enrolled in VA healthcare, along with an estimated 112,000 women of reproductive age in the Civilian Health and Medical Program of the VA, or CHAMPVA, which provides coverage to veterans’ families, including children. The department has said it is complying with statute, and that it is adhering to the U.S. Department of Justice’s legal opinion issued prior to the finalization of the rule stating that the VA could not legally provide abortion care. The VA also said the government was under no obligation to subsidize or to “facilitate” abortion. The current policy also doesn’t allow reimbursement for travel expenses or special leave to seek abortion care, which was permitted under the 2022 rule. “As explained in this rule, VA can provide care to pregnant women in life-threatening circumstances under the medical benefits package,” the agency said in its response to public comments. “In all other circumstances, VA will not discuss options for abortions outside VA and will not refer veterans and CHAMPVA beneficiaries to abortions outside VA.” So far, no Republican elected officials or anti-abortion groups have filed briefs in support of the VA’s policy in the lawsuit. When the rule was initially proposed, Susan B. Anthony Pro-Life America, one of the leading national anti-abortion organizations, called it a “major win.” “We thank President Trump and VA Secretary (Doug) Collins for restoring the rule of law and ending the Biden administration’s illegal policy that forced taxpayers to fund abortions through VA hospitals and violated state pro-life laws,” SBA President Marjorie Dannenfelser said in a statement at the time. “Thankfully this injustice is now corrected.” Some of the states with the highest number of service members and veterans, including Alabama, Florida and Texas, also have some of the most restrictive abortion laws in the country. According to estimates from nonprofit National Partnership for Women and Families, more than 400,000 women veterans lived in states that already had an abortion ban in place or were likely to ban it in 2023. That figure represents more than half of the women veterans in the country. “The decision to rescind that rule was both harmful and cruel,” said Jordan Goldberg, policy director of the Reproductive Freedom Alliance, a coalition of state governors who support reproductive rights. All 47 Democratic U.S. senators and 165 Democratic U.S. representatives signed the brief in October asking the court to override the rule. In March, those senators voted in favor of a resolution that would have allowed Congress to block the rule, but it failed to pass in a 48-50 vote. Although Democrats will hold nine more seats in the Senate in January, Goldberg said there is a limited window of a few months during which an agency’s rules can be overruled, and that time has passed. Goldberg said some states with Democratic leaders, such as California, are working to adopt state-level policies that help veterans who need abortion care and can’t get it from the VA, but that has its limits too. “A state cannot take the place of the federal government,” Goldberg said. ‘In a precarious position’ When Sylvia Andersh joined the U.S. Air Force in 1974, women were so new to the military that there were still enlistment limits, and Roe v. Wade, the 1973 U.S. Supreme Court case that affirmed a constitutional right to abortion access, was barely a year old. Just before the end of the four years she spent on active duty, Andersh needed an abortion. At the time, she said military personnel were supportive of her decision and helped her access care at a private clinic. But if she were serving today, with the military’s current stance toward abortion and 13 states with restrictive laws, she doesn’t know what that might have meant for her care. She went on to have a son in 1986, and four years after that, she had a miscarriage at 13 weeks and needed treatment. “It’s been very painful to see that women who have served their country do not deserve the respect of having control over their own bodies,” Andersh said. Andersh, who left home at 18 to join the military as one of few women service members, said she thinks the new policy is designed to drive women away. “It puts them in a precarious position, because when you’re in the military, you’re supposed to be combat ready at any time, and how do you navigate that when you have responsibilities as a mother and a parent?” she said. articles.title: European spacecraft finds chaotic scene after asteroid deflection experiment
articles.description: "DART made a really, really large mess. However, we didn’t really know what kind of mess."
articles.content: Four years ago, NASA dispatched a small spacecraft on a suicide mission to show how humanity might deflect an asteroid on a collision course with Earth. The first-of-its-kind experiment worked beautifully as the solar-powered space probe slammed into asteroid Dimorphos, permanently altering its trajectory. Using telescopes, astronomers measured changes in the orbit of Dimorphos around a larger asteroid companion named Didymos in the aftermath of NASA's Double Asteroid Redirection Test (DART) mission. The spacecraft released some 10 billion joules of energy as it impacted Dimorphos in September 2022 at more than 13,700 mph (6.14 kilometers per second), shortening the asteroid's 12-hour orbit around Didymos by about 33 minutes, 25 times the most conservative expectation. But scientists could only learn so much from DART. The collision destroyed the spacecraft, as expected. DART recorded images as it took aim on Dimorphos, but only faraway telescopes and a small CubeSat that briefly detected the impact flash could see what happened next.Read full article Comments

articles.title: Mamdani wins against landlords in New York rent freeze lawsuit: ‘Housing is not a luxury’
articles.content: Judge upholds rent freeze on roughly 1m rent-stabilized apartments in victory for Democratic socialist mayor A New York City judge has upheld a rent freeze on the roughly 1m rent-stabilized apartments in New York City, delivering a big victory for the city’s Democratic socialist mayor, Zohran Mamdani. In an order published Wednesday, Manhattan supreme court judge Brendan Lantry dismissed a lawsuit brought by a group of landlords seeking to block the policy, which freezes rents on one- and two-year leases for rent-stabilized units beginning on or after 1 October. A spokesperson for Mamdani also did not immediately respond to the Guardian. But, in a statement to the New York Times, Mamdani described the decision as “a victory for tenants, for affordability and for the principle that working New Yorkers deserve a city they can afford to live in”. “Because housing is not a luxury,” Mamdani said. “It is a basic necessity.” The lawsuit was filed after the city’s rent guidelines board approved the measure in June. The landlords argued that the order was a result of a “sham process” and claimed that the board “ignored evidence of soaring landlord costs and manipulated the data to understate the impact of these costs”. In the judge’s order on Wednesday, he wrote that “the court’s review is not whether the Board’s determination was wise or if it may cause negative collateral consequences to the overall real estate market” but rather that it is to review whether the order “has a rational basis, that is, that it is not unreasonable, arbitrary, or capricious”. The judge concluded that the petitioners had “failed to establish” that the passing of the order “was unreasonable, arbitrary, or capricious” and thus, the court found that freeze “has a rational basis and must therefore be upheld as valid”. The ruling marks a win for Mamdani, who campaigned on the pledge “freeze the rent” for rent-stabilized tenants. Much of his campaign focused on making New York City more affordable, as many residents face rising costs for housing, food and more. But the rent freeze for rent-stabilized units, and its approval by the board, drew criticism from landlords and from some in the real estate industry, who argued that freezing those rents, while insurance, taxes, maintenance and other operating costs rise, will place additional financial strain on building owners. In the ruling on Wednesday, the judge criticized the mayor’s campaign pledge to “freeze the rent” calling it “reckless and irresponsible” as he noted that mayors have “no authority to unilaterally raise, ‘freeze’ or otherwise adjust the rent of stabilized units in this City”. That authority rests with the board. But, ultimately, the judge wrote that the group of landlords had “failed to establish” that the passing of the order by the rent guidelines board in June was “unreasonable, arbitrary or capricious” and found that the freeze “has a rational basis and must therefore be upheld as valid”. It is not clear whether the landlords will appeal. One of the lawyers representing the plaintiffs, Randy Mastro, a former first deputy mayor under Eric Adams, said in a statement to the Guardian that he was “disappointed by the court’s ruling” and said that “we are continuing to review the ruling and considering next steps”.

Trump says he will meet with Abdul El-Sayed on healthcare: ‘He’s a smart guy’
articles.content: The newly elected Democratic senator from Michigan, Abdul El-Sayed, may have found an unlikely ally in his effort to enact universal healthcare in the United States: President Donald Trump. In a wide-ranging interview Tuesday night in the Oval Office, Trump called El-Sayed a “smart guy,” according to the New York Post. The president went even further, saying he would meet with him to discuss the prospect of universal healthcare. “I know I’ll be meeting with him,” Trump said. “Maybe there’s some place in the middle that we could go.”He did not specify a date or location for the proposed meeting. Trump’s comments come after El-Sayed posted an image of a gold credit card emblazoned with “TrumpCare” on Nov. 12, urging the president to pursue some form of universal healthcare.“Donald, this is on the table. Guarantee healthcare for every American, from cradle to grave,” he wrote in the post, which Trump later reshared. El-Sayed, a physician who will become the country’s first Muslim senator, has reiterated his commitment to advancing Medicare for All once in office, a key plank of his campaign platform. He did not immediately respond to MS NOW’s request for comment on Trump’s remarks about a possible meeting, but told NBC’s “Meet the Press” on Sunday that “plans are in the works” for a meeting.Earlier this month, Trump also told Fox News that “there’s a chance we could get great healthcare and a lot of other things, and we do it in a bipartisan way.”

articles.description: "Our entire country is in an outbreak," says Oakland County Health Officer Kate Guzmán. The post What losing measles elimination status in the US means for metro Detroit | The Metro appeared first on WDET 101.9 FM.
articles.content: “Our entire country is in an outbreak,” says Oakland County Health Officer Kate Guzmán. The United States has lost its measles elimination status, which it had held since 2000. That means the virus has spread in the country continuously for more than a year. There have been more than 5,800 cases nationwide and 12 deaths this year. And it’s not only children. More than 40% of those cases were in adults. Fewer kids are getting their shots as Americans’ confidence in major institutions, including the medical system, is near record lows. Here in Michigan, health officials have 37 confirmed measles cases. The state’s biggest outbreak is in Washtenaw County. Kate Guzmán is the Oakland County Health Officer. articles.content: As more data centers rise in Michigan, Rep. Rashida Tlaib explains why she wants to stop the bill supported by Democratic leader Chuck Shumer and President Donald Trump. Rashida Tlaib on The Metro, Nov. 25, 2026 Three buildings, together the size of 28 football fields, are rising on what was farmland in Saline Township. It is Michigan’s first hyperscale data center. Just east, in Van Buren Township, Wayne County has ordered a halt to construction on a second massive data center, this one for Google. The county says the developer did work without the permits it needed and violated the county’s stormwater rules. The developer, Panattoni, says it’s working with the county. Data centers like these need enormous amounts of power, and DTE Energy has agreed to supply both. Getting that power to them takes new power plants, power lines and pipelines. A bill in Congress would change how the country approves big energy projects: the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act. The bill is built on a trade. It promises faster, more certain approval of energy projects. In return, communities get less time to weigh in and fewer ways to stop a project they believe will harm them, from solar farms to gas pipelines. The Senate passed it on Nov. 19, and Michigan’s two Democratic senators, Elissa Slotkin and Gary Peters, voted yes. The House still has to approve it. Congresswoman Rashida Tlaib represents Detroit, Dearborn and Southfield. Her caucus has called the bill a gift to Big Oil and Big Tech. She joined The Metro’s Robyn Sfeir-Vincent to talk about what the bill would mean for data center opposition in Michigan and what she would pass instead.
