The Humans Who Helped Get Underdog Will Lawrence to Congress
articles.description: A massive network of volunteers who knocked on doors for House candidate Will Lawrence helped push his campaign across the finish line.
articles.content: In one of the most expensive congressional races in the country, East Lansing native Will Lawrence knew he’d have to run a different kind of campaign for Michigan’s 7th Congressional District if he was going to win the seat. And to be clear, no one thought he was going to win, Lawrence told East Lansing Info, freshly returned to the city after wrapping up new member orientation for elected U.S. Representatives in Washington D.C. Lawrence was not widely projected as a frontrunner in the Democratic primary for 7th U.S. Congressional District which determined who would face Republican incumbent U.S. Rep. Tom Barrett. The race in the general election became one of the most watched in the country and Lawrence’s victory became part of a wave for Democrats in the U.S. House as the party made historic gains in securing a majority. “Nobody thought I was going to win the primary, and didn’t think we’d even be here talking about a general election, and so it was important to run the campaign in a way in which I could win even if I lost,” Lawrence said, talking to ELi over the phone while doing last minute Thanksgiving shopping at Costco. Bringing people together, building community, and showing up in-person to repair some of the divides the current political climate has deepened would be a victory even if the campaign failed, Lawrence said. On door-knocking days, Melany Mack’s house was filled with the smells of different soups and the laughter of volunteers coming back from their routes to share stories from people’s doorsteps, the Dewitt-based volunteer for the Lawrence campaign said. “My whole dining room table for the whole summer was nothing but clipboards and buttons and literature,” Mack said. “It was just a great experience. We made lasting friendships, and I think it’s more than a campaign. … It’s the beginning of a movement. The friendships just blossomed.” Since the beginning of the race, the Lawrence campaign reports it’s knocked on more than 350,000 doors to share literature and have conversations with voters and Mack said she personally knocked on several thousand of those doors in Clinton County. But what the campaign can truly be proud of, according to Mack, was a consistent priority of hearing out the needs and concerns of individuals across the political spectrum. Lawrence comes from an organizing background, largely known locally for advocating for affordable housing. Mack said throughout Lawrence’s extensive efforts to show up in-person in communities across the district, he advised volunteers that “it’s better to listen than to talk.” Mack recalled one particularly hot afternoon when she knocked on a door in Dewitt and a man answered the door, saying he was a Republican. “I looked at him and I said to him, ‘Will you help me understand, please? What does that mean now?’” Mack said. “He shut his door. He stepped out on the porch, and he said to me, ‘I don’t know.’ And we had a great conversation about getting beyond labels and about looking at what the person stands for. … And I had several conversations like that, all of them with Republican men.” People are not as different from each other as political ads would lead them to believe, Mack said. Speaking to people in neighborhoods while they’re walking their dogs and holding their children provided a good opportunity to break through silos and talk about issues that were important to them, not what social media was saying was important. “Mom of the Campaign” was a title Lansing resident Kathleen Rogers wore proudly as she set up sloppy joes, enchiladas, bratwursts and other potluck foods at Lawrence’s campaign office in Lansing. With volunteers putting in long hours to knock on doors and come into town from other parts of the district, Rogers said it was important to provide “mom” support when they returned to the office, getting a hot meal and an opportunity to share stories from the day. “They call me the mom … I’m a calm person, a consistent presence. I can be there for someone that needs a ride. I can be there for a shoulder, to cry on a little bit or hugs. We brought food in … but there were a lot of moments where we as older people also gathered together and had some joy,” Rogers said. Seeing young people engaged in elections was an incredible experience, Rogers said. Baby boomers like she and her husband Andy need to step up to the plate to support candidates like Lawrence who are looking to make life better for the next generation. This is why she started the organizing group Boomers for William Lawrence for Congress which gathered baby boomer generation volunteers together to get involved in the campaign in ways younger people might not be able to. Amongst the divides the country is facing in politics, there is a lot of anger towards the baby boomer generation, where younger generations say the group has hoarded wealth it accumulated from a friendlier housing market and cheaper college tuition and left the next generation out to dry, Rogers said. It was important to her to mobilize people in her circle to use the time and resources that have been afforded to them to promote a campaign seeking to improve life for young people. “We knew that boomers had the ability. There are a lot of old hippies out there and if we could sway them to be role models and bring them in, we really felt like that the 18 to 44 year olds were going to be the major voters, but Boomers for Will mattered because we have the time and the means financially to assist Will and there’s a lot of savvy people that have experience,” Rogers said. Lawrence made a genuine bid for connection amid an era in politics where many campaigns try to find footing in the issues that divide communities, Lansing resident and political organizer Lyra Opalikhin said. Putting a federal moratorium on new data center developments and placing limitations on artificial intelligence developers were consistent priorities for Lawrence as he spoke at city council meetings and in communities all over Michigan’s 7th U.S. Congressional District. Though Lawrence didn’t hide his progressive politics, it was clear he wasn’t talking about issues like accountability for artificial intelligence developers to garner support from progressives or the Democratic party, Opalikhin said. Rather, Lawrence as a candidate focused on areas that united neighborhoods, which includes the bipartisan interest in holding tech companies accountable. Opalikhin knocked on doors, phone banked and participated in tabling events on Michigan State University campus to engage students voters in the election. People can want to be engaged in politics, Opalikhin said, and the Lawrence campaign made it fun. She pointed to Lawrence making appearances at Greater Lansing bars to sing karaoke with students and talk to a crowd at The Avenue Cafe in Lansing while dressed as Abraham Lincoln for Halloween. “Having someone who emphasizes that sort of positive connection and then makes the effort to actually go out and connect with people is what I think brought a lot of people to the campaign because they really saw how genuine he was,” Opalikhin said. “He wasn’t doing it for any other reason, but because he wanted to show up, and he shared those same values as many other people, values that were rooted in just shared humanity and like to live authentic lives.” The campaign was the definition of grassroots, and Lawrence’s ability to bring people together to flip a Republican controlled congressional seat may seem surprising from an outside perspective, but for those who know him personally, it’s just the kind of impact Lawrence has, Lansing-based artist Kelsey Brianne said. Lawrence was involved in the founding of housing rights groups such as the Michigan Rent Is Too Damn High Coalition and the Mid-Michigan Tenant Resource Center, which have advocated for policies to bridge gaps between vulnerable populations and housing opportunities. For the last three years, Brianne has worked on advocating for fair housing policies in the Michigan state legislature with Lawrence. She said she’s watched him foster a collaborative environment where he’s empowered others to take on advocacy work without his help. But when someone needs help, Lawrence is a helper, Brianne said, sharing that Lawrence sat with her through eviction hearings during her own housing security struggle and currently is letting her cat live at his house while she works through her options. From dinner tables to sewing circles, Brianne describes her efforts to support Lawrence during the election as a simple act of having more intentional conversations with the people around her about the issues that matter to them. “It was a lot of bridge-building … like whenever I would meet someone, I’m just a real social person. I would meet someone, see what town they’re in and be like ‘oh, you live in this town? You should vote for my friend Will Lawrence. He’s watching my cat,’” Brianne said. Lawrence could have made a larger career outside of Michigan and made a lot of money using his connections and organizing abilities, Brianne said. Lawrence has not held elected office prior and secured endorsements from the likes of former presidential candidate Bernie Sanders, even before the Democratic Primary. And whereas Barrett has caught criticism for his lack of in-person town halls in the district he represents, Brianne points out that Lawrence proudly talks about his East Lansing background and shows dedication to the community he’s been a part of. Hometown support for the campaign came from various eras of Lawrence’s local advocacy and roots in East Lansing, including a text campaign authored by his high school prom date When it was time for the class to pick partners for group projects, Lawrence was the partner all the kids wanted to team up with, Marianne Peel Forman, Lawrence’s 8th Grade English teacher at MacDonald Middle School in East Lansing said. “He’s always been very welcoming to everybody. You know how some students have that ability to make everybody feel comfortable,” Forman said. .”He was always very creative, but he was also willing to listen to other people’s ideas.” Forman moved to Kentucky after wrapping up a 32-year teaching career, but with family and friends still in Michigan, Forman said she was hopeful that if she talked enough about her former student online and to her peers, they would get people on board with his campaign. A lot of people are despondent with the state of affairs of government and have trouble seeing how their vote can make life better for themselves and the people they care about, Forman said. From a young age, Lawrence demonstrated a rare form of leadership that allowed his peers to feel empowered to share their ideas and talents and it’s clear from his House campaign that he has not lost that ability. “He was a candidate that I think everybody was hungry for and could believe in, who could move toward change, which we desperately need right now. And he was willing to put himself out there. I contributed to his campaign several times over the last couple months, I just believed in him,” Forman said. “When I saw him running, I was absolutely elated. I thought he would be a good candidate, and as it turns out, he really was.” East Lansing High School Sophomore Jabril Carter met Lawrence back in March at a No Kings protest when he saw Lawrence in the crowd after missing his speech earlier in the event “While walking out, I saw a pretty tall guy. I mean, if you know about Will, he’s like about six-foot-six, he’s pretty easy to spot in the crowd and I was able to go up to him. He seemed really genuine, seemed like he loved to talk to me. I shook his hand. I asked him a couple questions about what his campaign was trying to do, who he was, his background … and he had really good answers for me,” Carter said. articles.title: Thousands of Flint water settlement claimants may learn award amounts this week
articles.description: When the more than $600 million settlement fund was set up by the state of Michigan and others in 2020, the bulk of the money was earmarked for the youngest victims of the Flint water crisis.
articles.content: Thousands of young people may soon learn how much money they are receiving from the Flint water settlement.When the more than $600 million settlement fund was set up by the State of Michigan and others in 2020, the bulk of the money was earmarked for the youngest victims of the Flint water crisis.Flint’s drinking water source was switched to the Flint River in 2014. The improperly treated river water damaged aging pipes, releasing lead and other contaminants into Flint’s tap water. Flint returned to a Detroit-supplied water system 18 months later. But tens of thousands of people, including children, had already been exposed to high levels of lead in their drinking water. Lead is linked to serious health problems, particularly in young children, including developmental and behavioral issues.In a federal court filing Tuesday, Special Master Deborah Greenspan wrote a structured settlement program has been established to preserve the funds for minor claimants.“Under the Amended Settlement Agreement (“ASA”), consistent with Michigan law, the payments to current minors must be distributed through a mechanism that will preserve the funds for the minor’s benefit," Greenspan wrote. "The ASA provides that payments can be made in the form of a structured settlement or to a court approved trust. There are two court approved trusts for Flint Case Water Settlement claimants – a Special Needs Trust and a Settlement Preservation Trust. The structured settlement program has been established, and the Court has previously approved the form of fund settlement agreement and periodic payment options offered to eligible minor claimants."She said there are approximately 4,400 claims from minors included in this payment group, with letters going out starting this week.The process of getting to this point has been complicated as the claims administrator has struggled to get needed signatures and other documents from all the people who originally qualified for a share of the money.

articles.title: Google search alternative Kagi launches Gmail rival
articles.description: The pitch is an unusual combination of privacy promises and AI features.
articles.content: Kagi, a small, Palo Alto, California-based software company that provides a subscription-based search engine as an alternative to Google, has launched a Gmail-like e-mail service. Dubbed Kagi Mail, it makes many of the same claims as the search engine product: privacy, personal data sovereignty, customization, and control. Additionally, Kagi is rolling out a calendar as part of the mail service. Right now, both the email and calendar interfaces are web-only, but native Android and iOS apps are planned for the fourth quarter of next year. The email interface, currently in public beta, is minimalist. It emphasizes keyboard commands, as well as a private and ad-free experience. (You can see more details in Kagi's blog post about what they mean by private.) Other feature offerings include unlimited aliases and domains, an anti-lock-in policy for user data, 50GB of storage, rule-based filtering with Sieve, an MCP server, and several optional, off-by-default AI features, like chatting with an agent to search email history, do large-scale re-labeling, or define additional filtering rules.Read full article Comments

articles.title: FCC approves SpaceX plan to put AI data centers in space
articles.description: The FCC dismissed some of the key concerns raised by opponents, including potential threats to scientific research, because the agency determined they fell outside its regulatory authority.
articles.content: SpaceX was given conditional approval by the Federal Communications Commission on Wednesday to deploy and operate a constellation of up to 1 million satellites for its orbital data center business, a regulatory victory for Elon Musk and his bid to move AI data centers into space. The FCC authorization was granted despite objections from Amazon, Viasat, and the American Astronomical Society, which flagged concerns over orbital debris and congestion, radiofrequency interference, and environmental consequences. Amazon, which is building a competitor to SpaceX’s Starlink service, argued in its petition that the application lacked basic details and described it as a “lofty ambition rather than a real plan.” Despite that lack of detail, Amazon also said the proposal “risks real harm.” The FCC dismissed some of the key concerns raised by opponents, including potential threats to scientific research, because the agency determined they fell outside its regulatory authority. FCC Chair Brendan Carr said in a statement that the action “opens a bold new frontier for the computing infrastructure needed to power America’s leadership and growth.” Musk thanked Carr in a post on X, writing “Much appreciate. This will be a great asset to America and the world.” This initial regulatory approval doesn’t mean orbital data centers are imminent. SpaceX faces a number of technical and economic challenges, including how to dramatically reduce the cost of manufacturing and launching satellites, cool processors in space, and even how to secure financing for chips that are destined for orbit. The company must also clear other regulatory hurdles. The FCC has not yet approved SpaceX’s plans to handle orbital debris for satellites that would operate above 600 kilometers, for instance. SpaceX requested a waiver of existing FCC rules, which requires satellites ending missions below 2,000 kilometers reenter Earth’s atmosphere within five years of completing those missions. The company is interested in moving some of these retired satellites into other orbits around Earth or even around the sun, according to the FCC authorization document. SpaceX has said it plans to deploy the satellites, known as Starmind, at altitudes ranging from 500 to 1,002 kilometers. The FCC’s approval gives SpaceX the authority to use radiofrequency communications to maintain contact with and control its orbital data centers from Earth if their primary communications systems fail. The Starmind satellites would primarily communicate using lasers to connect with other satellites, including SpaceX’s Starlink. The FCC has given SpaceX time to sort out these issues. Under the approval, SpaceX has seven years to get its first operational satellite into orbit and 14 years to deploy the entire constellation. Al Jazeera Italian PM warns Ukraine after attack on Russian vessel in Mediterranean Sea Українська правда NATO sees no Russian naval buildup in the Med after strike near Libya, but analysts warn of wider risks Breaking Defense Libyan Forces
articles.content: Two Libyan naval officers have died following the Ukrainian drone attack on a Russian warship in Libya that opened a new theater in the conflict, thousands of miles from the front lines of the Russia-Ukraine war, and a highway fire near the Egyptian capital killed at least 30 people. Iran’s Revolutionary Guard said a liquified petroleum gas tanker hit a mine as it was passing through the Strait of Hormuz. And in Yemen, the Iran-backed Houthi rebels claimed responsibility for attacks on ports, a refinery and a financial district in Saudi Arabia. Here is the latest news from the Middle East on Wednesday. Read our full coverage here. A crash involving a fuel tanker ignited a massive fire on Ring Road, a key artery that encircles Cairo on Wednesday evening, killing at least 30 people and injuring 25, officials said. At the scene, rescue workers were pulling people out of burning cars. An Associated Press video shows firefighters working to put out the fire spreading amongst the cars. Hundreds of people gathered near the scene in the Warraq district of Imbaba, a Cairo suburb. More than two dozen cars and motorcycles were left charred, the Public Prosecutor’s office said in a statement. Iran’s paramilitary Revolutionary Guard said on Wednesday that the tanker was trying to pass through the Strait of Hormuz when it hit the mine. It added that the tanker had deactivated its positioning systems. The Revolutionary Guard has warned that tankers violating Iran’s restrictions could hit mines. The two officers died on Tuesday of their wounds sustained in the attack on a Russian warship moored in eastern Libya, the self-styled Libyan National Army said in a statement late Tuesday. The LNA is the most powerful group in Libya, a country fractured by years of civil war and chaos, and has close ties to Russia. President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Ukraine deployed seven sea drones in the operation that struck the Russian ship on Sunday. Libyan authorities said it had docked to refuel and resupply. The Iran-backed Houthis said Wednesday that their attacks on the Saudi Arabian ports of Jeddah and Jizan came in response to Saudi Arabia’s attacks on Yemen, including the targeting of the port of Hodeidah. The Houthis said that with their attack, they have established an equation of “ports for a port.” They claimed there was damage in both locations, without providing evidence. The Houthi rebels also claimed responsibility Wednesday for strikes on a refinery in Saudi Arabia and the financial district in the kingdom’s capital, Riyadh. The Saudi-led coalition said Tuesday that a Houthi drone targeted a tower in the King Abdullah Financial District. In a statement early Wednesday, it said four drones targeting the Ras Tanura refinery in the eastern region were intercepted. Houthi military spokesperson Yahya Saree claimed Wednesday, without providing evidence, that the rebels had carried out the two attacks. The AP could not independently verify the claim. The Houthis say their attacks on Saudi infrastructure aim to pressure the kingdom into lifting its blockade on Yemen. At least six women were among those killed by strikes on southeastern Sudan, according to Emergency Lawyers, a rights group tracking the Sudan war. It blamed the killings on the Rapid Support Forces paramilitary group. The rights group said the strikes on neighborhoods in Damazin, capital of the southeastern Blue Nile province on the border with Ethiopia, also wounded 15 people. Sudan’s government had rejected an Ethiopian government effort to mediate talks between warring parties to end the four-year conflict, claiming it supports the RSF. Ethiopia denies the allegation. The overnight airstrike on the Shati refugee camp killed four people and wounded six more, according to health officials. The strike killed Hamas’ director of internal security services in northern Gaza, Mohammad Majid Abu al-Ouf, his wife and two teenage daughters. Israel’s military confirmed it targeted and killed al-Ouf. It came after Israel carried out several strikes on Gaza this week, killing at least nine people between Monday night and Tuesday, including another top security official. More than 74,746 Palestinians in Gaza have been killed since the war began three years ago, according to the Gaza Health Ministry, which is part of the Hamas-run government. Its figures are generally considered reliable by the international community. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s yearslong effort to shake off corruption charges was given a boost on Wednesday, when judges recommended dropping one of the three cases against him and reconsidering a second one. The attorney general, who has a contentious relationship with Netanyahu, can decide whether to accept the judges’ recommendation. The judges have made similar recommendations in the past, including this summer, to drop the bribery charge, which centers on alleged business deals in exchange for favorable media coverage. But on Wednesday they said they had “serious doubts” the prosecution will be able to meet the legal threshold for conviction after hearing testimony. The other two cases revolve around fraud and breach of trust. Responding to the judges’ recommendation, Netanyahu on Wednesday evening said that the cases against him amounted to years of “character assassination.” He called for the charges to be dropped immediately. Khaled and Magdy reported from Cairo, Akour from Amman, Jordan, and Lidman from Tel Aviv, Israel. This report will be updated throughout the day as new developments emerge.

Michigan airport officials expect smooth holiday travel despite groundstop fallout
articles.description: By ALEXANDER BOESCH/Capital News Service Recent disruptions in aviation have cast doubt on the industry’s ability to get people around the country this holiday season following the mid-November nationwide grounding […]
articles.content: By ALEXANDER BOESCH/Capital News Service Recent disruptions in aviation have cast doubt on the industry’s ability to get people around the country this holiday season following the mid-November nationwide grounding of commercial planes and the resulting fallout. The Federal Aviation Administration issued the nationwide ground order on Nov. 13 due to complications from maintenance problems. The ground order was lifted the following day, but many stranded passengers needed multiple days to get back on track. U.S. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy and U.S. Rep. Tom Barrett visited the Capital Region International Airport in Lansing on Thursday, Aug. 13. Mike Ellis/City Pulse Cortez Strickland, the communications and public relations manager at the Wayne County Airport Authority, said his agency does not make decisions on cancellations or delays, but the airport encourages travellers to check flight information ahead of time. The authority, which oversees the Detroit Metropolitan Wayne County Airport (DTW), is anticipating more than four million passengers throughout the holiday travel season that stretches from Nov. 20 to Jan. 3. “We continue to remain focused on providing a world-class experience for our customers and guests just like we would any other day of the calendar year,” Strickland said. Strickland said that the airport is opening a new short-term waiting area for pickups, reducing traffic at the pickup curb. The lot is expected to open before the holiday season. “It’s in a more convenient location than the previous North Cell Phone Lot, which is intended to reduce congestion at the curb and create a safer environment for everyone moving through our airport,” Strickland said. Kevin Klein, the CEO of Cherry Capital Airport in Traverse City, said the airport anticipates around 2,000 passengers a day for the holiday season, with travel typically peaking around the Thanksgiving holiday and then picking up again in mid-December. It’s the state’s third-busiest airport after DTW and the Gerald R. Ford International Airport in Grand Rapids. Klein said that he does not expect lingering fallout from the nationwide grounding on Nov. 13 to disrupt the holiday season. “The system didn’t stop, and that’s the one thing that I want to make sure people are reassured by the fact that yes, there was an issue with some communication, but the system didn’t stop,” said Klein. “It still kept operating. It just was diminished, and when it was diminished, it was very similar to almost like a heavy snowstorm,” said Klein. U.S. Secretary of Transportation Sean Duffy said the outage was due to either faulty equipment or an installation error during routine maintenance, which disrupted communication and the radar feed. “When we see that, your safety is paramount. We shut down the airspace, and we do it safely. We get you on the ground, and then we work on isolating the problem and then opening the airspace back up, which is what we did yesterday,” Duffy said at a press conference the day after the shutdown. Duffy reiterated that the FAA system is outdated, and that the administration needs additional funding to overhaul systems from analog to digital. Duffy said that delays would become more common as the system ages.

articles.title: OpenAI says heavy ChatGPT users may hit limits sooner as it merges Chat and Work
articles.description: OpenAI will introduce a single usage meter across ChatGPT as it combines the Chat and Work experiences.
articles.content: OpenAI has started rolling out a unified Chat and Work experience in ChatGPT to a few of its users, amid criticism from some subscribers that the merger could restrict their usage. The ChatGPT maker began introducing the update to a small group of Pro subscribers, product lead Thibault “Tibo” Sottiaux said in a post on X on Tuesday. The rollout follows OpenAI’s earlier announcement of the merger in an email to users. An OpenAI spokesperson told TechCrunch that while most users are not expected to face more frequent usage resets, a small fraction of its heaviest users may hit their limits sooner. That’s among the concerns raised by some ChatGPT subscribers on social media and OpenAI’s community forum recently. The users fear that merging the usage limits for Chat and Work could leave them with less access to advanced reasoning models than they currently have, even as they continue paying the same subscription fees. Under the new system, Chat and Work will share a single usage meter across ChatGPT, the OpenAI spokesperson told TechCrunch. Conversations using the Instant model will, however, remain unlimited and will not count toward the shared allowance. Users can also continue using Instant after exhausting their usage limits. The spokesperson added that OpenAI would continue working to improve efficiency so subscribers could get more out of their plans. While the rollout has started for a small group of users, OpenAI plans to bring shared usage limits more broadly in December, per its support page. Similar to OpenAI, rival Anthropic also moved to bring its conversational chat service Claude and work-focused Cowork under one interface in September. The changes come as AI companies face mounting infrastructure costs and growing demand for increasingly capable models, putting pressure on their computing resources. Bringing conversational and work-related tools into a single interface could also make AI chatbots simpler to use, allowing users to move between chats and more complex tasks without switching tabs. articles.title: Anthropic’s Dario Amodei calls accusations of surrendering human control to AI ‘absurd’
articles.description: Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei pushes back against rivals’ accusations that he favors surrendering human agency to AI, even as leading AI companies increasingly automate their own research and model development.
articles.content: Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei is pushing back against claims that Anthropic believes we should “surrender human free will” to AI systems. In a long X post on Wednesday, Amodei called the suggestion “absurd.” “We should never sacrifice legitimacy or self-determination at the altar of efficiency or security,” he wrote. This argument against autocracy applies word for word against governance by AI, and I feel equally strongly that turning over governance to AI is a bad idea…No one who had carefully read my writing or my interviews could reasonably conclude that I believe anything different.” The statement comes after a growing chorus from Anthropic rivals suggesting that human agency could be at risk if AI is developed irresponsibly. Earlier this month, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman said he wanted to ensure people continue to have “agency over the future.” Meta’s chief AI officer Alexandr Wang also wrote in an essay on X that we “should not be okay with a ‘handover’ of society to AI.” “It is hard to imagine a world where humanity can maintain control over fully unconstrained recursive self-improvement,” Wang wrote. “Now that we are at a point where the scientific and technical problems on capability progress are likely solved, we must not only make progress in the extremely urgent areas of safety, alignment, and security, but we have to start thinking through how we progress thoughtfully.” But in published essays, Amodei claims he has repeatedly advocated for democratic oversight of AI, saying the technology should strengthen democratic institutions and that humans should retain ultimate decision-making power. Amodei noted that there’s a difference between surrendering human free will broadly and the idea that “as AI systems advance, they become capable of doing specific tasks in a more automated way.” As examples, he gave AI driving a car, designing a cancer drug, or writing end-to-end software. Amodei suggested drawing a line at recursive self-improvement (RSI), or AI that can improve itself without human assistance. Many safety experts see RSI as inevitably leading to a loss of human control, a point Amodei implicitly acknowledged, writing, “we may want limits on this process.” Still, Anthropic is laying the groundwork for RSI by incorporating AI into an increasing share of its own research and development. The company said in June that Claude authored more than 80% of the code merged into Anthropic’s codebase. An independent assessment published this month by AI safety research nonprofit METR found that Anthropic’s models are improving at about twice their historical rate, primarily driven by AI-assisted research. In its own IPO filings, Anthropic describes how each successive generation of Claude accelerates the development of the next, a process it refers to as “closing the loop.” “As we said publicly in early November, we don’t expect it to be safe for Claude to build successive frontier models fully autonomously, without meaningful human supervision or understanding,” Amodei wrote. The problem with “meaningful human supervision or understanding” is that AI is already advancing faster than engineers and safety experts can fully audit it, leaving them increasingly reliant on other AI systems to act as judge and jury. The issue compounds when AI models engage in deceptive behavior, particularly when they recognize they’re being evaluated, making them harder to trust and control. Still, Anthropic is by no means the only company that is pursuing RSI or building AI systems to automate more and more human tasks. This week, OpenAI claimed to have solved one of the biggest open problems in computer science — the exact speed limit of matrix multiplication, which is the mathematical engine behind modern computing, including deep learning and physics simulations. In his post, Amodei accused competitors of engaging in a “vibes-based commercial and political positioning,” disingenuously throwing around phrases like “human control and agency” or “AI should just be a tool” without approaching the AI race any differently. “Certainly the products that they offer don’t differ materially in their orientation towards automation of tasks; every company seems to be releasing models more and more capable of task automation,” Amodei wrote. “Every company claims to understand there are risks and downsides of such automation and to offer safeguards.” When you purchase through links in our articles, we may earn a small commission. articles.title: Michigan legislators challenge prison officials over inmate’s medical care and mold claims
articles.description: Following an October federal appeals court ruling allowing a lawsuit alleging toxic mold conditions within the state’s only women’s prison, one of the plaintiffs is seeking a permanent transfer from the Women’s Huron Valley Correctional Facility. That plaintiff, Krystal Clark, has become a focal point of criticism of the Michigan Department of Corrections, as she […]
articles.content: Women's Huron Valley Correctional Facility in Saline Township, Michigan. | Photo by Jon King/Michigan AdvanceFollowing an October federal appeals court ruling allowing a lawsuit alleging toxic mold conditions within the state’s only women’s prison, one of the plaintiffs is seeking a permanent transfer from the Women’s Huron Valley Correctional Facility. That plaintiff, Krystal Clark, has become a focal point of criticism of the Michigan Department of Corrections, as she faces what her attorneys described as a medical deterioration from toxic mold exposure, which led to an emergency court motion to transfer Clark to Duane Waters Health Center in Jackson in July. But in laying out their own findings of fact in court proceedings, the department is expressing doubts that Clark has many of the health conditions cited in her request for a more longstanding court order keeping her out of Women’s Huron Valley, describing Clark’s claims as “exaggerated and inaccurate.” This includes doubts about Clark suffering from mold growing in her ears, which was the centerpiece of testimony from state Rep. Laurie Pohutsky (D-Livonia) at a House Oversight Committee hearing in February. State Rep. Laurie Pohutsky (D-Livonia) testifies to the House Oversight Committee on health and sanitation concerns at the Women’s Huron Valley Correctional Facility. Feb. 24, 2026. | Screenshot. The filing from the state’s legal team alleges that Clark has refused a biopsy that would be able to conclusively confirm a diagnosis of aspergillosis, a respiratory illness or infection caused by breathing in spores of mold, and has otherwise refused treatment from the department’s doctors. “Clark claims to suffer from several health conditions, including an ear infection, difficulty breathing, nosebleeds, a severe mold allergy, and coughing blood,” the filing reads. “At various times, she has also complained of a facial droop, vomiting blood, and difficulty walking, but these claims are based on Clark’s self-reported symptoms and lack corroboration in her medical record.” Pohutsky, as well as state Rep. Emily Dievendorf (D-Lansing), both of whom have openly criticized the department, were critical of the department’s categorization of Clark’s claims as fabricated. “MDOC has already drawn the conclusion that Krystal Clark is healthy and that her complaints are part of a grand manipulation towards getting money out of the department,” Dievendorf wrote in a statement to Michigan Advance. “The assumption of ill intent toward Clark may be the most disturbing and dangerous of MDOC’s responses because it hangs questions over legitimate health conditions that require a serious response and likely require improvement on the part of MDOC to prevent the same health issues in other incarcerated individuals across MDOC’s facilities.” GET THE MORNING HEADLINES. SUBSCRIBE The Department of Corrections has repeatedly denied any issues with mold at the facility and released findings of independent environmental testing done by a private contractor, which concluded the facility did not have dangerous systemic black or toxic mold conditions. In response to the emergency motion that temporarily removed Clark from Women’s Huron Valley, the department released a response that disputed the medical need for that transfer. “Allegations contained in the plaintiff’s motion are not supported by the medical evidence or facts known to the department,” a spokesperson for the department wrote to the Advance in response to the concerns raised by the legislators. “Extensive medical records have been publicly released as part of the response to the plaintiff’s motion for emergency relief. Ms. Clark was not experiencing any emergent medical condition that warranted transfer from Women’s Huron Valley Correctional Facility (WHV).” However, both legislators state that they have personally seen Clark and attested to her need for medical care outside of Women’s Huron Valley. “I have witnessed Krystal’s physical condition myself,” Dievendorf wrote. “Krystal has very real health issues that require action, yet her necessary care is being pushed to the month she is expected to be paroled, almost 6 months from now.” For years, Clark has alleged that black mold at Huron Valley has made her sick. She said she has struggled to breathe and developed rashes, swelling and headaches. (Jay Love/Survivor Speaks) Clark will be first eligible for release on May 9, 2027, according to Michigan’s Offender Tracking Information System, but could be incarcerated up to a maximum date of May 9, 2040. Pohutsky described what she witnessed of Clark’s condition, specifically the alleged mold in her ear, saying, “It is black and fuzzy, and it completely covers her ear.” Both legislators also contested the department’s claims that there are no issues of mold within the facility, with Pohutsky calling it “laughable” and adding, “The idea that they’ve eliminated the mold, so she must be lying about any of these conditions being linked to it, is absurd, and they know it.” Pohutsky added that she sees the statements made by the department in Clark’s case as demonstrating a broader issue with medical care in MDOC facilities. “Their insistence that none of these symptoms or issues can be true because there’s no medical record of them being true. The whole point is that none of these folks, not Krystal Clark, not anyone else that has been at Huron Valley, not anyone else that is in any of the other MDOC facilities, is getting adequate medical care. So the fact that they keep pointing back to their own medical records, or lack thereof, is sort of beside the point, because they’re not getting adequate medical care,” she said. “People are not receiving adequate care, and their immediate tactic is to act as though it is just simply not happening, and everyone who characterizes it other than completely sufficient and appropriate medical care is wrong. I think it’s insulting.” Dievendorf added that, when they have expressed concerns to the department, “I have yet to hear MDOC take any responsibility for unsafe infrastructure, unfair conditions of confinement, and inadequate medical care. I have yet to witness MDOC admit it can and should do better.”

US Supreme Court to weigh bans on AR-15s, similar guns in big Second Amendment case
articles.description: After a man used a semiautomatic rifle to kill five children and wound dozens of others at a California elementary school in 1989, officials in sprawling Cook County, Illinois, banned what they called assault weapons — certain firearms such as the AK-47 and AR-15. Decades later, the U.S. Supreme Court is set to decide whether […]
articles.content: The U.S. Supreme Court on April 9, 2026. (Photo by Ashley Murray/States Newsroom)After a man used a semiautomatic rifle to kill five children and wound dozens of others at a California elementary school in 1989, officials in sprawling Cook County, Illinois, banned what they called assault weapons — certain firearms such as the AK-47 and AR-15. Decades later, the U.S. Supreme Court is set to decide whether Cook County’s ban — and similar restrictions across the country — violate the Constitution. The Supreme Court will hold oral arguments on Dec. 2 in a potentially landmark gun rights case that could sweep away the power of states and localities to prohibit popular models of firearms used in numerous mass shootings. The decision could also stop Congress from imposing new prohibitions on some semiautomatic weapons after a previous ban expired in 2004. “The safety of our communities is at stake,” Cook County State’s Attorney Eileen O’Neill Burke said in a statement. “There is absolutely no reason that AR-15s, AK-47s and other weapons of war that were designed to inflict mass carnage should be available to the public.” States at odds The case has pitted red and blue states against each other. Democratic state officials have urged the Supreme Court to uphold the bans, while Republicans say they must be invalidated under the Second Amendment. Eleven states and the District of Columbia ban “assault weapons,” according to the advocacy group Everytown for Gun Safety, which defines them as high-powered semiautomatic firearms. They include California, Connecticut, Delaware, Illinois, Maryland, Massachusetts, New Jersey, New York, Rhode Island, Virginia and Washington state. Several major cities, such as Denver, Indianapolis, New York and Philadelphia, also have restrictions. Chicago is the county seat in Cook County. The Supreme Court has spent nearly 20 years bolstering Americans’ rights to have guns and limiting the government’s power to restrict them. The justices first ruled in 2008 that the Second Amendment guarantees an individual right to bear arms for self-defense. The court then said in 2022 that restrictions must be rooted in the country’s historical tradition of firearms regulation. The new standard spurred fresh challenges to modern-day laws limiting guns. The justices will now decide whether bans on AR-15s and similar semiautomatic weapons — high-powered guns that fire and automatically reload each time the trigger is pulled — clear that high bar. Suits by gun rights advocates The case before the Supreme Court has been known as Viramontes v. Cook County, but it involves two lawsuits: one challenging Cook County’s ban and another challenging Connecticut’s ban. After oral arguments, the justices will likely release a decision in the case in the spring. Cook County residents Cutberto Viramontes and Christopher Khaya, members of the Firearms Policy Coalition, a gun rights advocacy group, first sued over the county’s ban in 2021. On Oct. 29, Viramontes asked the Supreme Court to drop him from the case without providing a reason. The court granted the request on Nov. 23, but Khaya and other challengers remain and the case will proceed for now. Gun rights advocates argue that under the court’s previous decisions, guns in common use, such as the AR-15, cannot be banned. A nationwide online survey of more than 51,000 adults this summer found that 25% of gun owners currently own an AR-15- type rifle. In total, 30% of gun owners own at least one rifle commonly referred to as an “assault weapon,” according to an analysis of the results by William English, a political economist at Georgetown University. “This is one of the most important Second Amendment cases in American history,” Brandon Combs, president of the Firearms Policy Coalition, said in a statement. “The question is simple: Can the government ban some of the most popular firearms in America?” For the Firearms Policy Coalition the answer is an emphatic “no.” In a brief to the Supreme Court, the FPC and other petitioners say there are many reasons why Americans may prefer AR-15s and similar semiautomatic rifles, including that they tend to be more accurate than handguns and are lighter and have less recoil than other rifles and shotguns. The brief says that “by any objective measure the handgun is the most dangerous weapon to modern society,” given its use in violent crimes. And because the Supreme Court already struck down the District of Columbia’s handgun ban in 2008, the semiautomatic rifles in question should also be protected by the Second Amendment, the brief argues. Regulations of dangerous weapons Supporters of the ban counter that the right to keep and bear arms under the Second Amendment, like other constitutional rights, is not absolute. The nation’s history is filled with examples of regulations of especially dangerous weapons, they say. In their brief to the Supreme Court, Cook County officials trace the AR-15’s military origins as the civilian version of the M-16, the rifle widely used by the U.S. military in the Vietnam War. They highlight the history of gun sellers marketing the firearms as “assault weapons” or “assault rifles.” The Chicago-area ban on the AR-15 and similar weapons is compatible with the nation’s historical tradition of firearm regulations, Cook County argues, because the rifles are offensive weapons of war designed for maximum lethality and not typically used for self-defense. During the 2010s, just over a third of mass shootings involved semiautomatic assault weapons, according to data from the Gun Violence Archive, a nonprofit group that tracks incidents of gun violence, that was analyzed by The Trace, a news organization focused on gun violence. Mass shootings were defined as incidents that took place in public areas where four or more people died. “When weapons are introduced into society that have the capability to perpetrate some of our most tragic and frightening crimes, from mass shootings to assassination attempts, democratically elected legislators are permitted to respond with appropriate regulation,” Cook County’s brief says. Federal appeals courts have issued conflicting decisions about the constitutionality of the bans, though most appellate decisions have upheld the restrictions. The U.S. 7th Circuit Court of Appeals found Cook County’s ban acceptable in a 2025 decision. Two months later, the 2nd Circuit sided with Connecticut in a challenge to its ban. But the 3rd Circuit ruled against New Jersey’s restrictions in July 2026 — a month after the Supreme Court decided to take the cases involving the Cook County and Connecticut bans. Dem, GOP attorneys general weigh in States have jumped into the fight on both sides of the Supreme Court case. Democratic state attorneys general in 18 states filed a brief urging the justices to reject arguments by gun rights supporters that AR-15 and similar semiautomatic weapons should be protected because of their popularity. Such a standard would break with common sense, they wrote. “It would risk opening the floodgates for other unusually dangerous weapons — just because sales of those weapons have cleared some arbitrary popularity threshold,” the Democrats argue. Massachusetts Attorney General Andrea Campbell and New Jersey Attorney General Jennifer Davenport led the brief. They were joined by Arizona, California, Colorado, Delaware, Hawaii, Illinois, Maine, Maryland, Michigan, Minnesota, New Mexico, New York, Oregon, Rhode Island, Vermont, and Washington, in addition to the District of Columbia. On the Republican side, Kansas Attorney General Kris Kobach, Tennessee Attorney General Jonathan Skrmetti and 25 other state attorneys general have pressed the Supreme Court to strike down state and local bans on AR-15s and similar weapons. They argue the weapons are commonly used for lawful purposes. The GOP state officials also reject comparisons between the AR-15 and military-issue weapons. In a brief to the Supreme Court, they note that the AR-15 semiautomatic rifle has never been issued to military service members. “The superficial similarity in appearance between the AR-15 platform rifle and standard service rifles simply reflects that certain ergonomic and design features translate well to both military and civilian use,” their brief, led by Kansas and Tennessee, says. Other states signing on to the brief include Alabama, Alaska, Arkansas, Florida, Georgia, Idaho, Indiana, Iowa, Kentucky, Louisiana, Mississippi, Missouri, Montana, Nebraska, New Hampshire, North Dakota, Ohio, Oklahoma, Pennsylvania, South Carolina, South Dakota, Texas, Utah, West Virginia, and Wyoming. Trump administration opposes bans President Donald Trump’s administration has also asked the Supreme Court to strike down the bans. U.S. Solicitor General D. John Sauer and other U.S. Department of Justice officials in their brief urge the justices to reject the term “assault weapon,” arguing that it is a political term that wasn’t in use prior to 1989. Sauer’s brief refers to FBI estimates that of the nearly 13,700 homicides in 2025, about 38% were committed with handguns. By contrast, just 3% involved rifles of any kind — semiautomatic or otherwise. “Holding that the Second Amendment protects handguns but not rifles would be ‘backwards,’” the brief says. But Julia Schardt wants the Supreme Court to listen to her experiences and those of other shooting survivors. Schardt was a second-grade teacher at Cleveland Elementary School in Stockton, California, on Jan. 17, 1989, when a 24-year-old man shot and killed five children and wounded some 30 others — at the time the worst non-college school shooting in U.S. history. The shooter had an AK-47 and other weapons. The shooting prompted a national outcry that helped lead to limits on some semiautomatic weapons across the country, including a nationwide “assault weapons” ban passed by Congress in 1994. Schardt and more than a dozen other survivors of shootings have signed on to a brief urging the Supreme Court to uphold the bans. They say their stories underscore the danger and lethality of the weapons. The brief recounts Schardt’s experience that day, including one student telling her that another was dead. The next day, Schardt viewed the body of an 8-year-old to help confirm the child’s identity and saw the massive head wound left by a bullet. “In Julia’s view, the assault weapons used allowed for so much carnage in so little time,” the brief says. “She believes it is hard to understand the damage these weapons can do to a child’s body without seeing it with your own eyes.”

The 2026 parade will feature plenty of local star power, with Rocket Companies chairman Dan Gilbert serving as the Grand Marshal. Parade Company CEO Tony Michaels says they invited Gilbert to participate in January. “He accepted immediately and we kept it a secret,” Michaels says. “It’ll be goosebumps on Thursday morning when he’s headed south on Woodward with his family.” Actor and comedian Dave Coulier, who was born in Detroit and grew up in St. Clair Shores, is also scheduled to appear in the parade. The parade will feature nine new floats, which Michaels says are massive. “They’re 120 feet long and they take a long time to design,” he says. “We have to get it right.” Michaels says he has seven artists who sculpt and build the floats. But it’s the volunteers who make the parade possible. “There’s close to 2,000 volunteers that do something with us throughout the year,” he says. “It’s a massive undertaking.” Mixed among the floats are marching bands, balloons, clowns, and people who wear large papier-mache heads depicting famous Detroiters. Several local companies sponsor the floats and other entries. Gardner-White has been the presenting sponsor since 2020. Michaels says they have extended their commitment through 2031. The FCC has authorized SpaceX to deploy 1 million satellites
articles.description: This constellation would increase the number of satellites in orbit by roughly 50-fold.
articles.content: This constellation would increase the number of satellites in orbit by roughly 50-fold. In an extraordinary decision, the Federal Communications Commission on Wednesday granted SpaceX conditional authorization to deploy a constellation of up to 1 million Starmind satellites designed to serve as orbital data centers. If fully deployed, this constellation would increase the number of satellites in orbit by roughly 50-fold. “The United States is moving decisively to ensure that this breakthrough technology creates opportunity, drives investment, and delivers lasting benefits for the American people,” FCC Chairman Brendan Carr said in a statement on Wednesday. “This action opens a bold new frontier for the computing infrastructure needed to power America’s leadership and growth.” The decision, announced a day before the Thanksgiving holiday in the United States, represents a major regulatory victory for SpaceX and its founder, Elon Musk, who has allied himself with the Trump administration. This announcement clears a major hurdle to deploying data centers in space, although it does not establish that orbital data centers are technically or economically viable. Nevertheless, the FCC authorization appears designed to give the company wide latitude as it works through these remaining issues. For example, SpaceX has seven years to deploy a single operational Starmind satellite under the order. SpaceX has until November 2035 to deploy 100,000 operational satellites, and November 2040 for the full constellation. SpaceX, therefore, has a 14-year regulatory runway to deploy the most ambitious industrial project ever approved for spaceflight. The authorization includes some conditional aspects. SpaceX has proposed operating in six orbits, ranging from 550 km to about 1,000 km. The company sought a waiver from FCC rules to allow satellites above 600 km to be disposed of into “Earth disposal orbits or heliocentric orbits.” That is, instead of burning them up in Earth’s atmosphere, SpaceX wants the flexibility to move retired satellites into other orbits around Earth, or potentially into orbit around the Sun. The FCC did not grant this waiver request “because SpaceX has not provided sufficient information for the Commission to determine whether its alternative disposal methods are compliant with the Commission’s requirements.” The company will need to obtain a waiver before deploying any Starmind satellites that are not intended to be disposed of via atmospheric reentry. However, in other ways the FCC appears to have been incredibly lenient with SpaceX. This is particularly the case with environmental concerns raised by numerous parties that commented on SpaceX’s application to the FCC. Half a dozen organizations, such as the Secure World Foundation and American Astronomical Society, raised concerns about deploying so many satellites into orbit, citing collision risks, orbital debris, atmospheric pollution from so many satellite reentries, impacts on astronomical observations, and more. The FCC also received approximately 1,500 public comments concerning SpaceX’s application. Some of these environmental issues, the FCC said, lay beyond the scope of its review. For example, on concerns about the environmental implications of thousands or potentially tens of thousands of rocket launches, the FCC said, “Potential concerns related to the emissions of rocket launches and the subsequent impacts on the human environment as an indirect result of the Starmind system are outside of the Commission’s purview.” The FCC also rejected calls for further environmental scrutiny of pollution from satellite reentries, including concerns about aluminum oxides and their potential effects on the ozone layer. “Other concerns, including impacts on the atmosphere caused by satellites burning up on re-entry, remain speculative and not supported in the record,” the FCC authorization states. As part of its decision, the FCC cited a significant policy change adopted in October, when the agency concluded that space-based activities generally fall outside its obligations under the National Environmental Policy Act. The FCC reasoned that as these activities occur beyond US territory, they don’t constitute federal actions requiring environmental review. As a result, the agency declined to conduct a comprehensive environmental assessment of SpaceX’s Starmind constellation.

articles.title: MSU's renowned horse breeding program is hiding in plain sight, and you can visit for free
articles.description: Founded with a stallion from W.K. Kellogg in 1934, Michigan State University’s Arabian horse breeding program trains students and welcomes free public visits.
articles.content: Michigan State University runs a historically significant horse breeding program. The program primarily focuses on one specific breed: Arabian horses. Arabians are a fine-boned desert breed prized for their endurance in tough climates and over long rides.The Arabian horse breeding program at MSU can trace its story back to when the breed was first brought to America, and has its start in breakfast cereal. Learn the history of the program with Michigan Archivist Mark Harvey, and take a tour of the facility with the new farm manager, Samantha Black, by using the audio player above. Here are five things you should know about MSU's program.1. Horses have been part of MSU since its founding in 1855Michigan State University began as what is widely recognized as the first land-grant college in the country in the mid-1800s. The school was always set up for teaching around the agricultural industry, including farm animal breeding and husbandry. The horses originally bred at the school would have been farm work horses, such as large draft breeds that could pull carts and farm machinery. MSU still maintains a small herd of draft horses to honor that legacy. Today, those draft horses are used for instruction at the university and in local parades.2. The founder of Kellogg's helped launch the program in 1934W.K. Kellogg invested some of his wealth from the cereal industry in an Arabian horse ranch in California. That ranch was the site of the original Arabian horses brought to American after the Civil War. Kellogg would eventually gift one of the prized stallions, Amidore, from that ranch to Michigan State. The Arabian breeding program at MSU began with Amador.3. Arabian horses aren't for everyoneArabian horses have narrow, dished faces and large nostrils that are perfect for cooling hot desert air. The also often have one fewer vertebrae than other horse breeds, which make the backs more sturdy for long, arduous journeys. Finally, Arabians are a smart, energetic breed. They are considered a "hot" breed, like Thoroughbreds, which gives them the personality and verve for long, hard races, but can also make them challenging to work with. They are not considered a beginner's horse. 4. MSU students train and care for the horses before many are soldAll of these unique features make the breed special to work with for students who are learning how to train horses at MSU. Students learn how to train, ride, and care for the 70 horses at the farm over the course of the school year. After students train them, most of the young horses are sold to the public. The money collected from those sales go back into the program at MSU.5. Anyone can visit the horses at MSU for freeMichigan State University maintains its land-grant legacy by being open to the public. That includes its farms that house horses, cattle, and sheep. Many young families show up to the horse farm throughout the week to visit the horses along the fence line. Interacting with many people helps the Arabians with their training and preparedness for life away from MSU. For more on how to visit, head to the MSU Horse Teaching & Research Center website.

articles.description: The U.S. economy grew at an unexpectedly high annual rate of 4.3% in the third quarter, the biggest bump in three years, federal data released Wednesday shows. It raises the likelihood of interest rate hikes that make borrowing for homes and investments more difficult. Increases in business investment and consumer spending led the bump, as […]
articles.content: People shop at an Ohio Walmart in April. Consumer spending driven by tax cuts and refunds, along with business investment in AI data centers, helped boost U.S. economic activity in the third quarter. (Photo by Marty Schladen/Ohio Capital Journal)The U.S. economy grew at an unexpectedly high annual rate of 4.3% in the third quarter, the biggest bump in three years, federal data released Wednesday shows. It raises the likelihood of interest rate hikes that make borrowing for homes and investments more difficult. Increases in business investment and consumer spending led the bump, as the artificial intelligence boom fueled investment while tax cuts and refunds kept shoppers going. The increase in gross domestic product could be a temporary bump, economists say. “This level of GDP probably won’t be sustained in 2027. A slowdown in AI investment is likely, and many consumers don’t have much cushion left to handle higher prices,” Heather Long, chief economist at Navy Federal Credit Union, wrote in a post on social media platform X. The federal Bureau of Economic Analysis announced the revision Wednesday for inflation-adjusted GDP, a measure of economic activity. The third-quarter estimate was up significantly from an earlier estimate of 3.4%. The 4.3% increase was the highest since 2023, when it was 4.5% in the third quarter. The bureau said the increase was driven by gains in the value of computer software and consumer spending on pharmaceuticals, recreational goods and vehicles, while economic activity dropped in healthcare. State estimates are not yet available for the third quarter. In the second quarter, when national growth was 2.2%, the largest annual growth was in New York (4.0%), followed by Delaware and South Carolina (both 3.5%). GDP decreased the most in West Virginia (down 2.3%), Wyoming (down 1.6%) and Alaska (down 1.3%), according to BEA statistics. E.J. Antoni, a conservative economist once nominated to head the BEA, wrote in an X post that the “red-hot” increase makes a Federal Reserve interest rate hike “guaranteed.” “Good news is bad news,” Antoni wrote. articles.title: Battleground poll reinforces what Lawrence heard from voters about healthcare
articles.description: Beginning in January, Democrats will hold majorities in both the U.S. House and Senate, taking power back from Republicans as voter frustrations over everyday costs resulted in a nationwide rebuke of President Donald Trump and Republican policies. While inflation and prices were a top issue for voters, polling from Hart Research commissioned by the advocacy […]
articles.content: Democratic Congressional candidate William Lawrence announces his final push to mobilize voters as he stands outside of U.S. Rep. Tom Barrett's (R-Charlotte) former office in Lansing on Oct. 27, 2026. (Photo by Kyle Davidson/Michigan Advance)Beginning in January, Democrats will hold majorities in both the U.S. House and Senate, taking power back from Republicans as voter frustrations over everyday costs resulted in a nationwide rebuke of President Donald Trump and Republican policies. While inflation and prices were a top issue for voters, polling from Hart Research commissioned by the advocacy group Protect Our Care and the Service Employees International Union, found that frustrations around healthcare helped deliver wins for Democrats in battleground districts across the country. Between Nov. 4 and Nov. 8, Hart Research surveyed 1,230 voters from 59 congressional battleground districts. Survey results found that healthcare was a “very important” factor in deciding 71% of participants’ votes. When voters were asked to rank their top issues, healthcare ranked second only to inflation and prices, polling above concerns around the war in Iran and jobs and wages. On a press call discussing the survey’s findings, U.S. Rep.-elect William Lawrence (D-Lansing) who ousted U.S. Rep. Tom Barrett (R-Charlotte) in Michigan’s 7th Congressional District, said the polling data tracked with what he heard on the campaign trail. “We talked to tens of thousands of voters and we heard again and again that healthcare is simply unaffordable, unreliable and it creates this cloud of anxiety over people’s lives,” Lawrence said. “Even those who have high-quality coverage now have no confidence that they’re going to be able to keep that coverage in the future, or that it will remain affordable because of how much volatility there has been in the healthcare markets and how Republicans have made this a political football that they seek to cut at every opportunity.” Polling from Hart Research shows affordable healthcare was a top concern for battleground voters. (Screenshot) Guy Molyneux, a partner at Hart Research, explained that while Democrats held a modest 6% advantage among the voters they polled, with 52% voting for Democrats and 46% voting for Republicans, voters who rated healthcare as their top issue overwhelmingly voted for Democratic candidates. Additionally, when voters were presented with a list of policy actions Republicans and President Donald Trump had taken in recent years, the three items that voters largely rated as a reason to vote against Republicans in Congress were all tied to healthcare. The poll also asked voters which issue was a higher priority, healthcare or lowering taxes – a major theme in Republican campaigns. Sixty-three percent of voters rated healthcare as their personal priority, while 34% said cutting taxes was more important. When asked which issue was of higher priority to each party, a broad majority of voters said healthcare was more of a focus for Democrats, while Republicans were more concerned with cutting taxes. Looking ahead to what voters want from their elected officials, 83% of voters said it was important for Congress to take action on the cost of healthcare. GET THE MORNING HEADLINES. SUBSCRIBE While 95% of Democrats surveyed said they’d like to see Congress act on healthcare costs, Molyneux noted that this issue was also vital to most Republicans, with 71% saying Congress should take action. As for what Congress should do specifically, the survey presented voters with six issues that Democratic candidates and party leadership have identified as possible priorities for the caucus. Each proposal drew support from at least two-thirds of the voters surveyed, with participants showing particularly strong support for capping insulin costs at $35, adopting reforms to bar insurance companies from overriding decisions made between doctor and patient and restoring funding to local hospitals. While survey data showed voters trusted Democrats far more than Republicans to deliver on affordable healthcare, the survey also found that voters were more concerned with Republicans blocking solutions than Democratic overreach. Forty-eight percent of voters said they were concerned about congressional Republicans or the president impeding efforts to make healthcare more affordable while 34% worried that Democrats would go too far in imposing government-run healthcare. Polling from Hart Research examines voter priorities on health care and tax cuts, as well as which they felt was a higher priority for the two major political parties. (Screenshot) Lawrence also noted that healthcare costs have put the squeeze on small business owners who provide healthcare to their employees, placing them in a situation of having to choose to either cover these rising costs or pass them on to their employees. Additionally, 23 Michigan health facilities have announced cuts, closed, or are at risk of closure, Lawrence said, while noting that care itself is becoming less available. Upon joining his Democratic colleagues on Jan. 3, Lawrence said he looked forward to undoing Republican cuts to the Affordable Care Act and Medicaid, “and doing so immediately before those cuts begin to bite deeper.” From there, Democrats need to work toward expanding healthcare access and increasing affordability, working down the road to universal and guaranteed healthcare, Lawrence said. Gabriella Jones-Casey, an executive vice president for SEIU Healthcare Michigan stressed that the voters gave members of Congress a mandate to put people first, and deliver affordable healthcare. “We are not asking. We are not begging. We are not pleading,” Jones-Casey said. “We voted for those who committed to improving care for our families in our communities, and we will not back down. Lawmakers must put care ahead of corporate tax breaks and strengthen the care that allows Michiganders to be healthy and to thrive.”

articles.content: In an announcement on Wednesday, the FCC says it authorized SpaceX to deploy up to 1 million AI chip-equipped satellites as part of the Elon Musk-owned company’s “Starmind” initiative. With several others also pursuing the idea of putting AI data centers in space, including Google and Blue Origin, this is the first approval the agency has granted for a full “constellation” of AI satellites. The FCC’s approval requires SpaceX to deploy at least one satellite by 2033, and meet the 1 million satellite milestone by 2040. The FCC also deferred SpaceX’s request to dispose of satellites located above 600km in space “graveyard” orbits, rather than having them burn up in the Earth’s atmosphere, saying the company hasn’t provided “sufficient information” about its disposal process plans. SpaceX has described its Starmind project as a way to “capture solar energy in space to power” AI capabilities on Earth. The company says Starmind will transmit data to Earth using high-speed lasers that connect to Starlink. It plans to produce chips for its satellites at an upcoming Terafab facility. Google has already taken its first steps toward putting compute into space, with the launch of a “Project Suncatcher” AI server satellite last month. Jeff Bezos’ Blue Origin will carry out the first dedicated heavy-lift launch for Project Suncatcher in 2029.

articles.title: Character.AI’s plan to auction off users’ private chats challenged by state AGs
articles.description: The proposed Character.ai bankruptcy sale includes sensitive personal data from more than 21 million U.S. accounts, including 2.1 million registered to minors, the state AGs said.
articles.content: What happens to your private conversations when an AI company goes bankrupt? If it’s Character.ai, apparently, the plan is to auction them off to the highest bidder. Now, a coalition of 42 state attorneys general is intervening in Character.ai’s bankruptcy proceedings in an effort to stop the chatbot maker from selling off sensitive user data, which includes the private conversations of millions of users. The attorneys general involved in the matter have put out individual press releases, claiming that Character.ai’s dataset includes chat histories from more than 21 million U.S. accounts, more than 2.1 million of which belong to minors. In addition, the sale would involve other personal data, like IP addresses, the statements said. Character.ai, which filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy in October, previously told consumers that their personal information would not be sold, the statements also noted. (In a blog post, Character.ai assured its users that their information would still be protected under its privacy policy.) Only one anonymous bidder for the chat data has been disclosed so far: Smirks and Pangs Acquisition LLC (Smirks), which was set up as a Delaware company on November 13, 2026. The following day, Character.ai picked it as the base bid for the auction, scheduled for December 1, California Attorney General Rob Bonta noted. It is unclear what the buyer’s plans are for the chats. The AGs are opposing this sale on the grounds that there are no protections for users — whoever buys the data can do as they like, including reselling the data without disclosure, they said. Buyers also won’t have to honor Character.ai’s privacy policy. Plus, Character.ai hasn’t provided the court with as much information as the bidders have been given about any potential safety or legal issues following the sale, the AGs claim. In addition, some states, including California, Colorado, New York, and Connecticut, have enacted chatbot safety legislation that will go into effect on January 1, 2027, which could trigger further violations if the sale goes through. “Character.AI promised consumers that their data would not be sold. This kind of behavior is illegal under federal and California law and bankruptcy should not be used to sidestep these consumer protections,” Bonta said in a statement. Connecticut Attorney General William Tong also criticized Character.ai’s business model. “Their chatbots drove vulnerable youth down a rabbit hole of emotionally volatile and sexually inappropriate chats,” Tong said. “Their reckless misconduct and broken business model drove their company into the ground. Now they want to abuse the bankruptcy process to do exactly what they said they wouldn’t do — auction off those private chat records and personal details to a shady buyer.” Tong added: “We objected to the Disney sale, and we’re calling on the bankruptcy court to reject this sale too as yet another guise to eviscerate legal liability and consumer protection.” The opposition to the Disney sale was led by a similar but not identical coalition of state AGs. They fought against a proposed $20 million licensing deal that would give Disney access to Character.ai’s intellectual property, but not to users’ chats. The deal has not yet received final court approval. (Disney also agreed to hire most of Character.ai’s remaining staff.) Character.ai suffered after its co-founders, Noam Shazeer and Daniel De Freitas, returned to Google, when the tech giant signed a non-exclusive license to use the AI startup’s tech. The company also faced lawsuits related to child safety — one involved the suicide of a 14-year-old Florida boy whose mother claimed he had become obsessed with a chatbot on the platform. California AG Bonta is joined in the effort to oppose the sale of Character.ai user data by attorneys general from Alaska, Arkansas, Colorado, Connecticut, the District of Columbia, Delaware, Florida, Georgia, Hawaii, Idaho, Illinois, Indiana, Kansas, Kentucky, Louisiana, Maine, Maryland, Michigan, Minnesota, Mississippi, Missouri, Nevada, New Hampshire, New Jersey, New York, North Carolina, North Dakota, Ohio, Oklahoma, Oregon, Pennsylvania, Rhode Island, South Carolina, South Dakota, Tennessee, Utah, Virginia, Vermont, Washington, Wisconsin, and West Virginia.
