Traffic crashes involving a pedestrian have been increasing in Michigan
articles.description: Traffic crashes involving a pedestrian have been steadily increasing throughout Michigan over the past several years. Kalamazoo’s efforts to address all crashes show there are ways to improve.
articles.content: After a drop in 2020, Michigan vehicle crashes involving a pedestrian have increased each year Kalamazoo’s efforts to reduce all traffic crashes have decreased crashes involving pedestrians In 2025, there were 27 days without fatal vehicle crash of any kind, according to Michigan State Police data Vehicle crashes involving pedestrians have been steadily increasing in Michigan since a roughly 25% drop at the start of the pandemic. From 2016 through 2019, Michigan saw on average 2,258 pedestrian-involved crashes each year, according to state police data. The number dropped in 2020, amid shutdowns and disruptions to daily life, to 1,691 crashes, or about 4.6 each day. The increase since then hasn’t been across the board. Kalamazoo, for instance, has seen spikes and dips in its year-to-year data, but going back to 2016 its overall trend has been a decrease. ‘Road diets’ and raised medians Dennis Randolph, Kalamazoo’s public works manager, told Bridge Michigan that the city has been working on reducing all vehicle crashes — including those involving pedestrians — since about 2017. The city has implemented “road diets,” reducing some four-lane roads to two. It also switched some one-way streets to two-way, added raised medians, additional signage and better lighting near intersections. The city has even looked to narrow lanes slightly when possible. “A lot of our emphasis has just been to make our streets feel like the appropriate speed,” Randolph said. “That’s working pretty good.” Related: As Michigan rolls out automated traffic tickets, new law blocks driver points Drunk driving crashes and arrests down for Michigan, but not for all counties Biking booms in the Motor City: More lanes, fun rides — and high fatalities State: New wrong-way detection system cut crashes on Michigan highway As of Nov. 19, state police data shows 27 pedestrian-involved crashes in Kalamazoo, about half of what it saw in 2016 and 2017. Traffic crashes involving pedestrians in Kalamazoo have decreased over the past decade, while those same incidents have been increasing across the state. A city official said work around intersections has helped. (Theresa Coty O’Neil/Bridge Michigan) Statewide through Nov. 19, there have been 1,744 vehicle crashes involving a pedestrian, a rate of about 5.4 each day. In 2025, there were 2,177 such crashes, a rate of about 6 each day, which was 118 fewer crashes than the 2,295 in 2017, the highest point in the past decade.Donate Each year from 2020 through 2025 has seen an increase in statewide crashes involving a pedestrian. In southeast Michigan, pedestrian fatalities increased from 2024 to 2025, according to a recent analysis of state police data by the Southeast Michigan Council of Governments. Total traffic crashes decreased by 1.3% in that time. The 100 pedestrian fatalities in 2025 matched the region’s total in 2020, which the organization said was the second highest in the last decade and just one less than in 2016. Jenya Abramovich, a planner with the organization’s transportation division, said in an October news release that shorter days due to Daylight Saving Time increase risks. “It is a particularly dangerous time of year to be walking and biking, especially in the morning and evening hours when it is darker,” she said. In 2025, pedestrians were involved in less than 1% of traffic crashes in southeast Michigan, but accounted for 22% of all traffic fatalities and 10% of all serious injuries, according to the analysis. While pedestrian-involved crashes in Michigan are on the rise, fatal traffic crashes have been decreasing statewide since 2021, when there were 1,078, compared with the 1,000 fatal crashes last year. Keeping Michigan pedestrians safe The Michigan State Police offer the following tips. What must pedestrians do to travel safely? • Use sidewalks whenever available. • Obey traffic signals, signs and markings. • Cross streets at a corner, using traffic signals and crosswalks whenever possible. • Face traffic and stay as far to the left as possible if traveling on the roadway. What should pedestrians do to travel safely? • Always stop at the edge of a parked car, curb or vehicle before walking out into traffic. • Look left-right-left before crossing a street and continue looking while crossing. • Make eye contact with drivers prior to crossing roadways. • Be visible: wear reflective clothing and lights at night and wear bright colors during the day. • Never allow children under the age of 10 to cross the streets alone. Young children do not have the skills to accurately judge traffic risks. What must drivers do to help keep pedestrians safe? • Stop before entering the marked crosswalk limit line. • Stop before entering the intersection if there is no crosswalk or limit line. • Obey traffic signals, signs and markings. • Yield to pedestrians in crosswalks, intersections and all traffic-controlled areas. • Obey the posted speed limit. What should drivers do to help keep pedestrians safe? • Never pass vehicles stopped at a crosswalk. There may be people crossing who cannot be seen. • Avoid distractions. • Stay alert and take extra caution at intersections, especially when making turns. • Make eye contact with pedestrians waiting to cross roadways. • Be extremely careful when backing up, checking for pedestrians who may move into the path of the vehicle. Matt Mencarini is a Report for America corps member who covers data and accountability for Bridge Michigan.

High school football picks, state championship games
articles.content: It is time to put a bow on the 2026 Michigan high school football season. Eight state championship games at Ford Field on Friday, Nov. 27, and Saturday, Nov. 28, will be the final acts of what has been another great year of Michigan high school football. Every team in August set out with the same goal to practice on Thanksgiving, but only 16 have earned that right with their play on the field. No Detroit teams will play for a state title in front of a home crowd for the first time since 2023. Two teams came close – Cass Tech and Edison – but both suffered semifinal losses to Romeo and Jackson Lumen Christi. Division 3 finalist Harper Woods, looking for its second state title in the last four years, will be the closest representative as a bordering neighbor on 8 Mile. The 2026 finals field also shares lots of similarities with recent state finalists. Five teams (Novi Detroit Catholic Central, Orchard Lake St. Mary's, Dearborn Divine Child, Grand Rapids West Catholic and Jackson Lumen Christi) can repeat as state champions. St. Mary's is going for three in a row, and Lumen Christi is going for five straight, which would tie the MHSAA record. Hudson also returns with a chance to win the D-8 title after finishing runner-up in 2025. Zeeland West, Frankenmuth and Beal City are making their second finals appearance in the last three seasons. The repeat chances will make for compelling storylines, both for the teams trying to cement that legacy and the opponents, who will do everything in their power to stop that from happening. Finals tickets cost $20 per day and grant you access to all four games. If you cannot make the drive to Ford Field, the title games will be exclusively streamed on the NFHS Network. The MHSAA no longer has a cable broadcast for state championship games. Here is a quick preview and a prediction of who will be taking home the 2026 MHSAA football championships. Games are ordered by division, with kickoff dates and times listed. [ Sign up for our new Michigan Sidelines statewide high school sports newsletter ] This will be the final game of the season on Saturday night, and there should be a big crowd in the building for it. Catholic Central filled up its side of Ford Field last year, while Romeo has had a consistently large crowd at every game this season. Romeo got some "divine intervention" in its one-point semifinal win over Cass Tech, according to coach Curt Rienas, with numerous clutch plays on the final two drives. The Bulldogs have a consistent rushing attack inside of a creative playbook with a few wrinkles that seemingly catch teams off guard once a game and a defense that is ferocious up front. Catholic Central looks to defend its state championship with an old-school recipe centered around running the football. The Shamrocks have held high-scoring opponents in check, starting with the pressure created by their defensive line. These teams will bookend the season with dates against each other. Mona Shores traveled over to St. Mary's in Week 1 and led most of the game until the Eaglets took the lead for good in the final minute. Mona Shores has not lost a game since, while St. Mary's rebounded from two late regular season losses with another high-scoring run to Ford Field. St. Mary's quarterback Jabin Gonzales has operated at a high level all year, accounting for over 40 touchdowns as the centerpiece of a talented offense with a great receiving core. Likewise, Mona Shores quarterback Owen Terpstra has been a dynamic player all season but has done it more as a dual-threat option in the Sailors' talented rushing attack. Expect fireworks on Friday night − and a new team wearing the D-2 crown. Free Press prediction: Mona Shores 38, St. Mary's 34. Harper Woods is seeking its first title since 2023, when its talented current senior class made themselves known as freshman. Zeeland West is seeking its first title since 2024 and its first under coach Jeff Bolhouse, who took over for the retired Hall of Famer John Shillito in 2025. Harper Woods avenged one of its two losses, knocking off Chelsea in the semifinal. Zeeland West took care of DeWitt, the defending Division 3 champion. The Dux have a great rushing attack in the Power-T, headlined by ball carriers Brandon Holman and Kenny Howe. Harper Woods just faced a similar offense against Chelsea and succeeded in shutting it down after some issues in the first matchup. Also, the Pioneers will have the biggest star at Ford Field, senior Dakota Guerrant, who will make sure he ends high school with a second wooden mitten. Free Press prediction: Harper Woods 35, Zeeland West 23. After waiting 40 years between its first and second state titles, Divine Child hopes the wait for the third is just 365 days this time around. Outside of a Week 8 loss to Warren De La Salle, the Falcons have cruised back to Ford Field with a balanced offense and a disruptive defense led by a turnover-generating secondary. Kenowa Hills plays in its first state title game since 1992 and is seeking its first football title. The Knights have won 12 straight games since an opening-week loss to DeWitt. Kenowa Hills has an explosive offense led by running back Lundon Hampton (Michigan), receiver Will Fussman (Central Michigan) and quarterback Grayson Fellows. Defensively, Kenowa Hills has held its last three opponents to 35 combined points. Free Press prediction: Kenowa Hills 31, Divine Child 24. West Catholic looks to add to its 21st-century dynasty, with the Falcons having eight state championships since 2010, including last year's D-5 title. West Catholic had to break in new faces on both sides of the ball but continued its championship standard in 2026. Senior running back/linebacker Collin Abram picked up where he left off from his All-State campaign as a junior as one of the primary driving forces for success. Frankenmuth continues its even-year success, making Ford Field for the D-5 finals every other year since 2020. The Eagles fell short the last three times but believe this is the group that can bring home the school's first football title. Quarterback Noah Main has been spectacular as the conductor of the offense, while the defensive line led by Avery Simmons has been stout, especially against the run. Free Press prediction: West Catholic 35, Frankenmuth 27. Lumen Christi has a few different opportunities at history on Friday. With a win, the Titans would tie the state's longest streak of consecutive state championships at five. Head coach Herb Brogan could also become the winningest all-time coach in Michigan high school football history after he tied John Herrington with the Titans' semifinal win over Detroit Edison. Lumen Christi has a balanced offense, led by quarterback Benny Gaston, receiver West Learned and running back Ayden Gatewood and a quality front seven. Almont came into the season eager for a chance to right a 2025 triple-overtime semifinal loss to Lumen Christi. The Raiders have handled every challenge on its schedule, including winning 11 of 13 games by a double-digit margin. Almont has an experienced backfield running the Wing-T offense, while a new-look offensive line has grown throughout the fall. Free Press prediction: Lumen Christi 24, Almont 21. These teams can put up points in bunches but have done it in different ways. Ithaca's Gibson Rondy has thrown for over 2,500 yards and 32 touchdowns as a dual-threat quarterback at the center of everything the Yellowjackets do offensively. Ithaca is led by a 13-player senior class that includes Rondy, two-way star Harper Merchant and returning All-State lineman Ben Munro. On the other side, Whiteford running back Brek Ruddy has topped 2,300 rushing yards and is averaging three touchdowns per game in the playoffs. The Bobcats started the season 0-2 as they dealt with a tough start due to an entirely new group of offensive line starters and training camp injuries. But Whiteford has won 11 straight by playing complementary football and stepping up late in close playoff games. Free Press prediction: Ithaca 28, Whiteford 16. These were Division 8's No. 1 and No. 2-ranked teams all season and meet as expected in Detroit to start the state final festivities. Beal City, which won the title two years ago, went undefeated for the second straight season and survived a one-point thriller against New Lothrop to get back to Ford Field. The Aggies have 16 seniors, including a half-dozen that were contributors to the 2024 title, including Cuyler Smith, a three-year starting quarterback. Hudson made it to Ford Field a year ago but fell to Harbor Beach. The Tigers have one of Michigan's most potent running attacks, led by All-State junior Beckett Campbell and sophomore Bronson Butts. Koen Hinzman, an Iowa State commit, leads both the offensive and defensive lines from tackle positions. Free Press prediction: Beal City 30, Hudson 26. Nominate a high school athlete for the Detroit Free Press boys and girls athlete of the week. Jared Ramsey covers high school sports for the Detroit Free Press. Contact him at jramsey@freepress.com. articles.content: In a powerful explosion that launched gray-white clouds over southeastern Iowa, the Army detonated 68 barrels containing 9,700 pounds (4.4 tons) of degraded lead azide on Wednesday at about 9 am CT, preventing a spontaneous unmitigated explosion of the crystallized, highly unstable compound. The detonation occurred at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant (IAAAP) in Middletown, Iowa, a town of fewer than 400 people. Residents within a 5-mile area of the facility were advised to evacuate, while people farther out were told to shelter in place, close windows and doors tightly, turn off fans, and set indoor air systems to recirculate. Local Iowa outlet KWQC caught the plume from the two earth-covered containers, which were detonated simultaneously. A KWQZ journalist, at a reportedly safe distance from the blast, said on the live broadcast that he could see and then feel the shockwave roll through the crop field in which he was standing. WHO recommends new oral treatment option for gonorrhoea and reports new data on antimicrobial resistance
articles.content: The World Health Organization (WHO) has conditionally recommended a new oral antibiotic, zoliflodacin, as an additional single-dose treatment option for gonorrhoea, marking an important step in expanding treatment. Gonorrhoea is a common curable sexually transmitted infection (STI), but treatment options are becoming more limited as Neisseria gonorrhoeae, the bacterium responsible, has developed resistance to successive classes of antibiotics used to treat the infection. In 2020 there were an estimated 82.4 million new infections among adults globally. The burden is disproportionately high among certain populations such as adolescent girls and young women in high-burden countries, sex workers, men who have sex with men and transgender women. The new interim WHO guidelines suggest a single 3 g oral dose of zoliflodacin as an additional option for treating uncomplicated gonorrhoea affecting the genital and urinary tract in adolescents and adults. The recommendation does not cover treatment of infections of the throat or rectum or severe infections. Based on the currently available evidence, the new drug is not recommended for treatment during pregnancy. Ceftriaxone 1 g administered as a single intramuscular dose remains WHO's recommended first-line treatment. “Gonorrhoea has repeatedly demonstrated its extraordinary ability to develop resistance to medicines, steadily eroding our treatment options,” said Dr Tereza Kasaeva, Director of WHO's Department for HIV, Tuberculosis, Hepatitis and Sexually Transmitted Infections. “The arrival of a new oral treatment option that can be administered without an injection is an important advance, with the potential to simplify treatment delivery and broadening the choices available to patients and health workers.” WHO also assessed a second new oral antibiotic, gepotidacin, but did not recommend it for general use in treating gonorrhoea. However, use may be considered in specific circumstances when the recommended first-line option cannot be used. The recommendations form part of wider efforts to expand treatment options for gonorrhoea. Their introduction should be accompanied by continued surveillance and antimicrobial stewardship to protect the effectiveness of both existing and new treatments. Equitable access and affordability of these new drugs will be crucial to ensure their benefits for public health. Alongside the recommendations, WHO has released its 2026 Enhanced Gonococcal Antimicrobial Surveillance Programme (EGASP) report, presenting new data from10 countries across five WHO regions to inform public health action. Resistance patterns varied substantially across participating countries. Resistance to ceftriaxone and cefixime was detected in four countries and to azithromycin in eight, with the highest country-level proportions of resistant isolates reaching 16% each for ceftriaxone and azithromycin, and 47% for cefixime. The findings underscore the need for sustained surveillance to detect emerging resistance early, monitor the effectiveness of recommended treatments and inform national treatment policies. Protecting the effectiveness of existing and new antibiotics will require their responsible introduction and use, supported by antimicrobial stewardship, surveillance of susceptibility and treatment outcomes, and timely investigation of suspected treatment failures. To support countries, WHO has also launched an online compendium of resources for antimicrobial stewardship in STI management, bringing together guidance and practical tools to optimize antibiotic use, strengthen surveillance and monitor treatment failures. Future efforts to improve gonorrhoea prevention and treatment must include stronger antimicrobial stewardship and surveillance, alongside sustained research and development of new antibiotics with novel mechanisms of action to broaden treatment options.

Private equity sets its sights on Michigan healthcare
articles.description: Private equity firms made more than 200 deals in Michigan from 2015 to 2023, according to public health researchers at Brown University, who say the acquisitions often result in rising costs and worse quality.
articles.content: Michigan has seen more than 200 healthcare private equity deals in recent years targeting physical therapy, eye care and other physician practices Economists say private equity can lead to higher costs and worse outcomes for patients as clinics close As some states work to regulate transactions, Michigan has little on the books to rein in private equity acquisitions When private equity first bought into his practice, Dr. Lawrence Handler saw an immediate benefit. “For the first four years, I loved it,” the Macomb County-based eye surgeon told Bridge Michigan. “I mean, we were humming along, and it took a lot of burden off of me.” Cashing out can be financially rewarding for doctors like Handler, and the new owners helped with the business end of his operation — payroll, human resources, purchasing and the like. But, he said, he would come to realize another cost: “You go from the boss to an employee.” The trade-off doesn’t stop there. When doctors sell to private equity, researchers say, patients often feel the impact: higher prices, more turnover among the staff who treat them and, in some cases, worse outcomes. In Michigan, private equity’s push into healthcare is well underway. Firms made more than 200 deals in the state from 2015 to 2023, the ninth most of any state, according to public health researchers at Brown University. Nationwide, researchers counted more than 6,000 transactions during that time. Private equity has spread across nearly half of Michigan’s counties buying into ophthalmology practices like Handler’s and other specialties like physical therapy, dermatology and cancer treatment. “Patients might feel like they’re not part of a deal, but it changes the way they experience care,” said Yashaswini Singh, a health economist and an assistant professor at Brown University. “There is enough consistent evidence that shows private equity increases the cost of care.” Downstream the deal Economists like Singh say healthcare-focused private equity firms often operate through consolidation, tying together similar, smaller practices into bigger entities that allow for improved market share and bargaining leverage. Despite using their negotiating power to get better pricing from insurers and medical suppliers, Singh said there’s no evidence private equity firms are passing along their savings to consumers. “There’s no incentive.” Among the cost concerns, research indicates some private equity-backed medical services have seen an increase in spending and utilization without a significant improvement in outcomes.Donate And then there’s quality — studies show staff are more likely to leave private equity-backed physician offices. Deaths at hospitals and nursing homes have been found to rise after being acquired. Private equity lobbyists like the American Investment Council contend the industry’s involvement in healthcare is welcomed by physicians, allowing practices to expand care, modernize operations and reduce administrative burdens without impacting patient experience. Aside from controlling a physician’s business operations through management services organizations, private equity firms can also structure complex real estate deals that separate healthcare providers from the buildings they operate in. In a sale-leaseback, a practice or hospital sells its property and rents it back, sometimes from the same private equity firm invested in its operations or from a real estate investment trust, or REIT. Research shows facilities affiliated with REITs have a higher chance of closure or bankruptcy than others. Related: Kalamazoo psych hospital had no doctors, state says. Closing it would leave a gap Michigan regulators set December deadline for Consumers dam sale decision Michigan bars big investors from buying more homes. Will it work? “We’ve seen PE’s footprint grow in virtually every specialty I can think of,” Singh said. Private equity’s reach extends to Michigan’s mental health system, too. In Kalamazoo, a psychiatric hospital is facing the loss of its license after regulators found it had no psychiatrist or other physician on site and noted reports of dozens of patient injuries. The hospital’s owner, South Bend-based NeuroPsychiatric Hospitals, has been backed by New York private equity firm Enhanced Healthcare Partners since 2020. Neither company responded to Bridge’s request for comment. Policy reform Most states have no way of knowing where private equity is in their healthcare systems, according to Nathan Hostert, the director for state policy at the Center for Advancing Health Policy through Research at Brown. Researchers at the university say their private equity tracker is likely an underestimate of the total transactions because of the lack of systemic reporting. Their team relied on industry datasets and reports to fill the information gap. Hostert said there’s been a “groundswell” of interest across states to control private equity in healthcare. His team has provided bipartisan technical assistance to regulators focusing on three areas: requiring ownership transparency, improving oversight of major healthcare transactions and strengthening conditions for physicians and the clinical workforce. Massachusetts and Indiana now require investors to disclose who owns healthcare businesses, while Maine and Delaware temporarily froze certain hospital deals. Oregon and California have tightened rules meant to keep investors out of doctors’ medical decisions, and Connecticut is stopping hospitals from selling their buildings and leasing them back. Michigan does not have a broad effort to regulate private equity in healthcare, Hostert said, but points to a Republican package of bills that would, in part, require certain mergers and acquisitions to go before a state review board. The legislation remains in committee. “At a time when premiums and cost sharing is already extremely high, those prices are only going to continue to rise if private equity firms are widespread within a state,” he said. “There’s a lot of good reasons to take action here.” Seeing the future Originally, the private equity firm that bought Dr. Handler’s practice was based in Oakland County. The ophthalmologist could talk shop and sports with its investors. “There was a good working relationship,” he said. But things changed when Handler’s practice was acquired by Atlanta-based EyeSouth Partners. In an August announcement last year, the firm said the deal would allow it to enter the Michigan market. In all, the takeover allowed EyeSouth to expand its footprint across 19 practices and surgery centers across the state, Ohio and Pennsylvania. The new relationship, Handler said, was “not quite as chummy” as the one he had before. The doctor described working in a more corporate environment where he lost control of his office’s business direction and culture. His practice may soon change hands again. In March, drug distributor Cencora agreed to buy EyeSouth’s retina business for $1.1 billion, folding its physicians into Retina Consultants of America, a Cencora-owned network of retina practices. Handler warned the deal could decrease competition among independent practices that have to vie with a large, vertically integrated organization. That “reinforcing cycle of concentration,” he said, could leave patients with fewer options, potentially limiting access to non-affiliated members during drug shortages. While some patients may be oblivious to the machinations of private equity operating behind the scenes of their healthcare system, the eye doctor has a clear warning for them: “They’ll eventually see it.”

Michigan has spent $40M trying to fix foster care. Abuse is increasing
articles.description: Despite $40 million spent over 18 years, federal monitors say Michigan foster care safety is worsening just as the Whitmer administration asks to end oversight.
articles.content:
A woman enters a Michigan Department of Health and Human Services office in Detroit, July 28, 2017.(Ed White / Associated Press)The rate of abuse and neglect of foster care children in Michigan is on the rise despite 18 years of federal oversightMichigan is now seeking to end that oversight, arguing it is ‘archaic’ and no longer helping to improve the systemBut federal monitors say the rising abuse and neglect rates are an ‘urgent safety threat to children’The rate of abuse and neglect of foster care children in Michigan is on the rise despite 18 years of federal oversightMichigan is now seeking to end that oversight, arguing it is ‘archaic’ and no longer helping to improve the systemBut federal monitors say the rising abuse and neglect rates are an ‘urgent safety threat to children’After 18 years and at least $40 million spent on the court-monitored overhaul of Michigan’s child welfare system, abuse and neglect are on the rise in state foster care.That “represents an urgent safety threat to children,” federal court monitors wrote in a recent report, the latest development in the long-running saga.The warning came as the Whitmer administration seeks to end the oversight, arguing the more than $2 million a year it is spending on those federal monitors would “be far better spent on children and families in Michigan.”The work to reform Michigan’s child welfare system began two decades ago, with a 2006 class action lawsuit claiming the system “inflicts numerous harms” on the children it is responsible for protecting.Those reported harms included maltreatment and neglect for children in foster care, a lack of “basic” healthcare, excessive lengths of stay in the system and frequent changes in their primary caregivers once the state got involved.Rather than defend itself, the state settled the suit in 2008, agreeing to give federal monitors extensive authority to oversee mandated improvements.Two administrations and several state health directors later, Michigan has failed to meet 19 of 24 performance measures and is “moving in the wrong direction” when it comes to preventing abuse and neglect of children in state care, federal monitors wrote in their July report.About 9,200 children were in state care last year, and the monitors cited 447 substantiated abuse or neglect incidents in their July report — 163 more than the minimum standard. They also reviewed a random sample of 150 state abuse and neglect investigations and found that a third “were not undertaken adequately.”Under the current agreement, Michigan is judged by the rate of child victimizations for every 100,000 days in foster care. That rate topped 14 last year, up from 5.6 in 2021 and higher than the 9.07 federal benchmark.Those findings were revealed one month after Michigan urged a federal judge to end the long-running monitoring.Despite struggles to meet the federal benchmarks, most Michigan children in foster care are safe, according to an expert the state hired as part of the case.Though “initially beneficial,” the consent decree governing the foster care program “has become archaic” and is “premised in outdated theories of child welfare,” Assistant Attorney General Neil Giovanatti wrote in a June filing.It now “imposes unnecessary and harmful burdens on both the state and children in foster care.”In their latest report, federal monitors said the rate of abuse and neglect in Michigan foster care homes is on the rise.

(Asha Lewis / Bridge Michigan )Samantha Bartosz, an attorney for Children’s Rights, the group that filed the 2006 lawsuit, opposed the state’s request, arguing in a court filing that “(d)ifficulty or inconvenience” in meeting required metrics does “not legally justify the modification of a consent decree.”The state’s request to end the federal oversight should “absolutely not” be granted, said state Sen. Jim Runestad, who organized a foster care reform rally at the Michigan Capitol last spring.“The state of Michigan never takes this seriously,” he said. “There’s always failures in every single audit report I’ve seen. Colossal failures.”Runestad, a White Lake Republican who also chairs the state Republican Party, said public safety should be the number one priority for governments, and protecting children is the “number one of the number one.”“And they fail at that,” Runestad said of the state. “And they never, ever will put forth the resources to fix the problem.”‘Where’s the boat oar you beat your kids with?’A recent Clinton County trial detailed the consequences that can fall on children when a system fails.Michigan Attorney General Dana Nessel said Tamal and Jerry Flore “subjected their foster and adopted children to prolonged, routine and systemic mental and physical abuse all for personal financial gain” over the span of 14 years.When she first brought charges in 2023, Nessel said the allegations “highlight not only a moral and legal failure of those entrusted with the children’s care, but a failure in our systems to ensure children placed in custody are properly taken care of.”The couple took in some foster children, who were later adopted.At trial, testimony from police, medical experts and adopted children described beatings with a 35-inch boat oar, meals withheld, bedrooms that could only lock from the outside, security cameras in the children’s bedrooms and children being forced to live in a laundry room as punishment.Authorities said the abuse began in 2009, but the criminal investigation leading to charges started in 2021 when Clinton County Sheriff Sean Dush, who was a detective at the time, accompanied a CPS investigator to the Flore home to execute a search warrant as part of a child abuse investigation.“I walked in the house and I went to Jerry and I asked, ‘Jerry, where’s the boat oar you beat your kids with?’” Dush testified. “… He walked right upstairs without saying a word and pointed it out in the closet in the master bedroom.”From 2010 through September 2021, the Flores received about $1.7 million from the state in the form of adoption subsidy payments, according to testimony.In late October, Tamal Flore, 59, was convicted on 11 felonies, including five first-degree child abuse counts that carry maximum sentences of life in prison. Jerry Flore, 61, was convicted on a second-degree child abuse charge and faces up to 10 years in prison at sentencing, which is scheduled for January.Jerry Flore plans to appeal his conviction, his attorney told Bridge Michigan. Tamal Flore’s attorney declined to comment.The CPS investigator who was with Dush during the 2021 search of the Flore home was later suspended and then fired, she testified, for failing to follow protocol.She interviewed some children, who still lived in the home, inside a sheriff’s office patrol vehicle, contrary to forensic interview protocol. She had received a six-week training course on the protocol when hired less than two years prior.She also made errors in her notes from the interviews and attributed some comments to the wrong child when submitting her report. She testified that those errors and others were caused by limited time and resources.State says money for monitor better used for MDHHS staffUnder the terms of the 2008 consent decree, Michigan is paying for the federal monitors who are tasked with overseeing improvements to the state’s child welfare system. Costs connected to the lawsuit and monitoring have exceeded $40 million, according to the state.In 2025 alone, the state spent about $2.7 million on monitors. But as it seeks to end the federal oversight, Michigan argues it could better serve children and families by using that money to hire an estimated 18 additional “CPS investigators, foster care case managers, or other staff.”Staff shortages were among the initial problems detailed in the 2006 litigation, and the consent decree set specific caseloads standards, which required the state to add staff.National standards at the time called for one caseworker for every 10 to 15 children in the system. But Michigan caseworkers were sometimes managing 25 to 40 children each, according to the 2006 lawsuit.Despite adding staff, the state struggled with high turnover rates and inexperience, said Sarah Font, who was hired as a Michigan child welfare worker in 2008 and is now a researcher at Washington University in St. Louis.During her 2 ½ years with the state, Font said she had three different supervisors, and after just six months on the job, she had new employees shadowing her. Most of her eight-week training was spent on learning the internal data system and applicable laws, and not much time on the investigative process, Font told Bridge.“Parents just don’t admit to whatever the allegations are,” she said. “You need really strong investigation and observational skills to know what’s going on.”The confrontational nature is present in well-run systems, she said, so CPS investigators have to be comfortable walking into someone’s home where they’re not wanted and facing hostility. Font said it’s not uncommon for reviews of child fatalities to show that an investigator was timid or had limited access to the child.“And that’s where, I think, really serious risks or safety issues get missed or unaddressed,” Font said.In January, the family of 5-year-old Ethan Belcher, who was killed by his mother and her boyfriend, sued the state in federal court. Ethan was killed less than two years after a CPS investigation was opened, and the lawsuit claims the state failed to properly investigate, the Detroit News reported.Child welfare systems are “probably the most difficult public service to operate,” said Jill Berrick, a University of California, Berkeley expert who added that a CPS investigator is trying to make the best estimate about a child’s safety under difficult circumstances.“It’s a system of scarcity,” she said. “There’s scarcity of time. There’s a scarcity of money. There’s a scarcity of great community members stepping forward to be a part of kids’ lives.”State: Most abuse, neglect happens in kinship homesMichigan’s rate of child victimization per day in foster care has exceeded the federal benchmark for abuse and neglect in each of the past three years.But in general, “children in foster care are safe” despite those metrics, Joseph Ryan, a University of Michigan professor, said in his expert report submitted as part of the state’s request to end the federal monitoring.While there were 447 substantiated instances of abuse and neglect in Michigan over the prior year, children were in the foster care system for a collective 3.1 million days. “This translates into one (instance) for approximately every 7,000 days of foster care,” Ryan wrote.The state had hired Ryan, director of U-M’s Child and Adolescent Data Lab, to provide an assessment of permanency outcomes, the use of emergency shelters and the incidents of abuse and neglect in state care.From 2021 to 2024, about 1% of foster care children in Michigan were abused or neglected, Ryan wrote. That is higher than the 0.6% national average and put Michigan among the 10 worst-performing states. But, he cautioned, comparing rates between states is “not advised” because they have different policies, reporting systems, investigatory practices and data quality.Ryan also found that “the largest share” of Michigan’s maltreatment in care incidents occurred in what’s known as kinship care, when a child is placed with relatives.As of 2024, more than half of Michigan foster children resided in kinship homes, according to his analysis, which found that unsupervised and unapproved visits with biological parents are frequent factors for these incidents.Bartosz, the Children’s Rights attorney, pointed to Ryan’s analysis when arguing to a federal judge that the federal monitoring should continue. articles.description: France blames an Iranian cyber unit for sabotaging hundreds of supermarket freezers.
articles.content: One night in October, hackers staged one of the most unusual cyber attacks in history: cranking up the temperature in refrigeration systems at hundreds of supermarkets across France and destroying millions of euros of food. Hackers have targeted commercial fridges and freezers before, but never at this scale and never in the heart of Europe. The brazen attack left cyber professionals unsure as to who might have executed such a madcap operation. But French intelligence agencies found traces of Farsi and other clues in the digital trail pointing to an elite hacking unit of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps. The unit allegedly behind the hack, Shahid Kaveh, was already well known to Western intelligence agencies. Named after Mahmoud Kaveh, an Iranian commander who died during the 1980s Iran-Iraq war, it is one of several hacking units overseen by the Revolutionary Guards’ Cyber Electronic Command.Read full article Comments

Michigan hunters love to hate game officers (and have guns): A day in the life
articles.description: Michigan has more than 200 conservation officers spread out in every county of the state. They police hunting and fishing, but what does that look like? Bridge Michigan rode along on an officer’s morning patrol to find out.
articles.content: Michigan conservation officers police hunting and fishing and participate in searches and rescues, respond to general emergency calls and can even write speeding tickets There are more than 200 conservation officers in Michigan, typically two patrolling each county According to the Michigan Department of Natural Resource, only about 3% of conservation officer interactions resulted in a citation in 2025 Cody Bourgeois approached two waterfowl hunters in a docked boat on Harsens Island at St. Clair Flats State Wildlife Area on Friday. The hunters wore camouflage and the boat was covered in a straw-like material to better blend in with the marshy surroundings. “Hunting licenses first,” said Bourgeois, a conservation officer with the Michigan Department of Natural Resources, tasked with not only policing hunting and fishing but also participatingin searches and rescues, responding to general emergency calls and even writingspeeding tickets. The two men presented their licenses, then Bourgeois checked their guns to make sure they were legal. Next he checked their shotgunammunition, little cylinders called shells. Waterfowl hunters in this managed area are only allowed to have 25 on them. One of the hunters had more. He apologized, saying it was an accident. Bourgeois wrote him a citation. RELATED: Dead deer and small fish: Michigan students learn to investigate poaching As GOP targets Michigan DNR, Ted Nugent blasts agency’s ‘insane’ regulations Michigan approves electronic kill tags for hunters. How will they work? “That gentleman was very nice,” Bourgeois said back in his truck. “There was no backlash towards me.” That’s not always the case. According to Bourgeois, people can sometimesget upset when he catches them hunting when they weren’t supposed to or killing too many animals. In such instances, he can take the animals and the hunters may incur thousands of dollars in fines. When they get mad at him, Bourgeois tries not to let it ruin his day. “I didn’t pull that trigger. I didn’t make you go hunting today. I didn’t do anything,” he said. “Now you want to swear at me and yell at me and act like I’m the big bad person, which I’m not. I just caught you.”Donate Michigan Department of Natural Resources conservation officer Cody Bourgeois prepares to hand over a ticket to a hunter at St. Clair Flats State Wildlife Area on Harsens Island. (Erick Diaz Veliz for Bridge Michigan) Most conservation officer interactions don’t result in a citation — about 3% did in 2025, according to the department. But some people think the DNR over-polices the outdoors. Sign up for our outdoors newsletter Want more coverage like this delivered directly into your inbox? Sign up for the Bridge Michigan Outdoors newsletter here. One state representative, Ken Borton, famously ran for office after being ticketed for having a feeder in his backyard that attracted deer, which was illegal at the time. Last year, Michigan-born rocker Ted Nugent called wildlife regulators “insane” and “the enemies of conservation” during a legislative hearing on supposed DNR overreach. More than 200 men and women serve as conservation officers in Michigan. They go through about six months of training that involves physical fitness and learning fish and game rules, how to identify animals and examine their dead bodies, first aid and more. Recruits also get trained to do their job on boats and off-road vehicles. Weeks of training for officers continues each year even after they’re hired. “Over the years, our mission has evolved beyond that of a traditional ‘fish and game cop’ to include recreational safety and resource protection,” said Brandon Kieft, DNR Law Enforcement Division chief. “Our officers patrol daily to ensure people across Michigan are hunting, fishing, snowmobiling, boating, kayaking, operating off-road vehicles and enjoying other outdoor activities safely and legally.” The DNR’s Law Enforcement Division was allotted $56.4 million, 10% of the DNR’s budget in the 2026 fiscal year. According to wages posted on a state website, conservation officers make between roughly $45,000 and $128,000 per year, with supervisors able to make a little more Each county typically has two officers but could have as many as four. They primarily patrol alone to spread out resources. In rural areas, they may be the only on-duty emergency responders and can be the first on the scene in life-threatening, general criminal and search-and-rescue situations. Earlier this year, the DNR honored a conservation officer who’d been the first to arrive to the Barry County home of a man in cardiac arrest and helped save the man’s life. Bourgeois, now 31, grew up hunting and fishing in New York and knew he wanted to be a conservation officer, or a game warden — which is what they call them in New York — since he was a kid. “I was fishing with my dad. I had a game warden pull up and he checked us for our fishing licenses,” he said. Afterward, Bourgeois’s dad explained the game warden’s job and Bourgeois responded, “That sounds like the coolest job ever!’” Now in the role, he loves it. He gets to make his own hours, often working early in the morning when hunters and anglers get going, taking a break in the middle of the day and then picking back up in the afternoon when outdoorsfolk go back out. He also likes the variety. “It’s nice because it’s always rotating,” he said. Michigan Department of Natural Resources conservation officer Cody Bourgeois inspects the hunting gear and registrations of Lindsey McDonald, 33, left, and Tim Taylor, 64. The father and daughter duo spent their morning hunting at St. Clair Flats State Wildlife Area on Harsens Island. (Erick Diaz Veliz for Bridge Michigan) Now, he’s focused on policing trapping as well as duck and deer hunting. Once winter hits, he’ll transition to ice fishing and snowmobiling. In the spring, he’ll check on anglers participating in the walleye and salmon runs. In the summer he polices boating. But the job isn’t without its stresses. “The biggest difference between our job and normal police officers’, especially this time of year, (is that) everybody that we encounter has a gun,” Bourgeois said. Which he said can be nervewracking. Hunters have pointed loaded guns at him, like the time he confronted some coming out of the woods after dark. “I just turned my flashlight on, announced myself, and they just pointed their gun right at me,” he said. The state’s hunting and fishing policies can be made by lawmakers, but they are primarily crafted by a governor-appointed body known as the Natural Resources Commission, which receives policy recommendations from the DNR. Bourgeois said that, when a new regulation is put in place that hunters and anglers don’t like, conservation officers get the brunt of it “because they see us first. So they take their anger out on us. And it stinks.” But plenty of interactions are perfectly civil — if not jovial. Back in the St. Clair Flats State Wildlife Area, a father and daughter pulled up in a boat with their dog. “Any luck today?” Bourgeois asked. “Yeah, we got a couple,” responded Lindsay McDonald, 33, of Kimball Township. They killed a goose, a couple of black coots and a mallard, with its metallic emerald neck and head. While the dog, Lola, came ashore and shook off, Bourgeois checked the hunters’ licenses and their guns. They were all clear. “Thank you guys,” Bourgeois said. “Have a great year. Happy Thanksgiving!” “You, too,” the father and daughter responded.

articles.title: How will data centers impact Michigan’s renewable energy goals? It’s complicated, new research says
articles.description: As data center proposals pop up across Michigan, concerns about the amount of energy and water used by hyperscale facilities across the country has been at the forefront of arguments against the projects. With a facility under construction in Saline Township expected to use 1.4 gigawatts of electricity – roughly equivalent to the power usage […]
articles.content: DTE Monroe power plant (Photo by Susan J. Demas/Michigan Advance)As data center proposals pop up across Michigan, concerns about the amount of energy and water used by hyperscale facilities across the country has been at the forefront of arguments against the projects. With a facility under construction in Saline Township expected to use 1.4 gigawatts of electricity – roughly equivalent to the power usage of 1.2 million Michigan homes – and another in Van Buren Township expected to demand 1 gigawatt from the grid, environmental advocates have raised concerns over how the electricity demand from facilities like these will impact Michigan’s clean energy goals. In 2023, the Democratic-led Michigan Legislature passed a series of clean energy bills, including legislation requiring Michigan energy companies to supply power from a portfolio of 100% clean energy resources – which can include nuclear energy and natural gas facilities using 90% effective carbon capture and storage technology – by 2040. Along with the clean energy standard, the law also requires energy companies to secure 60% of their power from renewable sources including solar, wind, geothermal energy and the movement of water by 2035. GET THE MORNING HEADLINES. SUBSCRIBE While the law has benchmark requirements for energy providers to build up their portfolio of renewable energy resources, organizations such as the Michigan Environmental Council have argued that increased energy demand from data centers could extend the lifespan of fossil fuel plants, and incentivize companies to build additional gas plants. In a recent research brief, the nonpartisan Citizens Research Council of Michigan examined how data centers could impact the state’s efforts to meet that 60% renewable energy standard within the next nine years. Currently, only about 13% of Michigan’s electricity is generated from renewable energy sources, the report notes. The state is also facing separate challenges in building up its renewable resources, including ongoing legal challenges to the law around renewable energy siting, expiring tax credits from the federal Inflation Reduction Act, the growing cost of energy generation and the difficulties connecting energy resources to the grid. The brief also noted that Michigan’s clean energy law was crafted in 2023, meaning policymakers hadn’t considered the possibility of rapid growth in electricity demand from hyperscale data centers when setting these goals. It also points to comments from the Data Center Coalition, an industry group, acknowledging that increased electricity demand from data centers “may challenge the utility’s ability to procure or develop sufficient clean energy sources, implicating statutory or regulatory clean energy and emissions reductions targets.” Construction underway on Related Digital’s hyperscale data center in Saline Township, Michigan. June 20, 2026. | Photo by Jon King/Michigan Advance Data center tax breaks come with a clean energy requirement When Michigan lawmakers penned the bills creating the sales and use tax exemption for data centers, they included requirements for data center developers to procure 90% clean energy. However the brief explains that the law does not specify how data centers would demonstrate this, leaving certification of the clean energy requirement to the Michigan Strategic Fund. Under the fund’s guidelines, a data center can meet the clean energy requirement by contracting with an electric utility that is “actively pursuing compliance” with Michigan’s clean energy law. If the utility does not comply, the data center does not lose certification for the tax credit, the brief explains, noting that this effectively makes the 90% clean energy requirement a non-factor in meeting the requirements for a tax exemption. Considering the difficulty that new data center energy loads will impose on the utilities, the Citizens Research Council said that could prompt utilities to delay complying with the state’s clean and renewable energy requirements, through the law’s “off-ramp” provision. Given that two utilities – DTE Energy and Consumers Energy – supply 90% of Michigan’s electricity, the Citizens Research Council examined each company’s plans for meeting the state’s renewable energy requirements. Consumers Energy is already supplying power to a hyperscale data center, which the council defines as a facility using more than 100 megawatts at peak demand. Additional data center contracts are pending local approval. In its most recent integrated resource plan, Consumers Energy acknowledged it must accommodate an additional 2,000 megawatts of electricity demand that it had not anticipated in its 2021 plan. It must do so while replacing 3,000 megawatts of fossil fuel generation as it retires the J.H. Campbell coal plant in Ottawa County and winds down operations at the Dan E. Karn Generating Plant in Bay County by 2031. Consumers Energy has said closing the J.H. Campbell plant was expected to save Michigan ratepayers $600 million by 2040. (Photo/Sarah Leach) To meet that demand, Consumers plans to add 3,000 megawatts of solar energy generation and 1,200 megawatts of wind by 2031, continuing at a similar pace through 2041. The company expects to bring 17,500 megawatts of renewable energy online over the next 15 years, which its analysts say will allow it to meet the state’s clean and renewable energy benchmarks. DTE Energy, meanwhile, is contracted to provide power to both the Saline Township and Van Buren Township data centers. The Saline Township project includes an agreement for the data center to fund 1.4 gigawatts of 4-hour battery storage capacity, which would be owned by DTE. While battery storage is complementary to renewable energy use, the council notes that the batteries do not generate renewable energy. In order to meet the state’s renewable energy portfolio standards while supplying power to the Saline Township data center, the council’s brief says DTE will need to bring more renewable energy resources online than previously planned. As for the Van Buren Township project, Google, which is developing the data center, plans to ensure 40% of the power it receives will be generated by renewables. Google will also be funding 480 megawatts of energy storage and 1.6 gigawatts of renewable generation capacity, although the report said the renewable energy credits created by these sources will not be available to DTE. In order to serve the Google data center and maintain compliance with the state’s renewable portfolio requirements, DTE estimates that it will need to increase its long-term renewable energy target by 10.8%, which will be funded by a surcharge on Google’s bill. According to the company, the Google data center will be funding 40% more renewable energy than it uses In its briefing, the council noted that funding for renewable energy and battery storage from these two data centers is critical to DTE’s recently proposed Integrated Resource Plan. While these agreements will help bring more renewables online, the Citizens Research Council said these data centers will also bring substantial, unanticipated energy load growth, creating a challenge for DTE to provide enough power for these energy loads while it works to retire 3 gigawatts of coal by 2032. However, DTE expects to meet this challenge while complying with the state’s renewable portfolio requirements by building roughly 15 gigawatts of renewable generation, 4.5 gigawatts of battery storage, and two new natural gas plants for peak energy demand with a combined generation capacity of 2.1 gigawatts. Wind turbine in mid-Michigan, Feb. 7, 2023 | Laina G. Stebbins Data centers bring both opportunities and risks for renewable energy While the two utilities have provided plans to meet Michigan’s renewable energy requirements while supplying power to data centers, the Citizens Research Council does acknowledge concerns from environmental advocates that these companies would not need to develop a combined 3.5 gigawatts of new natural gas generation if they were not serving data centers. Although it is theoretically possible to meet current and future energy demand with renewables alone, the council said that could prove difficult, and could be “unacceptably costly.” It notes that while fossil fuel energy generation can be turned on and off to meet demand, renewable energy is contingent on climate and weather. Power transmission could also present a challenge, the council said, as redistributing energy generation from a few large fossil fuel plants to several smaller renewable sites could require a substantial investment into transmission infrastructure that would ultimately be paid for by energy customers. According to the council, if Consumers and DTE did not plan to build this additional natural gas generation, they would need to build at least 10 gigawatts of additional renewable energy alongside additional battery storage and transmission infrastructure to make that power available where it is needed. “Michigan’s utilities are obligated to meet Michigan’s renewable goals, but they are also obligated to do so without impairing reliability or incurring excessive costs,” the council’s brief stated. Although DTE and Consumers plans appear to meet their regulatory obligations, the council said these plans may not reflect real-world constraints. While together the utilities have planned to build more than 30 gigawatts of solar generation and substantial wind and battery storage, the addition of solar alone would require 150,000 acres of land, or 235 square miles, the brief explains. Identifying suitable land and securing leases from landowners will be difficult, the council states. It also notes that utilities may struggle to obtain project approvals and secure labor and materials at the required pace. While the council set out to determine whether data centers would make it more or less difficult for Michigan to meet its 60% renewable energy standard, its final conclusion is complicated. In the short term, the additional electricity demand from data centers will make it more difficult for Michigan utilities to meet the state’s renewable energy requirements by 2035, the council found. The projects will require a rapid expansion of renewable generation, while potentially increasing the reliance on natural gas. Over the longer term, however, the data centers could help utilities meet those requirements by funding new renewable energy generation and battery storage. Contracts that allow data centers to reduce their electricity consumption during periods of high demand could also ease pressure on utilities. However, the council cautioned that utilities may nevertheless need to delay compliance with the state’s renewable energy targets. 10:44 amThis story was corrected to reflect that the council's brief referred to DTE, not Google, as needing to bring additional resources to bear on the Saline Township data center.

articles.title: Has vibe coding made open source the new normal for synths?
articles.description: The emergence of powerful vibe-coding agents and tools like Reverse Engineer Anything has caused chaos in the music gear world, leaving companies scrambling to figure out how to respond. While some, like Roland, have remained silent for now, others have embraced the modding community. In the last several weeks, as it's become clear that no piece of music gear is safe from Claude and a subreddit full of curious tinker
articles.content: The emergence of powerful vibe-coding agents and tools like Reverse Engineer Anything has caused chaos in the music gear world, leaving companies scrambling to figure out how to respond. While some, like Roland, have remained silent for now, others have embraced the modding community. In the last several weeks, as it’s become clear that no piece of music gear is safe from Claude and a subreddit full of curious tinkerers, companies have begun making more and more of their devices open source. The biggest name to decide “if you can’t beat ’em, join ’em” is inMusic, the parent company of Akai, Moog, Native Instruments, and more. “We’re going to provide a toolbox to the community, we’re going to provide the inner workings of, say, an MPC or Sample so that people can do what they want,” inMusic CEO Jack O’Donnell tells The Verge. That includes a recently launched SDK and several open-source devices, including the recently teased MPC Sample Key. Akai is trying to walk a fine line, offering modders access while keeping its products reliable for professionals. O’Donnell says the company will “try to give them a reset button” so “they can experiment with it, and then not lose what they have.” Behringer has also rushed to cash in, announcing a slew of open-source devices. In just a matter of weeks, it announced a $150 clone of the MPC One called Kick, a clone of the E-mu SP-1200, the Anima DJ controller, the Ignite sequencer, and the Polykeys 61 MIDI controller, all of which are open source. It’s unclear when any of these products might launch. M-Vave’s FM-1 helped kick-start the whole movement. The $70 pocketable clone of the iconic Yamaha DX7 became the synth of the summer not just because of its dirt-cheap price and faithfully re-created ’80s tones, but because it also turned out to be infinitely hackable. There are well over a dozen different custom firmwares for the FM-1. M-Vave responded by releasing an open-source firmware with more features for developers to build on. The company also confirmed that a successor, the FM-2, is in development and will be open source as well. Other companies have also embraced the modding community. Erica Synths recently released the source code for its LXR-02 drum machine, but founder Ģirts Ozoliņš isn’t necessarily fully on board with vibe coding. “Inventions succeed if they solve some fundamental problems, right?” he tells The Verge. “So, I’m still wondering what fundamental problem vibe coding solves.” While he can’t imagine a producer simply stacking his studio with a bunch of hacked FM-1s running various synth engines, he’s curious to see what the community cooks up for the LXR. And he does see a benefit in making music tech a little less disposable. “What I like on the upside of this is that there is some trace of sustainability. Instead of buying five or 10 plastic boxes, you can try options on one,” he says, though he’s under no illusions about the environmental impact of vibe coding. “Of course it by far does not offset data center impact on the planet and on ecology and stuff like that.” Polyend has also gotten on board, open-sourcing its line of Tracker grooveboxes. The Polish company’s decision to open its arms to vibe coders isn’t too much of a surprise. Last year it released the Endless guitar pedal, which lets users vibe-code their own effects. Opening its other instruments to AI tinkering feels like a natural extension. Elektron is less thrilled about the emergence of vibe-coded mods. The company banned links to custom firmware from its official forums, saying, “We would always warn against modifications to our firmware and/or machines that could brick them (potentially rendering them unusable), prevent future updates, affect warranty coverage.” Elektron’s CPO Christian Alsing told YouTuber EZBOT that he was sympathetic to the hacker community and that the company has roots there with its first instrument, the Sidstation (based on the iconic SID sound chip from the Commodore 64). He also said that he believes users have a right to modify their devices as they see fit. But he pushed back on the idea that Elektron is “withholding features,” an accusation that Akai also faced. Ģirts also defended Elektron, saying, “people tend to blame the company, saying they are hiding features ... you design an instrument, you have a specific concept in mind, and you cannot foresee millions of possibilities ... it’s not about hiding features; it’s more about having an idea of how an instrument should look and work.” Other major music manufacturers, like Roland, Korg, Arturia, and Novation – all of whom did not comment for this story – have yet to issue any public statements about the explosion of AI-aided custom firmwares.

articles.title: Trump to meet Abdul El-Sayed: Will he agree to a renamed Medicare-for-all?
articles.content: After offer to rename policy ‘TrumpCare’, US president calls Democratic victor ‘a smart guy’ weeks after a bitter Senate race in Michigan. United States President Donald Trump says he will meet Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed to discuss the Democrat’s push for a single, low-cost government health insurance programme, which El-Sayed has suggested renaming “Trumpcare”. One month ago, Trump was using anti-Muslim rhetoric against El-Sayed during his race against Republican Mike Rogers in Michigan. But on Tuesday, the US president appeared to have changed his tune. During a 45-minute interview in the Oval Office, he told the New York Post, “He’s a smart guy,” as he answered questions about El-Sayed’s offer to rename “Medicare for All” as “Trumpcare”. “He did a good job. He actually did a very good job,” the president said. “I know I’ll be meeting with him,” he added. “Maybe there’s some place in the middle that we could go.” He did not give a date for the meeting. Since the Republicans’ crushing defeat in the November 3 midterm elections, in which they lost their majorities in the US Senate and the House of Representatives, Trump has already indicated that he plans to make liberal use of his presidential veto to block “insane” Democratic policies. However, he has also suggested that he may be open to negotiations, telling Fox News that he would “veto, veto, veto” but the Democrats would eventually call him hoping to do a deal. “Congratulations to the Democrats. They did a good job,” Trump said. “I congratulate them and look forward to working with them for the good of our country.” In the New York Post interview, Trump praised El-Sayed’s idea of putting his name on the healthcare programme as “very smart”. He also said he and Democrats could work together on healthcare but “Obamacare hasn’t worked”. Obamacare was an overhaul of the individual health insurance market under former President Barack Obama that had slowed increases in insurance costs and halved the number of uninsured Americans. Trump added: “I’m just going to veto everything there is, and then at some point, I think they’re going to want to negotiate.” El-Sayed first floated the idea of renaming the proposed healthcare plan on November 6 in an interview with Zeteo editor-in-chief Mehdi Hasan. “If he wants to pass Trumpcare for all, I’m OK with it. He seems to like to put his name on things,” El-Sayed said. On November 12, he posted a mock-up of a gold “TrumpCare” insurance card bearing the president’s signature on X. “Donald, this is on the table,” he wrote. “Guarantee healthcare for every American, from cradle to grave.” In a video posted on November 17, El-Sayed addressed the president as “habibi”, an Arabic term of affection. “Trumpcare for all. It’s really popular. People really want healthcare,” he said. “You can put your name all over it.” The White House was initially dismissive. Spokesperson Allison Schuster called the proposal “Medicare for none” and described it as a socialist government takeover of healthcare. But on Saturday, Trump reshared El-Sayed’s post on his Truth Social platform without comment. NBC News later reported that Vice President JD Vance’s office had contacted El-Sayed’s team to set up a meeting. On the NBC TV network’s Meet the Press programme the next day, El-Sayed called the plan “the ultimate Trump card”. He said he did not care what it was called as long as universal healthcare coverage passed. In a post on Monday, he wrote: “The point of winning elections is to do something good with the seat.” The warmth displayed by the president is a reversal of his previous approach to El-Sayed. During the election campaign, Trump repeatedly questioned El-Sayed’s loyalty to the US and tried to tie him to the Muslim Brotherhood. At an October 25 rally in Port Huron, Michigan, Trump said he was there “to keep a jihadist Muslim Brotherhood member from becoming a United States senator”. There is no evidence that El-Sayed has any affiliation with the group, and he has denied any. Democrats denounced the attacks as targeting El-Sayed’s faith and his Egyptian heritage. Vance told a rally in August that there was “something about Abdul El-Sayed that is very, very evil”. El-Sayed, a physician and former head of Detroit’s Health Department, hit back throughout the campaign and at one point called Trump an “unserious fool”. He defeated Rogers to become the first Muslim member of the US Senate. While most other wealthy countries have built universal health systems paid for from taxes, the US has relied largely on voluntary private insurance, leaving a substantial share of the population without coverage. Despite decades of calls for national public insurance, it was not until 1965 that Washington created its two main public programmes: Medicare for people aged 65 and older, and Medicaid for people on low incomes. Medicare, which also covers some younger people with disabilities, now serves nearly 70 million people. Most Americans under 65 with health insurance rely on a patchwork of employer-provided insurance; private plans bought through the Obamacare, or Affordable Care Act, marketplaces; and Medicaid. According to the US Census Bureau, 26.7 million people, or 7.9 percent of the population, were uninsured for all of 2025. The Affordable Care Act, passed in 2010, made almost all lawfully present residents eligible for more affordable coverage than they had before. But taking it up remains largely voluntary, and millions still go without insurance, often citing cost as the barrier. The US insurance model has proved expensive for the nation as a whole. The US spends more on healthcare than any other country in the world, and the gaps in coverage have deepened over five decades. In 1970, it spent about 7 percent of its gross domestic product (GDP) on healthcare, roughly in line with comparably wealthy countries, which averaged about 5 percent. By 2024, the latest government data available, that figure had risen to 18 percent of GDP. Per person, the US spent an average of $14,775 on healthcare in 2024, compared to an average of $7,860 in comparably wealthy countries, according to Peterson-KFF. Medicare for All is a policy proposal that would extend government insurance to every resident, not just those over 65, with disabilities or with low incomes. The main bill on the table is Senator Bernie Sanders’s Medicare for All Act. It would replace most private insurance with a single public plan with no premiums, deductibles or copayments. Sanders has called on Democrats to start by reducing the Medicare eligibility age from 65 to 55. Polling has traditionally been mixed but may now be rising. Pre-election polling by KFF, a nonpartisan health policy research organisation, suggested support for Medicare for All was 66 percent. Mollyann Brodie, who leads KFF’s polling, called it “the highest level of support … we’ve ever found”. El-Sayed wants one public plan to cover every American “from cradle to grave”. In a book he cowrote, he described this as “an enhanced version of the traditional Medicare program that tens of millions of seniors rely on today”. Doctor visits, prescription drugs and emergency care would be covered, and patients could see any participating provider without out-of-network charges. Coverage would also no longer depend on a job or family circumstances. “Turn 26, get a job, lose a job, get married, get divorced: None of these would cost you your health insurance under Medicare for All,” he said in testimony to the Senate in 2022. In the November 3 midterms, Democrats flipped nine Republican-held Senate seats and won a 56-44 majority, including two independents who caucus with them. They also won a majority in the House – raising the number of their seats from 214 to 258. When the new Congress meets in January, it will be able to pass legislation without having to find Republican votes in the House and, on some measures, in the Senate. But Trump may veto any bill. Overriding a presidential veto requires a two-thirds majority in both chambers: 67 senators and, with all seats filled, 290 House members. Democrats are 11 votes short in the Senate alone, so an override would need a significant number of Republicans to break with the president, which is unlikely to happen. Trump has signalled he will use the veto freely. A day before the midterms, he pledged to become “Mr Veto” if Democrats took control of Congress. The easier route then is for Trump not to veto legislation. That is the bet El-Sayed is making: that Trump, ever the politician, might sign a popular bill if he gets the credit for it. Analysts doubt the talks will deliver the system El-Sayed wants, but they see room for a deal of some kind. “I do not think it will lead to anything like the single payer system El-Sayed favours,” Ian Lesser, a senior fellow at the Policy Center for the New South, told Al Jazeera. “But as with Mayor [Zohran] Mamdani in New York, they may have a strangely positive relationship.” In November last year, Trump heaped praise on then-mayor-elect Mamdani after the two held surprisingly cordial talks in the White House. That too was an about-turn from Trump, who, during the mayoral election campaign, had caricatured Mamdani as an anti-Semitic communist and threatened to strip him of his US citizenship while Mamdani called Trump a “despot” in his election victory speech. Lesser said the El-Sayed exchange followed “very much the same pattern we saw with Mayor Mamdani: curiosity and the president’s focus on personalities above all”. “The president could be inclined toward some new health reforms if he can put his own stamp on them,” Lesser added. Scott Lucas, professor of international politics at the Clinton Institute at University College Dublin, said a meeting with El-Sayed would be part of an effort by Trump to salvage his legacy after the midterms defeat. “He wants the good photo ops,” Lucas told Al Jazeera. “He’s going to have to try to do some photo ops that aren’t just simply his standard insult, trashing people, … because clearly voters rejected that type of politics earlier this month.” Lucas said El-Sayed’s victory had also forced a rethink. “They threw everything at him – not just the state Republicans in Michigan but the national Republicans in the Trump camp – and he still won,” he said. “Trump or those around him have to realise that the proposal to do something about healthcare resonated with voters.” Trump, 80, enters the last two years of his presidency after elections that are widely seen as a rebuke of his administration and Republican Party. His second term has been marked by an unpopular war with Iran, rising living costs and cuts to public health coverage. “I think what has happened now with the midterms is that that was shown up abroad because they couldn’t win in Iran. They couldn’t win in Greenland. They did win in Venezuela. But he’s been shown up as a bit of a paper tiger beyond that, and now he’s being shown up as a bit of a paper tiger at home,” Lucas said. A major healthcare law with his name on it could give Trump a signature domestic achievement. However, his record points the other way. In 2018, he dismissed the idea as “Medicare for none”, and as recently as August, he said Medicare for All “doesn’t work”. Lucas said he does not expect Trump to sign off on El-Sayed’s plan “at this point”. “Trump doesn’t understand the details,” he said. The real question, he said, was whether officials around the president and Republicans who will be in the minority from January would make it a priority. For now, he said, the gesture “doesn’t cost Trump anything” because Medicare for All would first have to win over Democrats. The US healthcare system is “extremely complex, it’s extremely tangled” and replacing it with universal national health insurance is “not simple at all”. Lucas said a better test of whether Trump is serious would be whether Republicans agree to restore the expired Affordable Care A

Courtesy of Bedrock.The Detroit City Council voted 7-2 on Tuesday afternoon to OK the redevelopment plan for the Renaissance Center and a portion of the city’s riverfront. The $2.2 billion project would demolish two Renaissance Center towers to make way for new housing and a riverfront park. The developers, Bedrock and General Motors, had requested $548 million in tax subsidies for the project.
