articles.title: AI may soon change what it means to be a theoretical physicist
articles.description: Frontier AI is already solving problems that once took top physicists a full day.
articles.content: About six months ago, Suvrat Raju, a professor of theoretical physics at the International Centre for Theoretical Sciences in Bengaluru, India, asked a frontier AI model to solve a physics problem. He didn’t ask because he needed to know the answer. He had actually solved this particular problem already. But he had never published the solution—which made it a perfect question to test how good AI was at physics. LLMs have been trained on the whole Internet, so if a physics problem has been discussed online, it’s likely the model already knows about it and may have memorized the answer. So a fair test of AI capabilities needs to focus on problems that have never appeared online. The model didn’t answer Raju’s problem correctly, but it did better than he expected—well, enough to get him thinking that the experiment should be repeated and formalized. With the help of a colleague, he set out to create a theoretical physics benchmark for AI.Read full article Comments

articles.title: What is GraphRAG? A practical guide to smarter AI retrieval
articles.description: Learn what is GraphRAG, how knowledge graph RAG works, and where it beats standard RAG. See use cases and how ElevenAgents handles RAG for voice agents.
articles.content: Introducing Eleven v4Meet Eleven v4, our most emotive model yet. Generative AI responses sound helpful until you ask a complex question like “I’ve canceled my purchase, why have I not received a refund?” Answering difficult queries relies on combining information from different databases. That’s where GraphRAG comes in. GraphRAG is a technique that allows AI models to provide accurate, helpful, and consistent answers for complex questions beyond their foundational training data. Organizations use GraphRAG to support genAI applications that require contextual relevance across multiple subtopics. This guide explores what is GraphRAG, how GraphRAG works, common use cases, performance against RAG, and applications of knowledge graphs in AI. GraphRAG, which stands for Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation, is a retrieval technique that uses graph-like structures to improve a generative AI system’s response. GraphRAG helps address LLMs’ inference constraints that rely solely on learned knowledge. It also improves upon a baseline RAG’s semantic search approach, which retrieves information in isolation. You can think of GraphRAG as a student who pieces together relevant information from pages in different chapters of a book before attempting to answer a question. Generative AI models may not always provide relevant answers to queries that require complex reasoning and connections between entities. For example, if a customer asks an AI model, “I upgraded my subscription last week. Why was I charged twice, and why am I still on my old plan?”, the model can’t provide detailed, factual answers on its own. By using graph data consisting of entities and their relationships, a GraphRAG-powered system can better understand the query's context, thereby retrieving detailed information that is highly relevant for answer generation. Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) allows an LLM to improve its answer and reduce hallucination by accessing relevant data from a vector database. A RAG system typically goes through these stages. Before RAG can process queries, you need to set up a vector database. A vector is a series of numbers that represent the information. A vector database is a specialized storage system that stores numerical representations of information. The vector database stores closely related information close together, and the AI model connects to it. Common RAG knowledge bases include product guides, FAQs, and business policies. To meet model limits, the RAG system first splits internal data into smaller chunks. It then uses a process called embedding to convert each chunk into a vector and stores it in the vector database. RAG uses semantic search to retrieve information from the vector database. When the AI model receives a query, the RAG system converts it into vectors. Then, the RAG system searches the vector database and retrieves embeddings with similar numerical representations. This way, it retrieves only information highly relevant to the query. Next, the RAG system combines the original query with content retrieved from the vector database and sends it to the LLM. If needed, RAG rewrites the prompt to optimize the LLM's response. Finally, using the additional context RAG provides, the LLM generates the answer. The final answer is precise, helpful, and relevant to the query. Learn more in our guide to retrieval-augmented generation. GraphRAG, unlike baseline RAG, uses a knowledge graph as its main structure to retrieve relevant information from internal knowledge bases. Many implementations still use a vector database or vector search to find the first entry point into the graph, but the graph relationships do the heavy lifting. Below is the process that supports GraphRAG retrieval. A knowledge graph connects different entities. An entity is a self-contained object, such as a person, place, or event. Each entity can be related to more than one entity. Let’s take an illustrative payment dispute scenario (a hypothetical example, not a real customer case). A knowledge graph that helps GraphRAG investigate the root cause requires several entities, including: A typical GraphRAG implementation creates clusters of different entities segregated by topics. Some GraphRAG implementations group clusters into communities. These communities vary in size and may form a hierarchy. The system then generates summaries describing each community's important entities, relationships, and attributes. LLMs use these summaries to understand the distributed entities when running a GraphRAG search. When the AI system receives a query, it extracts the entities and uses them to search the knowledge graph. Graph data search can happen in several ways. The system might search depth-first or breadth-first to find the initial nodes. Or it may use simpler vector search to find the starting node. Then it traces adjacent nodes to find linked entities. For example, in this illustrative scenario, a support agent asks, “Why was this customer charged twice, and why are they still on their old plan?” To answer, GraphRAG traces the customer account and retrieves connected subscription records, invoices, payment transactions, and CRM events. By following the graph, the system discovers a CRM synchronization error that stopped the subscription upgrade from being recorded. Depending on the GraphRAG system, the traversal algorithm may return other related entities that connect to the primary entities in the original query as additional context. After retrieving connected entities from the knowledge graph, the GraphRAG system prunes the result to remove redundant entities. Then, it augments the original user query with the remaining entities to generate an AI answer. Using the same illustrative billing dispute example, the AI system replies, “The customer was charged twice because a CRM synchronization error prevented the plan upgrade from being recorded. As a result, the customer is still on the old plan.” Knowledge graphs help AI systems provide accurate responses by serving as domain-specific ground truth. A knowledge graph represents entities as nodes, and relationships between them as edges. By traversing interconnected nodes, AI systems can improve their reasoning capabilities, which can reduce hallucination, especially for complex queries. Even before generative AI became publicly available, tech companies already used knowledge graphs at scale. For example, Google uses knowledge graphs to return more relevant search results. By surfacing contextually relevant nodes, it can differentiate Apple as a brand vs. a fruit. Now, knowledge graphs help AI systems interpret contextually dense relationships between entities. In other words, knowledge graphs can help keep different AI systems aligned. As organizations build, deploy, and integrate AI at scale, a shared understanding is more important than ever. Many enterprise applications benefit from GraphRAG’s relationship traversal capabilities. Instead of searching disparate databases separately, GraphRAG offers an effective mechanism for relationship-heavy retrieval that grounds answers in domain-specific context. GraphRAG excels at retrievals that involve multi-hop reasoning (answering a question by following several linked pieces of information, such as customer, subscription, then invoice) and relationship-heavy questions spanning multiple topics. Meanwhile, a baseline RAG suits simple, straightforward information lookup. For example, if you’re building a knowledge base management system that answers questions like “If feature A failed, what other processes are affected?”, GraphRAG can outperform RAG’s vector search. However, setting up GraphRAG is complex, as you need to build an entire knowledge graph that accurately represents entities relevant to your product, services, or business. Therefore, for simpler searches like “What is the refund policy?”, a standard RAG is more than sufficient. Because RAG search has a direct search path, it’s generally faster for a single-hop query. RAG remains important for grounding AI responses with proprietary data an AI model wasn’t trained on. RAG was created to overcome LLMs’ limitations in responding beyond their learned knowledge. Even as LLMs’ context windows have increased, enabling users to provide more information, RAG is far from obsolete. Instead, RAG has evolved from a simple document repository into more sophisticated retrieval approaches like GraphRAG, which can handle relationship-heavy questions that basic vector search struggles with. ElevenAgents supports retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) that allows voice agents to retrieve supporting information from your documents. You index each knowledge base document for RAG, then enable RAG on the agent from the ElevenAgents dashboard or through the API. ElevenAgents RAG uses semantic vector search over your documents. Depending on the configuration, the agent can retrieve information on every turn, or on demand when it decides it needs more context, to deliver more accurate responses. To ensure low-latency responses, we’ve optimized our RAG retrieval architecture for real-time conversations, effectively reducing median latency from 326ms to 155ms, mainly by racing several query-rewriting models in parallel and using the first valid response.* This keeps voice agents natural and responsive while providing answers augmented by internal data. Get started with ElevenAgents today and learn how to set up RAG for your voice agents or contact sales for more information. *Based on internal benchmarking of ElevenAgents RAG retrieval architecture. Results may vary by configuration and use case. RAG is a technique that allows AI models to use external resources when answering questions. RAG helps reduce AI hallucinations by augmenting the original prompt with knowledge it doesn’t have, such as company policy, product features, and pricing guides. Graph retrieval-augmented generation (GraphRAG, also sometimes written as graph RAG) is a retrieval technique that uses graph-traversal algorithms to improve AI responses. GraphRAG retrieves connected entities from a knowledge graph, allowing AI systems to provide relevant, helpful, and accurate answers to complex, multi-hop queries. AI systems use knowledge graphs as a shared source of truth to reduce hallucinations and generate helpful answers. Common use cases include recommendation systems, customer support agents, enterprise knowledge management, and compliance audits. articles.title: Fixing the front door to government, one voice agent at a time
articles.description: The front door to government for millions of people is an outdated IVR phone menu. Governments are now adopting AI agents for several kinds of calls.
articles.content: Introducing Eleven v4Meet Eleven v4, our most emotive model yet. Call almost any government agency and you know what's coming: a robotic voice, a confusing menu, and a reminder that your call is important. You press 2, then 4, then 0 because none of the options quite fit. Then you wait. If you can't stay on hold through your lunch break, you hang up and try again tomorrow. Some people never call back, and they go without the benefit, permit, or answer they needed. According to the US Inspector General, in 2025, 25 million calls to the Social Security Administration’s number ended without service. People hung up, missed the callback, or couldn’t be reached. In January 2025, Social Security’s average hold times peaked at 1 hour 40 minutes. Service did improve by the end of the year, and the Inspector General credited a new phone platform and more automation for much of that. Automation alone isn't the answer, though. At the IRS, the phone is still the main way taxpayers reach out, and in 2025 the agency began routing nearly 8 million calls to voice bots. According to the National Taxpayer Advocate's 2025 report to Congress, the bots answered only 29% of those calls. The other 71% were disconnected or abandoned, most likely because callers wanted to talk to a person. A scripted bot that can't understand people or finish the job just adds one more way for a call to fail. This broken interaction is the front door to the government for millions of people. At ElevenLabs, we're working to fix that front door with voice agents that understand what callers need and can actually get it done. Governments are already using voice agents for several kinds of calls. The first job is replacing the outdated automated IVR phone menu. A voice agent can understand the question, answer it, or send the caller to the right department the first time. Think of a city's 311 line: an agent can handle routine questions and triage the rest, so staff can spend their time on calls that need human judgment. It can also answer in the caller's language and after hours, providing service to people who may need it the most. In Ukraine, the Ministry of Economy's voice agent, built on ElevenAgents, answers the State Employment Service hotline 24/7 and hands calls to a person when needed. In its first 80 days it handled 2,698 calls, about a quarter of the line's volume, and cut the time to answer from 30–40 seconds to 18. When air raid alerts sent operators to shelters, the agent kept the line open. Callers want to check where an application or refund stands, book or move an appointment, or update their information. These are among the most common reasons people call. The agent can’t handle them by talking alone: it has to verify who it's talking to and connect to the agency's systems. With that access, it can resolve the request instead of just passing it along. In Poland, ElevenLabs powers the voice agent for Centralna e-Rejestracja, the central appointment system in the national e-Health platform. It calls patients who only have a landline to remind them of appointments and reschedule when they need to. With 40 million appointments a year and no-show rates of 10–20%, even a modest reduction in missed appointments can meaningfully improve access to care across Poland. In partnership with Brazil’s National Electoral Court (TSE), we gave a voice to its Electoral Assistant, making election information more accessible to citizens. We also used our No Go Voices technology to protect the voices of several senior political figures, including presidential candidates, and Supreme Court justices, and blocked nearly 2,000 impersonation attempts. A voice agent can walk someone through a multi-step benefits or permit application, collect what's needed along the way, and hand it off to a caseworker when judgment is required. In Deloitte's 2026 Digital Citizen Survey of 1,000 Americans, 55% said they expect AI to improve public services, and 48% named step-by-step guidance when applying for government services as an important need. In India, we recently signed a partnership with the state of Karnataka. We're working with the state's technology agency to explore voice AI pilots, starting with grievance redressal, public helplines, and entitlement schemes, in Kannada and other Indian languages among the 14 we support across the country. Language. According to the Government Accountability Office, 26 million people in the U.S. have limited ability to read, speak, write, or understand English. A menu with two or three language options leaves many of them out, and translation is expensive: the National Weather Service spent about $2.7 million between 2022 and 2025 to bring AI translation to five languages. ElevenLabs’ latest voice models support more than 90 languages, which puts language access within reach for more agencies. Connectivity. Not everyone can just go online. The FCC's 2026 broadband report found about 10.5 million Americans still can't get high-speed home internet over a wired or fixed wireless connection, and more than 9 million of them live in rural areas. Pew Research finds that one in five rural adults relies on a smartphone with no home broadband. For them, a phone call is the front door, and in an emergency it may be the only one. 24/7 availability. Most government phone lines are staffed during business hours, and many people with jobs, kids, or shift work can't call then. A voice agent picks up at 2 am on a Sunday with the same patience it has at 10 am on a Tuesday. Government phone lines are already stretched. Soon, many of the calls won't come from people. Gartner predicts that by the end of 2030, more than 10 billion autonomous AI agents will clog public services by the end of 2030, finding benefits, checking eligibility, and filing claims on their users’ behalf. Government agencies are already seeing a sharp rise in inquiries to government agencies’ support sites. Some of those agents will belong to scammers. The IRS's 2026 Dirty Dozen list of tax scams includes AI-enabled impersonation calls that use voice mimicry and spoofed caller ID. The Inspector General lists audio deepfakes among the ways AI can be exploited to commit benefits fraud. Every automated call that ties up a line means a longer wait for a real person, and agencies can't deflect that volume forever. They'll need AI of their own to serve legitimate agents efficiently, catch fraudulent ones, and keep the line open for the people who need it. Fixing the front door also means securing it. The front door is where we start, but we think AI can help rebuild the whole house. Government services are fragmented because they are organized around agencies rather than people's lives. For example, starting a small business means dealing with at least three different agencies. Some governments are already bringing services under one roof. Greece's single digital portal, gov.gr, now offers more than 2,200 services. In May 2026, we signed a partnership with the Greek government to explore bringing voice AI to its call centers and to gov.gr, so citizens can reach those services in any language. That includes the Greek diaspora and people who find the internet hard to use. In the U.S., the federal government launched America.gov in September 2026, an AI-powered portal that draws on more than 29,000 federal websites. For now, it answers questions in text; applying, enrolling, and tracking progress are planned for 2027. Now imagine that same front door with a voice. You pick up the phone, explain what you need in your own language, and get routed to the right part of government. Behind the scenes, agents across agencies talk to each other and resolve the issue, while you stay on one call. Public trust depends on how this is done. Governments need voice agents that: For most people, the phone line is where they meet their government. For too long, that has meant ineffective menus and hold music. It can be a conversation instead, in the caller's language, at any hour, on any phone. We're starting with the front door, and we don't plan to stop there. He focuses on government affairs, government and civil society partnerships, and policy development. Before ElevenLabs, he worked with OpenAI, Meta, and WhatsApp in a variety of policy and partnerships roles. articles.title: The Invisible Toll: New Study Calls for Timely, Predictable Funding to Protect Kenya’s Children
articles.content: The Government of Kenya launches The Invisible Toll: Rising Debt, Shrinking Aid and Kenya’s Children, alongside the Annual Public Debt Management Report 2025/26 Nairobi, 25 November 2026 – Today, the National Treasury and the State Department for Children Services, in partnership with UNICEF, launched The Invisible Toll: Rising Debt, Shrinking Aid and Kenya’s Children, that shows how rising debt, shrinking aid and economic pressures can delay or disrupt crucial services for children. The study recommends timely release of funds, a guaranteed minimum level of spending on children and stronger oversight to keep those services on track. The report was launched alongside the Annual Public Debt Management Report 2025/26. The study examines health and social protection, tracing public money from borrowing and revenue decisions, through cash releases and budget execution, to health facilities and households. It finds that budgets protect children when funds are released on time and spent as planned. According to the report, debt service absorbed more than half of ordinary revenue in the 2024/25 Financial Year. Net official development assistance fell from nearly USD 4.0 billion in 2020 to about USD 2.6 billion in 2023, while tax revenue stood at around 14–15 per cent of Gross Domestic Product. Despite these constraints, the Government now finances about 90 per cent of the health budget from domestic resources and has sustained cash transfers to vulnerable households through the Inua Jamii National Safety Net Programme. “The study and its launch carry forward a message delivered by H.E. President William Samoei Ruto on 22 September 2026 at the UNICEF High-Level Dialogue on Debt, Development and the Next Generation in New York: that debt is not only an economic issue, but also a development, equity and children’s issue. Kenya will honour its obligations, and we will protect our children. These are not competing commitments; they are two sides of responsible fiscal management. A budget’s value lies in what reaches the frontline, on time. The National Treasury will strengthen cash management, budget execution and the quality of borrowing, and we will draw on these findings in the 2027 Budget Policy Statement, so that every shilling delivers for Kenya’s children today and for the generations who will inherit our decisions,” said Hon John Mbadi Ng’ongo, Cabinet Secretary, The National Treasury and Economic Planning. The report finds that the impact on children stems less from budget cuts than from the timing of fund releases. In the 2024/25 Financial Year, releases to counties were uneven, with delays, often exceeding six months, reported by more than 70 per cent of sampled health facilities, 68 per cent of pre-primary units and about half of sampled nutrition units. Children make up more than two in five Kenyans, about 22 million, and more than half experienced multidimensional poverty in 2022. Recent gains, including a rise in facility births from 61 to 88 per cent and a fall in stunting from 26 to 18 per cent between 2014 and 2022, face risks: infant immunization coverage declined from 82.7 to 73.3 per cent between 2021 and 2025, only about one in ten children receives a child cash benefit, and the KES 2,000 Inua Jamii transfer has not kept pace with the cost of living. Children in poorer households, arid and semi-arid counties, informal settlements and refugee-hosting areas are most affected by delays. “Children do not sit at the table where fiscal decisions are made, yet they live longest with the consequences. This study brings their interests into those decisions. With predictable releases, reliable social assistance and protected funding for child-critical services, today’s fiscal choices can widen children’s futures rather than narrow them. Together with the National Treasury, county governments and partners, we will take forward child budget tagging and turn this evidence into results for every child, starting with those furthest behind,” said CPA Carren Achieng Ageng’o, Principal Secretary, State Department for Children Services. The study sets out options for the 2027 Budget Policy Statement and the 2027/28 Financial Year budget. It proposes quarterly minimum cash releases for child-critical services at national and county levels, and a costed spending floor for immunization, nutrition, pre-primary and primary education, water and sanitation, child protection and social assistance. It also recommends child budget tagging in the Integrated Financial Management Information System (IFMIS), an annual child budget statement, and timely Cash Transfer for Orphans and Vulnerable Children payments that keep their real value. To support the transition from aid, it calls for costed domestic financing plans and timely clearance of service-related arrears, alongside child-sensitive debt decisions, including stronger project readiness and transparent debt-for-development mechanisms such as debt swaps. “Children experience fiscal policy not as a budget line, but as a vaccine given on time, a meal served, a safe classroom and a cash transfer that arrives when it is needed most. By launching this study alongside its debt report, Kenya is showing real leadership in looking at public debt through the eyes of its children. As part of the UN family, UNICEF is proud to support this nationally owned agenda. Together, let us make the 2027/28 Financial Year budget, one that can be followed, shilling by shilling, all the way to the child. Every child counted. Every shilling tracked. Every service delivered,” said Dr. Shaheen Nilofer, UNICEF Representative to Kenya. Read the full study to learn more: https://www.unicef.org/kenya/reports/invisible-toll The National Treasury and Economic Planning is the Government of Kenya ministry that formulates financial and economic policies and oversees the effective coordination of Government financial operations. Its mandate, derived primarily from the Public Finance Management Act, 2012, covers economic policy management, formulation of the national budget, resource mobilization, public debt management through the Public Debt Management Office, and oversight of national and county government financial management systems. For more information about the National Treasury and its work, visit: www.treasury.go.ke. Follow: X (KeTreasury) and Facebook (The National Treasury and Economic Planning) UNICEF works in some of the world’s toughest places to reach the world’s most disadvantaged children. Across more than 190 countries and territories, we work for every child, everywhere, to build a better world for everyone. For more information about UNICEF and its work for children, visit www.unicef.org. Ahead of Thanksgiving, more Americans struggle to put food on the table
articles.description: KANSAS CITY, Kan. — It doesn’t take long for the line to pile up at Cross-Lines Community Outreach as more people flock to the nonprofit food pantry to help stock their cupboards. As the queue grew at the check-in counter two days before Thanksgiving, Andreas Leal and his wife perused the dwindling meat freezer and […]
articles.content: Andreas Leal and his wife peruse the shelves at the Community Market, a food pantry operated by Cross-Lines Community Outreach in Kansas City, Kansas. Food banks and pantries across the country are experiencing surging demand amid declining federal food assistance and higher grocery prices. (Photo by Kevin Hardy/Stateline)KANSAS CITY, Kan. — It doesn’t take long for the line to pile up at Cross-Lines Community Outreach as more people flock to the nonprofit food pantry to help stock their cupboards. As the queue grew at the check-in counter two days before Thanksgiving, Andreas Leal and his wife perused the dwindling meat freezer and the hodgepodge of donated items on the toiletry shelves. A 75-year-old retiree, Leal said every bit helps when trying to keep up with rising prices. “It’s very expensive,” he said. “Everything is expensive right now.” Leal said his monthly Social Security benefit can’t keep up with rising costs. While the federal program boosted benefits by 2.8% this year, he said he just received notice that his residential property tax bill will jump 30%, costing him some $600. The increases require constant trade-offs. For example, to save on gas, the couple forgoes trips to visit their son who lives about 45 minutes away. Leaders of Cross-Lines Community Outreach say such stories are more and more common. Its Community Market, a food pantry resembling a grocery store, serves about 1,900 families per month — a 35% increase over last year. “Daily, we have to turn people away,” said Executive Director Susila Jones. The market previously aimed to provide a couple pounds of frozen ground beef each month to every family. But those costs are now too high, pushing Cross-Lines to buy ground turkey or chicken — if prices are low enough. People shop at the Community Market, a food pantry operated by Cross-Lines Community Outreach in Kansas City, Kansas.(Photo by Kevin Hardy/Stateline) Cross-Lines serves people across Wyandotte County, one of the most populous counties in Kansas with a poverty rate that exceeds state and national averages. In recent years, the food pantry has become more lenient about its income requirements and welcomed people who seek aid from multiple organizations. “This is not what people want to do and so we really just let people come to us when they need to come to us,” she said. “Because we know even if you are working, if you’ve had steady income, just one paycheck can put you over the edge.” Rising costs of groceries, housing and gas have pushed more people to seek emergency food assistance. At the same time, those charitable organizations are seeing a wave of Americans who have lost access to the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, or SNAP, the nation’s largest food assistance program. About 5.5 million Americans have lost SNAP benefits since last July’s passage of the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, which cut taxes and federal safety net programs. The law changed SNAP eligibility rules, ended certain work requirement exemptions and shifted new costs to states that administer the federal program. More people are expected to lose SNAP aid as the legislation is fully implemented in the coming years. And earlier this month, the Trump administration proposed enrollment rule changes that would cut eligibility for another 6.3 million people. Without congressional action, few experts see much relief ahead, further stressing the nation’s patchwork of churches, food banks and nonprofits laboring to keep people fed. “Unfortunately, it has become a big part of people’s lives because they keep cutting off SNAP benefits,” said Gina Plata-Nino, the SNAP director at the anti-hunger nonprofit Food Research and Action Center. “…And you have these volunteers at food banks trying to do their best, but they are suffering in terms of being able to keep up.” ‘A huge demand’ The line of cars waiting to pick up ingredients for a full Thanksgiving dinner stretched a mile long last week in Detroit’s East Side. The Capuchin Soup Kitchen had to close its line a few hours after opening when it became clear that the annual giveaway would quickly deplete its 500 turkey meal kits. “If we had 750, we still would have to shut the line down,” said Brother Fred Cabras, director of social services at the nearly century-old Catholic nonprofit. “I imagine that whatever number we set, we will probably hit every time because there is a huge demand.” The organization serves about 1,000 hot meals each day across two locations and operates a food pantry for thousands of families. Food pantry visits have been surging in recent years. In 2022, the operation served about 15,000 families. Cabras expects that figure to reach 34,000 to 35,000 by the end of this year. “This is definitely worse than the pandemic,” he said. The surging demand — and food prices — mean the Capuchin Soup Kitchen spent about $20,000 more on the food it bought last month compared with September. But private donations have remained strong. Cabras said the coronavirus pandemic and last year’s unprecedented disruption to SNAP benefits because of the federal government shutdown heightened the public’s awareness and compassion about growing hunger. “People also realize it because they’re spending more money on groceries,” he said. “And they’re like, ‘Well if I have a decent job, and I’m struggling, I can’t even imagine for the folks who are not getting great wages how much they’re struggling.’” Vegetables are available at the Community Market, a food pantry operated by Cross-Lines Community Outreach in Kansas City, Kansas.(Photo by Kevin Hardy/Stateline) While people tend to donate more generously around the holiday season, high prices have also squeezed the budgets of many regular donors to charitable food groups. “Everybody’s struggling. People who were not struggling a year ago are in a different space, just because of the rising costs,” said Courtney Goff, associate director of United Crescent Hill Ministries in Louisville, Kentucky. The nonprofit, supported by local churches, businesses and individuals, serves about 50 people per day at its food pantry. That’s quadruple the amount of people it served last year, Goff said. With federal cuts to food pantry aid and rising prices for consumers, Goff said her organization is purchasing more food on its own and increasingly asking the community for cash and food donations. Still, the food disappears nearly as quickly as it’s stocked because so many people are struggling to afford the basics. “You have people who maybe they make enough money to pay their rent, but rent is so high that that means they don’t have money for groceries or they don’t have money for gas,” she said. “And so they’re picking what is the most vital in that moment, and then trying to scramble together for the rest of it.” Food banks increase spending St. Mary’s Food Bank in Phoenix, Arizona, which calls itself the World’s First Food Bank, has had to dip into its savings this year to meet rising diesel and fuel costs. “We bought more food than we ever have before,” said Jerry Brown, director of public relations. “And just like everybody else who goes to the grocery store, that food is costing more.” The food bank serves hundreds of communities across Arizona, which has experienced the nation’s sharpest decline in SNAP benefits. Between July 2025 and July 2026, about 450,000 Arizonans lost SNAP benefits — a decrease of more than 50%. St. Mary’s has seen an influx from those who lost SNAP, Brown said. But it’s also experienced more visits from retirees who are unable to keep up with rising prices. “They thought they had enough money to retire on, and then the price of everything skyrocketed, while the amount of money that they receive remains the same,” he said. In Texas, some food banks have had to ration food in the face of overwhelming demand. While individuals have lost SNAP benefits, food banks have grappled with separate cuts to federal food assistance. Last year, the Trump administration cut hundreds of millions in funding from a local food program for food banks and school meals. The U.S. Department of Agriculture also slashed $500 million that had already been allocated to food aid nationwide through The Emergency Food Assistance Program. That’s pushed more food banks to purchase more of the food their communities need, said Celia Cole, CEO of Feeding Texas, a statewide network of 20 food banks. “And that’s a real concern because it’s not really sustainable,” she said. While she foresees no immediate relief from high food prices, Cole said politicians are increasingly recognizing the growing threat of hunger across the country. She’s hopeful that Congress will make changes to last year’s federal legislation cutting SNAP benefits. “I think everyone recognizes the importance of having a well-nourished population and sees how these changes to SNAP are leading to people losing access to what’s really the backbone defense against hunger in our country,” she said. “So I see a light at the end of the tunnel there because I think there is a lot of bipartisan concern.” Stateline reporter Kevin Hardy can be reached at khardy@stateline.org. articles.title: Human rights groups sue ICE alleging detention of pregnant, nursing immigrants
articles.description: The Robert and Ethel Kennedy Human Rights Center and several other groups filed a lawsuit Tuesday against the U.S. Department of Homeland Security and U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement alleging that the agency is illegally detaining pregnant, postpartum and nursing immigrants against its own policies. The suit, filed in the U.S. District Court for the […]
articles.content: Federal immigration officers are shown at the Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta International Airport in March. A lawsuit filed by advocacy organizations alleges the U.S. Department of Homeland Security and U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement is violating a 2021 directive by detaining pregnant, postpartum and nursing women. (Photo by Ross Williams/Georgia Recorder)The Robert and Ethel Kennedy Human Rights Center and several other groups filed a lawsuit Tuesday against the U.S. Department of Homeland Security and U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement alleging that the agency is illegally detaining pregnant, postpartum and nursing immigrants against its own policies. The suit, filed in the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia, cites a 2021 ICE directive, which states that agents “should not detain, arrest, or take into custody for an administrative violation” anyone who is known to be pregnant, postpartum or nursing. According to the complaint, ICE has stopped tracking the number of women who are pregnant, postpartum or nursing and being held in detention under the Trump administration. But one of the plaintiff organizations — the Women’s Refugee Commission — obtained data through a Freedom of Information Act request. Those documents showed an increase of pregnant women in ICE detention between January 2025 and March 2026 from nine to 128, or a 1,320% increase, the complaint states. The length of detention for pregnant women has also increased substantially, according to the complaint. “Since 2025, ICE detained more than 557 pregnant women for an average of 43 days,” the complaint reads. “Nearly 14% of these women were detained for 90 days or longer, with one woman detained for 219 days, almost seven months of her pregnancy.” A spokesperson from the Department of Homeland Security said in an email sent to Stateline that the 2021 directive is still in place, and that pregnancy in ICE detention is “exceedingly rare,” making up 0.15% of all of those currently in custody as of Oct. 31. The spokesperson said pregnant women in detention receive regular prenatal visits, mental health services, nutritional support and other accommodations. “This includes medical, dental, and mental health intake screening within 12 hours of arriving at each detention facility, a full health assessment within 14 days of entering ICE custody or arrival at a facility, and access to necessary medical appointments and 24-hour emergency care,” the statement said. “This is the best healthcare many of these individuals have received in their entire lives.” They added that women are provided services such as pregnancy tests, routine or specialized prenatal care, postpartum follow up and nursing services. They said the detention standards are higher than most U.S. prisons that “hold actual U.S. citizens” and that the agency is regularly audited and inspected to ensure the facilities are complying with national standards. The complaint details the experience of one woman detained in Kentucky, who asked for emergency assistance because she was pregnant and had been bleeding for more than a day. She eventually miscarried while shackled to a hospital bed, according to the document. Another woman who was detained in her third trimester of a high-risk pregnancy was told by ICE officers they would “take her baby away forever” after she gave birth, and she waived her right to see an immigration judge out of fear and was quickly deported, the lawsuit said. Others who are nursing have been separated from their infants and denied breast pumps, the complaint says. The 2021 directive also prohibited the use of GPS ankle monitors on this population of women if they were granted supervised release, but the complaint says women are being forced to wear them anyway, which one woman said is making her high blood pressure worse. Another, who was nursing an infant at the time, said she couldn’t receive treatment for a painful hernia while the ankle monitor was attached because of burn risks in the operating room. A hearing in the case will likely be scheduled in the coming weeks. The plaintiffs are asking the court to declare that the 2021 directive is still effective and order the agencies to comply with the policy. Stateline reporter Kelcie Moseley-Morris can be reached at kmoseley@stateline.org. Hunger in focus during Michigan’s holiday season. Where to get help, volunteer
articles.description: More than 160,000 Michiganders fell off of federal food benefit programs in the last year, but pantries say the need for food hasn’t changed.
articles.content: Michigan’s SNAP enrollment fell by about 160,000 between October 2025 and October 2026, according to state data Food pantries across the state say demand has been consistent and longstanding, though new families are seeking help for the first time Free help is available by calling 2-1-1 and through local food banks, and residents can support pantries by donating or volunteering Hundreds wrapped around the block near River Rouge High School on a chilly Monday morning in Wayne County. They lined up to drive through a parking lot full of student volunteers ready to load their cars with gravy, cranberry sauce and candied yams ahead of Thanksgiving. This story also appeared in Bridge Michigan Organizers were ready with 2,000 turkeys during the district’s annual holiday giveaway this year. While many people were in line for Thanksgiving staples Monday, Stevon Scott, River Rouge’s director of parent engagement and community outreach, stressed that the food giveaway was “not a one-off.” The school system, he said, is consistently feeding hundreds of families multiple times a week regardless of the season. “If anything, we really need to be more vocal and let people know that this is a place where you can come and get support because we have it to give,” Scott told Bridge Michigan. It’s the first holiday season since the federal government reduced funding for the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP) and imposed new work requirements and other restrictions under the One Big Beautiful Bill Act. The country is roughly one year removed from the 2025 federal shutdown that delayed benefits through SNAP — the food benefits program supports nearly 1 in 8 Americans. In the past year, more than 160,000 Michiganders, including nearly 53,000 children, have fallen off SNAP. Monthly benefit payments are down nearly $33 million in the same period, according to state data, as more than 1.2 million residents remain on the program. Related: 167K Michiganders fell off SNAP since last summer Michigan set to lose millions under Trump SNAP reforms Michigan food banks brace for SNAP ‘crisis.’ How to get or give help At the same time, food banks and pantries say they’re in constant demand, and advocates warn that an increase in state costs and more federal rule changes could force even more families from SNAP. “Our state lawmakers will face impossible choices between further restricting SNAP eligibility, cutting other essential services in our budget or raising taxes for everyone,” Julie Cassidy, senior policy analyst at the Michigan League for Public Policy, told reporters in September. ‘Holding steady’ Taylor Moore, director of food rescue at Goodwill Northern Michigan, said pantry visits in Traverse City have “not seen a significant increase” in demand amid the changes occurring in the food benefits system. But, he said, new families are rolling in. “You have people that are navigating a new terrain,” Moore said, explaining that some are just beginning to understand the changes occurring within their lives because of the economy and how they will impact their spending habits. “Folks are definitely being materially impacted in a way that they have less money to go buy food.” More than 2,000 turkeys were available at the pre-Thanksgiving food giveaway in River Rouge. (Eli Newman/Bridge Michigan) That also means more food is going unsold at big box stores. Food rescuers like Moore say they’ve been able to secure more fruits and vegetables as grocery shoppers buy fewer perishable items amid broader affordability problems impacting disposable income and gas prices. “People will buy less produce and focus more on essentials,” he said. The resulting changes have had some positive impacts, Moore said. “Food banks in the state of Michigan are working more collaboratively than ever before.” Glori Crowell, president of the Do a Little Good food pantry in Elk Rapids, said while demand among food pantries is “holding steady,” she worries about forthcoming federal Medicaid cuts set to take place at the beginning of 2027 and rising healthcare prices. Already, she’s seen troubling trends, including a rise in reports of first-time homelessness, unaccompanied minors and employment difficulties. “As we get through Thanksgiving and Christmas, I’m sure we won’t hear the demand for food because it’s everywhere and it’s widely available,” Crowell said. If you need help: On SNAP? Reach out to your local Michigan Department of Health and Human Services office with questions, or check MI Bridges for updates about your benefits Dial 2-1-1 or visit Find Help – Michigan 2-1-1 for free, confidential assistance and referrals to local food programs and support services Visit the Food Bank Council of Michigan or call 800-552-4483 to locate nearby food banks and learn about hunger relief efforts Call the Double Up Food Bucks hotline at 866-586-2796, operating 9 a.m. to 5 p.m., Monday through Friday, or visit its website for questions on additional resources If you’re a senior, adult with disabilities or a caregiver, you can contact a local Area Agency on Aging or call 517-886-1029 to check eligibility for home-delivered meals and nutrition assistance If you or a family member has a disability, you can contact a local Center for Independent Living for community resource referrals If you want to help: Donate to a food bank: Advocates say cash donations are typically preferred, as charitable food organizations can stretch dollars further by buying wholesale or getting extra food donations from suppliers. Find a local food bank here Check on friends, family and neighbors: Sometimes a simple phone call or a knock on the door can be enough to start a dialogue about getting help Join a mutual aid group: Some community support groups rely on volunteer participation and reciprocal cooperation. Many groups organize on social media to address specific local needs. Find a mutual aid group here Volunteer: Find opportunities through Volunteer Michigan or contact groups like The Food Bank of Eastern Michigan, South Michigan Food Bank, Greater Lansing Food Bank, Gleaners of Southeast Michigan, Forgotten Harvest, Food Gatherers – Ann Arbor, Feeding America – West Michigan, Manna Food Project Petoskey and Goodwill Northern Michigan How to weigh in on proposed SNAP changes: A proposed federal rule would end automatic SNAP eligibility for some people who receive cash assistance and for some households with incomes slightly above 130% of the poverty line. Public comments are due Dec. 10 and can be made in a variety of ways: Federal eRulemaking Portal: Go to regulations.gov. Follow the online instructions for submitting comments. Mail: Send comments to SNAP Program Development Division, Food and Nutrition Administration, 5601 Sunnyside Ave., Beltsville, MD 20705. Email: Send comments to: sm.fn.snappdbrules@usda.gov. Include Docket ID Number [FNA-2026-0661], “Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program: Reforming Categorical Eligibility” in the subject line of the message. articles.title: Holiday shopping? Here’s where to find the deals in Detroit
articles.description: Here are some Detroit businesses, markets and organizations you can support during the holiday season and year-round.
articles.content: The holiday shopping season is upon us and to find deals you won’t have to go far. Several Detroit businesses and institutions will be offering specials during the ultimate shopping weekend: Black Friday on Nov. 27, Small Business Saturday on Nov. 28 and Museum Store Sunday on Nov. 29. Beginning in 2017, more than 2,300 museum stores worldwide take part in the annual shopping event, with offers on exclusive discounts, special events and one-of-a-kind gifts. The Detroit Institute of Arts is one of the institutions in the city participating, as well as: Detroit Historical Museum Charles H. Wright Museum of African American History Michigan Science Center Pewabic Pottery The DIA will be celebrating the day with a DJ set by artist Zander Nash and a pop-up from Detroit clothing and accessories shop I Am A Genius from 1-5 p.m. This is the first time the museum will be working with store owner Candace Cox-Wimberley, said Monika Nyquist, director of retail operations at the DIA. “We’ll be selling two collections of hers. One is Motor City Genius and the other is Contemporary Genius,” Nyquist said. “We will have totes, pillows, journals – so really great giftables that I have no doubt people will want to either put in a stocking or wrap up as a gift for the holidays.” Museum members can also get 20% off all regular priced items at the DIA’s museum shop and the Georgia O’Keeffe Exhibition Shop, Nyquist said. The exhibition shop coincides with the institution’s “Georgia O’Keeffe: Architecture” show, which is on display until Jan. 3. “We have curated gorgeous mid-century modern jewelry,” Nyquist said. “We have the architecture nerd T-shirts and hoodie sweatshirts that are great. We also have gorgeous scarves that showcase the Brooklyn Bridge in silk, as well as magnetic brooches, so really a great variety of items that represent what I call the Georgia O’Keeffe aesthetic.” For those looking to add something new to their Christmas tree, the DIA has two special ornaments. There’s the 11th annual collector’s ornament for $26.95, which is a miniature version of the painting “Ellen’s Isle, Loch Katrine” by artist Robert S. Duncanson. Then there is the custom beaded ornament of the DIA building, which is featured in Museum Store Sunday’s gift guide. The ornament costs $24.95. Here are some Detroit businesses, markets and organizations you can support during the holiday season and year-round. This list is in no way exhaustive, and if you have suggestions of places to add, let us know! (City Bird in Midtown photographed on Nov. 23, 2026. Credit: Christine Ferretti, BridgeDetroit) Black Friday (Nov. 27) Midtown City Bird and Nest will have extended hours from 10 a.m. to 7 p.m. on Friday and Saturday, offering specials and promos both in-store and online. That includes 20% off all apparel at City Bird and 20% off plants at Nest, free wooden Detroit landmarks for the first 20 customers at City Bird and a chance to win a $200 shopping spree, no purchase necessary. The stores will also have other activities going on, such as photo ops with its classic Detroit Architecture carnival cut-out and a DJ spinning tunes throughout the day. The Michigan Science Center will offer deals from Black Friday to Cyber Monday on its annual memberships and gift shop items. The center is offering a BOGO deal for membership, with packages available from $65 for individuals and $99 for families. Those who purchase or renew a membership will get a gift membership at the same level for free. Gift certificates will be mailed by Friday, Dec. 4. The institution will also offer a 15% discount for the public and a 25% discount for members at its Science Store gift shop as part of both Small Business Saturday and Museum Store Sunday. Members receive year-long access to the museum, plus discounts on theater tickets, education programs, summer camps, special events and gift store items. They also receive invitations to special member events and previews, plus reciprocal admission to more than 250 Association of Science and Technology Centers globally. Downtown The Downtown Detroit Markets at Cadillac Square are back, operating until Jan. 3. Located across from Campus Martius Park, shoppers can browse and buy from local vendors like Bespoke By Feldman, Next Chapter Books, Ink Detroit and Yarn Nerds. Premier Pet Supply, which has 15 locations, including downtown Detroit at 1511 Washington Blvd., will have special offers running on Black Friday. Most of the offers will still be available for Small Business Saturday, where customers can get 10% off on dog and cat food, toppers, cat litter and wild bird seed. Stores will also offer 20% off everything else in the store. The Aroma Labs at 1435 Farmer St., Suite 122, a store where customers create their own scents, is offering a gift with any purchase from Friday to Sunday. Woodhouse Spa Detroit at 1447 Woodward Ave. is offering an online promotion on gift cards now through Saturday. Customers who spend $200-$249 get a $25 bonus card if they use the code DETBLK25 at checkout. Customers who spend $350 or more get a $35 bonus card, using code DETBLK35 at checkout. New Center/North End Comic book retailer Vault of Midnight is having a Black Friday super sale at all its locations, including its Detroit store, 2857 E. Grand Blvd. Discounts include 15% off board games, 15% off comic books priced at $20 or less, 15% off graphic novels and 15 % off vinyl, toys, plushes and statues. Hours are 11 a.m. to 10 p.m. Small Business Saturday (Nov. 28) Midtown Source Booksellers is partnering with late children’s author Richard Scarry to celebrate Small Business Saturday from 11 a.m. to 6 p.m. Customers can explore the neighborhood, support local businesses, and collect stickers in the store’s special sticker book. Plus, participants can earn fun prizes, including coloring books, tote bags, buttons and more. People can RSVP here. The Detroit Hispanic Development Corporation is hosting its Small Business Saturday celebration from 11 a.m. to 5 p.m. at its space in Corktown, 1211 Trumbull Street. Visitors can shop local vendors, enjoy live entertainment and take photos with Santa. The Grandmont Rosedale Development Corporation is hosting its annual Holidays on Grand River, beginning at 4 p.m. The community event will feature shopping, food, live entertainment, a scavenger hunt and a tree lighting ceremony. Folks can shop from neighborhood businesses such as Pages Bookshop and The Sisters Couch. Pewabic Pottery is hosting its Holiday Showcase Saturdays from Nov. 28 to Dec. 19, where customers can sip hot chocolate and enjoy sweets from On the Rise Bakery, partake in family friendly activities and shop from the studio’s winter collection. The Nov. 28 event will feature the St. Paul Lutheran Church Handbell Choir from 12 to 3 p.m. Sunday, Nov. 29 Eastern Market’s holiday markets are back for the season, from Nov. 29 to Dec. 20. From 10 a.m.-4 p.m., shoppers can expect to see Michigan-made gift options, including clothing, art, jewelry, beauty products and more. Saturday, Dec. 5 After taking a hiatus last year, Midtown’s holiday tradition Noel Night is back, taking place from 4-9 p.m. Organized by Midtown Detroit Inc., the event allows attendees to explore the neighborhood’s cultural district, such as the DIA, the Wright Museum and the Museum of Contemporary Art Detroit. Several Midtown businesses will also be open during Noel Night, offering special deals and programming.

Australia passes online safety law, putting Big Tech at risk of multibillion-dollar fines
articles.description: Australia passes online safety law, putting Big Tech at risk of multibillion-dollar fines AP News Australia passes law forcing internet platforms to take down harmful content Reuters ‘You’re protecting Trump’: Hanson-Young clashes with Liberal senator before digital duty of care legislation passes – as it happened The Guardian US Criticizes Australia Social Media Law as Harming Free Speech Bloomberg.com What Australi
articles.content: MELBOURNE, Australia (AP) — Australia’s Parliament on Wednesday passed online safety laws that could expose tech giants to multibillion-dollar fines for failing to prevent foreseeable online harms. The United States and the Australian opposition party warned that the legislation would lead to censorship of lawful speech. The Digital Duty of Care Act requires Big Tech to proactively reduce the risk of harm before it occurs, according to an Australian government statement. The legislation is similar to the European Union’s Digital Services Act, passed in 2022, and the United Kingdom’s Online Safety Act passed a year later. The legislation became law in the House of Representatives, where the center-left Labor Party government commands a majority, by 97 votes to 43. Prime Minister Anthony Albanese told Parliament the law would stand as a “powerful instrument to protect our children and our society from online harms by placing the onus on the tech platforms to ensure a safer online environment.” “This is a victory for our children and young people. The dangers were unforeseen when the digital world was young,” Albanese said. “But now that the digital world has matured, they can be easily recognized and they can be remedied.” Opposition leader Angus Taylor told Parliament he would repeal the legislation if his conservative Liberal Party wins elections in 2028. Taylor described the legislation as “authoritarian.” “This bill is a blank check for political censorship,” Taylor told Parliament. “The bill is an attack on free speech that is absolutely central to our democracy.” The government struck a deal with the minor Greens party on Tuesday to get the legislation through the Senate, where no party holds a majority. “Today, the safety and wellbeing of Australians and their children have finally been put ahead of Big Tech’s bottom line,” Greens chief negotiator Sarah Hanson-Young said in a statement after the bill passed the Senate by 36 votes to 23. “My message to Big Tech companies is, it’s time to make your platforms safe or we will see you in court,” she added. The Australian legislation sets minimum safety standards for online services, including games, apps and artificial intelligence chatbots, requiring them to protect Australians from seriously harmful material and conduct, the government said. The Greens’ amendments include increasing maximum penalties for breaches from 109 million Australian dollars ($72 million), as the government originally proposed, to 5% of a tech company’s global revenue. U.S. Ambassador to Australia David Brat said on Tuesday the then-proposed laws would “impose disproportionate compliance burdens on American companies relative to competitors.” “Vaguely defined ‘harms,’ backed by penalties of up to 5% of global revenue, will push platforms to censor lawful speech,” Brat posted on social media.

articles.title: Hollister showed Lansing what a mayor could do
articles.description: Moments before David Hollister’s public celebration of life began on Monday, who should come up to me but former Lansing Mayor Virg Bernero? His first line to me was this: […]
articles.content: Moments before David Hollister’s public celebration of life began on Monday, who should come up to me but former Lansing Mayor Virg Bernero? His first line to me was this: “If it wasn’t for Mayor Hollister, there would have not been a Mayor Bernero.” It took me a minute to register what he meant. Does that mean Hollister recruited him to run? Did Hollister go to bat for him in either of his campaigns, the one he lost in 2003 or the one he won in 2005? The answer to all those questions was no. What he meant was this: Former Mayor David Hollister showed Virg (and all of us, really) what a mayor could do to transform a city. If you had the right person in place – that was Hollister – you could use the office of mayor to do great things. Virg told me he never had visions of being the mayor of Lansing when he started his political career, first as a legislative staffer, county commissioner and legislator. He confided that he saw himself going to Washington someday as a member of Congress. The office of mayor was not on his radar. Terry McKane was Lansing’s mayor in the late ‘80s and early ‘90s when Bernero started his political career as a legislative staffer. At that time, Lansing was … well, not what it is today. Strip clubs once stood where Jackson Field is today. Entire blocks of Michigan Avenue were urban wasteland. Outside of Kewpee’s and the Peanut Shop, not much was going on downtown. But under Hollister, Lansing turned things around. Roughly $2.9 billion in public and private investment. A new downtown transportation center, a minor league baseball stadium and new state office buildings led to a livelier downtown and to Old Town became a real thing And then, of course, came Hollister refusing to let General Motors leave town. He brought together everybody – labor, government, business, community leaders – to figure out how to keep auto manufacturing in the region. Bernero said he saw what was possible. He wanted to be like Hollister. Do you remember how often Virg talked about Mayor Hollister during his campaigns for mayor? Having covered all of his campaigns for mayor, I sure do. It was a lot. Tony Benavides — who succeeded Hollister in 2003 and then lost to Bernero in 2005 – was so annoyed by Virg’s constant references to the former mayor that he once told Bernero, “You talk about Hollister so much, I can get you his pants for you.” There’s a lot to say about Bernero. However, it’s not disputed that he helped bring in $2 billion in private investment in Lansing. Does the Ottawa Street Power Station become the Accident Fund’s headquarters without him? Is the river trail system kept up as it is? Of course, Bernero wasn’t Hollister. Lansing Mayor Andy Schor is not David Hollister, either. But both have used Hollister as a guidepost to measure what a successful mayor in Lansing can accomplish. Both have governed with an energy and a determination so Lansing does not slip backward. They refuse to be complacent and push for progress. That enormous crane dangling over the new 28-story Tower on Grand, Lansing’s newest development, is proof of that. So is the new city hall, another Hollister vision that, interestingly, became a reality the exact day of Hollister’s celebration of life. “It’s one of the first things he talked to me about when I told him I wanted to run for mayor,” said Schor, adding that Hollister told him, “Find a way to make it happen.” “And we did so,” Schor said. If Lansing keeps electing collaborative, go-getting dreamers, the new David C. Hollister Lansing City Hall couldn’t be more appropriately named.

articles.title: David Campbell Hill returns from nearly five-decade hiatus with first solo novel
articles.description: There was a 46-year gap between Lansing author David Campbell Hill’s last novel, 1980’s “Invader,” and his latest novel, “Pandora’s Daughter” (Sunacumen Press, $24.95). “The number of years between books […]
articles.content: There was a 46-year gap between Lansing author David Campbell Hill’s last novel, 1980’s “Invader,” and his latest novel, “Pandora’s Daughter” (Sunacumen Press, $24.95). “The number of years between books astonishes me,” said Hill, 75, who co-authored “Invader” with his late father, Albert Fay Hill. “I did write a screenplay with my father and a novel on my own in the early 1980s, but at that point, it was clear I wasn’t going to get rich any time soon. Our agent was not interested in my solo book. David Campbell Hill (right) with his late father and two-time co-author, Albert Fay Hill. Courtesy “I started looking for real work,” he continued. “I never really stopped writing, but it was piecemeal and competed with a full-time job, another career change and getting married twice, not to mention 10 years in skydiving. The publishing market changed tremendously. I sent manuscripts out every now and then but couldn’t attract much interest.” He began “Pandora’s Daughter” in 2004. He retired in 2018, which freed up a lot of time. “I promised myself I would get back to writing and would show that I could complete novels without my father’s help,” he said. “I went to workshops, joined a couple of writing groups, got on the board of A Rally of Writers, cleaned up my old solo novel, finished ‘Pandora’s Daughter’ and started an entirely new book.” He spoke about the impetus to write “Pandora’s Daughter.” “After being stuck for a long time, I decided to give up on the idea of writing a bestseller and just write something that was fun,” he said. “Since I like history, geopolitics and physics, all I needed was an idea. That came when I read about the almost certainly apocryphal ‘Philadelphia Experiment.’ It doesn’t appear in the book at all, but it led to a chain of ideas that (became) ‘Pandora’s Daughter.’” In the book, barbarism and chaos run rampant throughout the galaxy. In the midst of it, a dying empire searches for an ancient fount of knowledge that holds the key to humanity’s perseverance. David Campbell Hill. Credit Libby Rice Emperor Stuart II fears that his empire, which has kept order for millennia, will collapse after his death. His daughter, Fuji, embarks on a six-month voyage into the decaying and lost realms of the empire in search of the wisdom that will hold it together. Aboard a powerful warship, the princess confronts an alien species that has taken a keen interest in her search for the lost planet that might harbor all the answers: Earth. “Emperor Stuart II is directly inspired by the Roman emperor Marcus Aurelius and his despicable son Commodus,” Hill said. “Fuji was supposed to be a love interest, not the main character. After all, I am a guy, and I wasn’t sure I could get inside a female character’s head. But as I continued writing, she took over the story, and my original protagonist fell into the role of love interest. I decided to go with it.” Hill self-published “Pandora’s Daughter” instead of having it traditionally published like he did with “Invader” and 1976’s “The Deadly Messiah” (which he also co-authored with his father). “I contacted over 100 agents and got a few nibbles, but nothing developed,” he said. “I had hoped that my publishing history might get me an ‘in,’ especially since one agent said he had worked for the publisher of ‘Invader’ and offered to read it, but I never heard from him again. I talked with many other writers and found agreement that self-publishing was the new normal. I had help from people who had already done it, which showed me a path forward.” The author discussed how the publishing industry has changed in the 46 years between novels. “It’s become bigger, faster, more commercial. There’s less interest in non-established authors,” he said. “I found a lot of agents wanted writing by traditionally oppressed groups. I used to send out manuscripts with stamped, self-addressed envelopes. Now it’s all done online, which is kind of cool, actually.” Major influences on Hill’s work include his interest in physics and history, particularly the Roman Empire, as well as “Star Trek: The Original Series” and the works of noted science-fiction authors Isaac Asimov, Arthur C. Clarke, Robert A. Heinlein and Larry Niven. His father was also a crucial influence. “He gave me the discipline to develop an entire story, then stick to the process of writing it. He also had contacts that helped get our two books traditionally published. We had long sessions firing ideas at each other. One of us would write a chapter, then the other would edit it, then we would pass it back and forth,” Hill explained. “My stepmom also did a lot of editing, which evened out our writing styles. Note to other potential father-son writing teams: It can be embarrassing writing sex scenes with your father. I also deduced a lot about my parents’ history from working with them. Sometimes, it’s definitely TMI!” Origin of “The North Avenue Irregulars” A World War II veteran and Purple Heart recipient, Albert Fay Hill was a pastor in New Rochelle, New York. During his time as senior pastor at North Avenue Presbyterian Church, Hill led the fight against organized crime, which had taken over the suburb. After local gangsters brutally murdered a young man for failing to pay his gambling debts, Hill began his own inquiries into the influence of organized crime and formulated a plan for reclaiming the community. When his efforts spread, he was contacted by U.S. Treasury agents. He agreed to form a citizen’s task force, but he encountered reluctance from his male parishioners to volunteer. However, when he approached women in the congregation, they enthusiastically agreed. Using the information gleaned from the women, Treasury agents organized raids on a number of gambling houses. Word of the team’s success spread, and one of the larger raids was featured on the front page of The New York Times. Look magazine followed up with an article on Hill and his task force. Soon thereafter, Cowles Publishing approached him about writing a book. In 1968, “The North Avenue Irregulars” was released. Walt Disney Productions purchased the movie rights, and in 1979, the film adaptation was released, starring Edward Herrmann (“Gilmore Girls”) and Cloris Leachman (“The Last Picture Show”). SOURCE: David Campbell Hill and IMDb. Hill and his father spoke about collaborating after Hill graduated from Northwestern University. “We discussed the unfortunate fact that we lacked abundant income,” Hill said. “My father had earned some money writing a book about his adventures fighting organized crime in New Rochelle, New York, called ‘The North Avenue Irregulars,’ so we thought that might work. We sketched out a plot before we got home, which turned into ‘The Deadly Messiah’ in 1976 and ‘Invader’ in 1980. I also remember hunt-and-peck writing on my parents’ old manual typewriter many years before that. I wish I still had some of that stuff. In those days, I couldn’t put together a plot or stick with it, but I had an active imagination.” Hill and his father aren’t the only writers in the family. “Friends get cross-eyed listening to conversations around the dinner table. Everybody reads,” Hill said. “My sister writes poetry and helped her daughter write her doctoral thesis. My brother is a published author and poet. My father published two more books after we stopped working together, and I have manuscripts for four other novels he wrote but never published. Plus, he published a medical study on his work with cancer immunology. My stepmom’s ideal day was sitting on a chaise lounge in the backyard, editing our work. My brother married a college professor who has her books in the Harvard Library. My brother-in-law has a book on golfing.” Hill’s writing has come a long way since “The Deadly Messiah.” “When our first book came out, I had delusions of being some sort of wunderkind. I got cured of that pretty quick. It’s been a long process of doing the work to learn the craft since then” he said. “I’ve had fantasies of rewriting the books I wrote with my dad or even the books he wrote himself. I think I could make them a lot better.” For Hill, writing is like meditating. “You get in a zone,” he said. “Everybody needs to create something.”

articles.title: Lansing’s DeSean ‘Whipdog’ Whipple found his voice through pro wrestling
articles.description: Media personality DeSean “Whipdog” Whipple was not always the outgoing figure our community recognizes from radio, television and podcasting. Heard on Power 96.5 (WQHH-FM), seen in a recurring role on […]
articles.content: Media personality DeSean “Whipdog” Whipple was not always the outgoing figure our community recognizes from radio, television and podcasting. Heard on Power 96.5 (WQHH-FM), seen in a recurring role on TV One’s “Fatal Attraction” and serving as a producer/board operator for “The WILS Morning Wake-Up” with Mike Austin, the Detroit native turned Lansing resident is also a highly regarded professional wrestler. He credits the sport for his success and confidence. Local media personality DeSean “Whipdog” Whipple credits his confidence to his experience as a professional wrestler. Mr. Joe Walker for City Pulse “I needed professional wrestling to get me to where I am today,” Whipple said. “Growing up, I was the tall, chubby, nerdy kid who didn’t like to talk to people. When I originally started professional wrestling, I was a shy, quiet guy who didn’t talk much, which is always surprising to people. Now I won’t shut up!” The “Whip thing,” as he described it, clicked for him. “I started feeling confident in the ring and in knowing who I am, which is applicable to real life,” Whipple said. “Once you know who you are, then you can make the world believe who you are.” These days, Whipple’s life is more about conversations than confrontations. As the creator, producer and host of “The Wrestling Heroes and Insiders Podcast,” aka “The WHIP Show,” he regularly interviews top talent from World Wrestling Entertainment, Total Nonstop Action Wrestling and All Elite Wrestling. Once ranked one of the top 500 wrestlers in the world by Pro Wrestling Illustrated, Whipple will step back into the squared circle on special occasions. “I don’t really consider it coming out of retirement,” Whipple said. “I won’t be back wrestling weekly, but I do feel being part of something for a good cause is necessary.” Whipple raises an elbow for one of his nine battle royale opponents at the Headlock on Hunger II fundraiser Nov. 14 in Jackson. Mr. Joe Walker for City Pulse Such a cause drew him to Jackson on Nov. 14. After a four-year hiatus, Whipple stepped into the ring for the fundraiser Headlock on Hunger II at the Salvation Army gymnasium. One of 10 competitors in the event’s over-the-top-rope battle royale, the ‘dog whipped seven guys from the ring to the floor before being eliminated himself. “Getting back in the ring in front of my people in Jackson felt amazing,” Whipple said. “I spent so many years wrestling for them. They literally raised me. Seeing many wrestlers from the city who used to watch me as a fan now get in the ring was definitely a full-circle moment.” Early in his career, Whipple found himself in a tag team with “Canadian Bad Boy” Steven Summers, whom he described as the talker of the duo. As Whipple grew in that space, he said he learned to speak more and gained the ability to be totally open with an audience. “Whether it’s professional wrestling, acting in a movie or commercial, or doing voiceovers or radio, you have to connect with your audience,” Whipple explained. “You have to make people notice something about you. Professional wrestling helped me do that.” A graduate of Cass Technical High School, Whipple spent two years at Michigan State University before finishing his business administration degree at Wayne State. But the core of his education, and eventual success, began as a WrestleMania III audience member at Pontiac Silverdome in 1987. “At 7 years old, I sat at the top of the arena, so high I could have high-fived Jesus,” Whipple said. “When I went to Philadelphia for WrestleMania XL and they checked in my name and gave me my lanyard that said “WrestleMania XL media,” I had to go to the bathroom and let a couple tears go. It just felt really good.”
